Mr. Chairman, I had addressed a few remarks to the committee before the adjournment some time ago. I wish to continue those remarks today and to start out by emphasizing the fact that under the estimates now being given consideration almost half the total expenditures by the government are provided.
It does not seem to me that during the time this subject was under discussion before there was any tendency on the part of the minister to take the House of Commons into his confidence as to the situation with which we are in fact confronted. There were generalities about the excellent morale of our men and women in uniform. There were sweeping statements about our ability to accept our responsibilities in defending this country against air attack. There were sweeping assertions as to our assumption of the responsibility at this time; but the fact is that at no point in his remarks did the minister say what he would have said, and that is: I regret to inform the committee that for reasons I shall now put forward the reserve forces, which are the backbone of the defence of Canada, are now confronted with serious problems; that we are not getting the men we need; that in many cases units are unable to go to camp with more than a fraction of the strength that has been authorized, and that in some cases units of great importance to the defence of Canada are actually going on parade with more officers than men.
Had the minister then explained to us what the reasons are for that situation, I am sure that hon. members of this committee would have been ready to join in any positive effort which could be made to meet that situation in the face of the gravity of the world picture now before us.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that you will permit me to read into the record a short summary of Soviet military power, prepared as appendix "A" to the report of the deputy supreme allied commander in Europe which was presented on May 24 last. I suggest that I be permitted to do this, because otherwise I would simply summarize paragraph by paragraph this short appendix. I believe it is in the most compact form possible, and therefore I propose that, with the consent of the committee, for the sake of brevity rather than otherwise, I be permitted to read this into the record. I do so rather than ask that it be printed because the facts are facts which should be in front of hon. members of the committee in dealing with this subject. I repeat, this is an appendix to a statement prepared by Field Marshal Montgomery and 83276-402
Supply-National Defence presented in the form of an address on May 24 and appearing as appendix "A" to that address:
1.	From 1947 to the present time, the numerical strength (175 divisions) of Soviet ground forces has remained fairly constant. Nonetheless, significant changes have been made in favour of increased mechanization with sturdy and efficient modern equipment. Sixty-five divisions of the present establishment are tank and mechanized divisions. Moreover, the rifle divisions have been provided motorized equipment; they also have organic tanks and additional artillery . . . Thus, the mobility and firepower of all Soviet divisions have been increased through the introduction of improved weapons and equipment.
2.	The U.S.S.R., Eastern Germany and the East European satellites today have over 6 million men under arms. Approximately 4-5 million of these are in the ground forces. A high state of preparedness is maintained by a rigorous training program.
3.	The number of satellite divisions has almost doubled since 1947, bringing their total to about 80 divisions.
4.	The U.S.S.R. has a ready-made spearhead for a rapid advance into western Europe. The spearhead is composed of 22 Soviet divisions in Eastern Germany, the bulk of these armoured divisions with nearly a complete complement of tanks and self-propelled guns. Behind this spearhead there are an additional 60 Soviet divisions located in the eastern European satellite countries and western U.S.S.R. (This does not take into account satellite divisions.)
5.	Their mobilization system is exercised periodically to insure its effectiveness, and by M 30 (30 days after mobilization day) the Soviet and satellite ground forces could number 400 divisions.
6.	The numerical strength of the Soviet air forces in recent years has been constant, having been stabilized at about 20,000 aircraft, but the rapid increase in the Soviet air potential is illustrated by the rate of changeover to jet aircraft. In 1951, about 20 per cent of their fighters were jet types. By early 1954, almost all of their fighters were jet types.
7.	A similar development has occurred with respect to their light bombers. In early 1951, jet light bombers had not been introduced into operational units. By 1954, well over two-thirds of their light-bomber forces were jets.
8.	In the medium-bomber category, the Soviets have, doubled, since 1951, the number of TU-4s (similar to the U.S. B-29) in operational units.
9.	Still newer types of jet fighters have recently appeared. Newer types of medium and heavy bombers, including jet models, also have been observed.
10.	The development of a comprehensive aviationtraining program has been one of the most significant contributions in the Soviet post-war program to improve the capability of the Soviet air power.
11.	The program for airfield construction is still in progress, with attention recently being directed to fields with very long runways. In the past three years the Soviets have about tripled the number of major airfields in eastern Europe which will accommodate jet fighters.
12.	In the past, the combat value of the satellite air forces has not been significant. In 1951, their aircraft were obsolete. By 1954, the numerical strength of the satellite air forces had been doubled with nearly half being jet fighters. Their facilities were improved and training had reached a fairly satisfactory standard.
13.	The growing complex of airfields throughout eastern Europe, the aircraft-control and warning systems and anti-aircraft artillery dispositions of

19.	To illustrate the magnitude of their total equipment stockpile, the Soviets have more than enough tanks, mortars and anti-tank guns for some 300 odd Soviet divisions. Their stockpile of field artillery and anti-aircraft artillery is several times that required to supply those divisions. Annual production of these items is continuing at a sizeable rate.
That is the carefully calculated statement by the man most competent to analyse Soviet military power at this time, Mr. Chairman. May I just for a moment again refer back to the last paragraph of that statement that the Soviet forces have more than enough tanks, mortars, and anti-aircraft guns for some 300-odd Soviet divisions, and then may I emphasize these words:
Their stockpile of field artillery and anti-aircraft artillery is several times that required to supply those divisions.
That is the cold, chilling reality with which we are confronted at this time, Mr. Chairman, when we discuss the estimates for the Department of National Defence.
As though that were not sufficient warning in itself, we then find that even within these past few days there have been further warnings of the rapid increase, not only in the enormous reserves of manpower, but in the supplies and quality of weapons for the Soviet forces. At Quantico, Virginia, only last Saturday, President Eisenhower was present at a meeting of senior staff officers and officials concerned with the general problem of defence, and at that meeting those who were gathered there were informed by the people best qualified to make a statement on the subject that Soviet production is not only expanding rapidly but that the lead in quality and technical novelty of weapons which have given the western allies their supremacy, in spite of a very great disparity in manpower, is rapidly closing in.


They warned, in the presence of President Eisenhower, that the Soviet forces both Russian and satellite are closing in very rapidly in the quantity, quality, and originality of design.
Those are the facts before us. Only yesterday in the celebration of air force day in Moscow, more than 600 planes of the largest and most modern jet type took part in a demonstration of Soviet air power. Those who listened to the radio description of that event heard that this was the largest demonstration of its kind that had ever taken place in the world in peacetime. They were told of the dropping of paratroops, and of all types of artillery of normal field standards, to give support to infantry and other lighter troops who were dropped by parachute.
Never in our history at any time, Mr. Chairman, have we been confronted so openly and with such accurate knowledge with the necessity for devoting whatever money we spend to the most effective defence possible, and with the necessity that our defence dollars produce defence and not just broad and sweeping statements about the general characteristics of our weapons, supplies, and organization.
Let us see what our position is. As of April 30 our active forces numbered 113,478. But, Mr. Chairman, that represents very largely the executive staff and various office employees necessary not only for the active forces, but also for the training, administration and supply of the reserve forces. It would be wholly wrong to think of those figures of active forces as fighting forces. We do not know exactly how many of those can be described as fighting forces.
It is fighting forces, after all, that General Montgomery is talking about when he speaks of six million men under arms. He is not talking about office staff or chauffeurs waiting outside the parliament buildings to take nonmilitary personnel to various non-military engagements. He is not talking about various details of that kind.
He is talking about six million men under arms. He is talking about 400 divisions in the field capable of going into battle within 30 days. He is talking about 300-odd Soviet divisions fully equipped, and not only with an adequate stockpile but with several times their requirements behind them for military purposes. These are the realities. When we examine it from that point of view, let us remember that with the enormous amount of money we are expending, and with all the satisfaction we may express in the training and morale of the young men and women in uniform, it is still a comparatively limited force compared with that reality.

Now, Mr. Chairman, the spokesman of our party, General Pearkes, has on more than one occasion emphasized our belief that there should be a reorganization of our forces in keeping with Canada's own particular military requirements, not only for the defence of our own vast territories, but to play our part in the over-all obligations to NATO which we have assumed. He has made it clear that he believes that the more we concentrate on air and airborne forces, the more we shall be capable of meeting our demands within our own boundaries and, in the unhappy event that the necessity should ever arise, of extending our effectiveness to distant points in other parts of the world.
On several occasions, Mr. Chairman, we have sought to obtain the report prepared by three senior officers of the armed forces in regard to the reserves. Let it be remembered that, while we talk of the active forces in Canada, the backbone of our defence is the reserve. We have never pretended at any time that we are a nation that seeks to maintain a standing army or a standing military force of air, land and naval units capable of meeting the demands of war. We have relied throughout the years on the strength of our reserve forces. That has been the backbone of our defence. It is the backbone of our defence today and it is the strength of the reserve that we should examine and about which we should have all the available information that can be given to us. We have asked several times for the production of that report. We have been told that this is a secret report; that it is a confidential report. But that, Mr. Chairman, is eyewash. That report is no more secret than was the report which was prepared twenty years ago and which formed the basis of the reorganization of the land forces of this country at that time. That report is no more secret than were the recommendations which were carried out twenty years ago and under which there was a conversion of half of our infantry units to artillery units, armoured units and other units of various types. That report was made public. That report was made public in detail. It was made public in detail for several reasons. It was made public because, as a result, it made it possible to obtain the support of the members of the house for the principles laid down and also to obtain the support of the general public, particularly the public in those communities where reserve units carry out their training. By making the general nature of that report public, support for the general plan of reorganization was gained in those communities which have a proud tradition of military training. Only one detail of that reorganization program was kept secret. That was the 83276-4024
Supply-National Defence part which referred to the specific units which should be converted or discontinued. I think the same principle could well apply to the present report.
There are obvious reasons why it is not desirable to present detailed recommendations with regard to the conversion or discontinuance of specific units until a general principle is settled and has gained support. If that procedure is followed, in the vexy nature of things the local pride in a particular type of service is bound to assert itself, often without due regard to the advantage there may be in the unit's becoming" part of a particular type of military service.
Mr. Chairman, I would certainly urge as well as agree to the idea that any recommendations with regard to specific units be withheld just as they were withheld twenty years ago when there took place at that time the sweeping reorganization which alone made it possible to mobilize on an effective basis in 1939. Let us, however, have the rest of the report. Any report can have the word "secret" or "confidential" put on it; but that does not mean that it is in fact secret or confidential. The members of the House of Commons have a right to know what assessment has been made of the strength of our reserve units, of their effectiveness at this time and of the possibility of suddenly mobilizing a force in the event that danger presents itself on a greater scale than that on which it is presented at this time.
I recognize that this matter presents one of the fundamental problems confronting every democratic legislative body. The balance between wide-open disclosure of all information and a measure of secrecy which) denies to the members of the elected legislative body adequate information for informed' discussion is one which today is engaging the attention of all those who are concerned about the effectiveness of our democratic system. Without in any way suggesting that it is our right, our duty or our prerogative to speak in critical terms of any other legislative body, I think it is appropriate that we should say that here in this chamber and in the parliament of Canada we certainly do not agree with certain propositions which have been put forward in Washington in recent days with regard to the full disclosure of all documents, no matter how secret those documents may be.
The proposition that any document made available in the utmost secrecy to a member of the executive or exchanged between governments should become available to any member of the elected body is, of course, one that would be intolerable to contemplate under our system. In fact, let it be said right

Supply-National Defence away that proper discussion between nations becomes more difficult when there is any uncertainty about the completely confidential character of those documents. But let it also be said right away that where there are truly secret documents-for instance, such documents as relate to secret military developments or to the assessment of new military power upon a highly confidential basis-they most certainly should not be disclosed. Having said that, however, we should not be placed in a position where, in the name of secrecy or confidential documents, we in this committee and in the House of Commons should be denied information that every member has the right to have.
This matter goes to the root of the whole effectiveness of the democratic system. The question before us is as fundamental as is democracy itself. The free election of men and women to sit in the House of Commons and be members of the parliament of Canada offers to the people of Canada no assurance that we shall, in fact, have either democracy or freedom unless those who meet here as representatives of the people have before them, for their knowledge, information and advice, the essential facts with regard to any matter brought before the House of Commons for consideration. We have not that information today. I hope the minister will not insult the intelligence of the members of this committee or the good sense of the people of Canada by suggesting that we have the essential information which makes it possible to discuss in a well-informed way those items that call for an expenditure of some $2 billion -during the current year.
We can obtain some of the facts in spite of the government's determined effort to hide them from us; and let no mistake be made about it, they are determined efforts, successfully carried out by the weight of their superior majority. For example, in the face of these cold and chilling facts that are presented in appendix "A" to the last statement of Field Marshal Montgomery, we are told about our ability to meet an air attack. We are also told that we rely on our reserve antiaircraft forces to meet that attack. Do hon. members of this committee know the strength of our reserve anti-aircraft forces? I happen to know the situation with regard to one of the best. They have less than one-tenth of the weapons they should have. They cannot even train effectively with that small number of weapons. They cannot train effectively because under the system they now have they often find they have more officers than men on parade. That would not be so if there were a sense of reality, of urgency and of duty in relation to the operation of these

reserve units. When I state that fact I do so simply because of personal contact. I have stated already with respect to a group of field artillery which is generally regarded as one of the best in Canada that in this year, when we are told that there are six million Soviet men under arms, that group, one of the best in Canada, will fire with 24 guns instead of 124. That group will go to camp in no single case with one of the regiments up to strength.
I am not talking about even full reserve field strength, as the minister implied in earlier remarks, nor am I talking about military strength for active service. I am talking about the reduced strength which has been established for training purposes. Not one of them will come up to that reduced strength, and some regiments will not even go as a single battery but only as troops of a battery because of their inability to man the guns, and that in this year 1954 when we are told that the military strength of the Soviet forces is mounting all the time.
There is another aspect of this problem which extends generally throughout the army. Because decisions have not been made with regard to the report to which I have referred, there are some units in a state of uncertainty today because they do not know what kind of units they are going to be. I know one of the best infantry units in the country that is scarcely able to train at all at this time because of the uncertainty as to what kind of unit it is going to be. These are merely examples which I put forward from personal contact. I do so with full responsibility as a member of this house. The members of the house should have before them a complete and detailed statement of the situation with respect to every reserve unit of the land, sea, and air forces right across Canada today. Without that, the estimates now before us and the general statements made are, in substantial measure, largely meaningless.
At this stage of the session, Mr. Chairman, it is still possible for the minister to say that in view of the situation that has developed it is his intention to present what has come to be known as the general's report. It is possible to place before this committee, this house and the parliament of Canada the essential information that has been found. Let us hope that, confronted with the threat of military might greater far than was ever presented by nazi Germany up to September, 1939, we will have reality and not blind generalities with regard to what we can do. I hope, in answer to demands of this kind, that we will not have statements by the minister that he is proud of the quality of

the training, of the effectiveness of the brigade in Germany, of the brigade in Korea, of our naval units on the seas of the world, of our airmen who fly the aircraft that we are getting in increasing numbers.
When I say I hope we will not hear that, it is not because we do not want to hear it. We have heard it already. We believe it and we believe it just as much as the government. We on this side of the house have just as much reason to be proud of the young Canadians in uniform as has any member on the other side of the house. Without reducing this to personalities may I simply, for the purpose of the record and for the knowledge of that younger generation who may not be aware of the facts, remind the house that the military spokesman of our party, General Pearkes, carries on his breast more decorations for valour than are worn by any other infantry officer in the units of the commonwealth today. I mention that not to glorify his military achievements, glorious though they are; but a man who wears the ribbon of the Victoria Cross, that highest of all decorations for valour, a decoration difficult to win and live, a man who wears the C.B., the D.S.O., the Military Cross and the many other decorations awarded to him for his service on the field of battle, a man who has risen from the rank of private in an infantry unit to divisional commander, is not a man who is going to place before this committee, this house, this parliament or the people of Canada any argument or any single statement that would reflect on the young men in whom he himself has such a deep and abiding pride.
Without extending it beyond that, Mr. Chairman, may I say that the same applies to a large percentage of the members of this house who have, in one service or another, done their best within their limited capacity to serve their country in time of war. I would not feel myself worthy of the remarks I am making if I did not concede and say with admiration that the Minister of National Defence himself is one of those who served gallantly on the field of battle, and from that service I would hope that he would be prompted to recognize the deep and grave concern of those of us who have seen the penalty of unpreparedness in the situation with which we are confronted in this country at this time.
As one whose contact with the reserve forces goes back for more years than I like to recall, I say without any reservation that on a comparative basis, in spite of the enthusiasm, the quality of training and the efforts of those in the reserve forces today, there has been no time in the last fifty years when the reserve forces of Canada were less
Supply-National Defence capable of immediately assuming the responsibilities they would be called upon to assume in the event of a sudden emergency. Surely that is not a situation we can contemplate with satisfaction. Surely that is a situation which should be fully examined, fully disclosed to us. Instead, we are simply told that under terms of secrecy and because the word "secret" or "confidential" appears on the document, we cannot have the findings which have been made.
This is becoming a habit, Mr. Chairman. It is not only in the case of the report to which I have referred that this same attitude applies. Only this morning an effort was made to obtain information respecting some inquiries that have been made, and that was denied on the ground that it was made in relation to other findings which have also been denied. That is one original way of denying information-deny the blanket and you deny everything under it. That is exactly what we have before us now. Then let us see some of the reports that there have been in regard to the various aspects of the military service. There was the Mainguy report on the navy; there was also the Gordon report on the national defence department within a limited field. There was the MacNab report; there was the Currie report; there was the Hendry report; and also there is the report which is known colloquially as the general's report and which perhaps is more accurately known as the Kennedy report from the name of the very distinguished general who acted as chairman of that committee.
During this past session, motion after motion has been presented to this house calling for the production of reports, including the Kennedy report, and they have been voted down by the solid voting strength of those supporting this government. So far as the supporters of the government are concerned, they are prepared to accept these blind assurances that all is well, in the face of the knowledge of many hon. members on the other side that all is not well and that we should have the information which is not available to us today. So far as the supporters of the government are concerned,
Theirs not to make reply.
Theirs not to reason why.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that no one is under the impression that any statement in the Currie report has been challenged because of the fact that the government still is able to exercise such a sweeping majority for the suppression of all information in other cases. Not one word of that stands effectively challenged. The rails were stolen; the horses were on the payroll-

Supply-National Defence
Oh, oh.
The horses were on the payroll-
No, no.

-just as they were found, Mr. Chairman, to be on the payroll, by a man declared by the Minister of National Defence Jhimself to be the best qualified for that inquiry. The tawdry objections made by members opposite, in sounds that will not be recorded in Hansard, merely indicate the extent to which the Liberal mythology has already written off the Currie report.
May I rise on a point of order?
No, on a question of privilege, but not on a point of order. If it is a question of privilege, that is a different thing.
The Leader of the Opposition is not chairman of this committee.
No, nor are you.

I should like to rise on a question of privilege to say that the question of the horses on the payroll was effectively dealt with in this house once and for all by the Prime Minister. Despite that fact the Conservative opposition has continued repeating this story about them. However, it was effectively dealt with once and for all in this house.
What point of order is that?

That is exactly the kind of answer, Mr. Chairman, that should make every hon. member in this house concerned about every answer given by the minister, because that is not so. The statement he has just made is directly contrary to the facts. The statement he has made is contrary to the Currie report, which stands unchallenged. The statement made by the Prime Minister disposed of this thing in no way. The statement by the Prime Minister skirted around this question, and the fact that the Minister of National Defence would give this absolutely misleading answer is one reason why we should have before us now every word in the Kennedy report, and not rely upon his interpretation of it. If he is not capable of interpreting the Currie report correctly at this time, he is no more capable of interpreting the Kennedy report to us.
Let us remember, Mr. Chairman, that it was not only horses on the payroll. Let us remember the whole siding that was stolen. Let us remember the hobby horses that were made; let us remember also the fraudulent invoices and the disappearing cement and the general's fish pond and everything else found in that report which stands, unless the


minister is prepared to get up in this house and say he does not believe Mr. Currie.
And include the Ontario highways.
The sound effects from the C.B.C., Mr. Chairman, are not an appropriate background for the consideration and discussion of national defence.
Just as important as yours.

I recognize that in this house the minister is much more important because he has behind him a majority that will deny to this house any information he wants withheld, including information about the C.B.C. He is, therefore, very important in this house, particularly when he is backed up by this majority.
You ought to get a few backers.

That is the only thing that does give him importance. Certainly, we concede that as long as he is in a position to deny to this house, through the majority that supports this government, the information we should have, then he is very important indeed, and important mainly because of his capacity to deny us effective information.
Hon. members in this house who were not members before, Mr. Chairman, should read the Currie report and read also the statement of the Minister of National Defence that Mr. Currie or Colonel Currie or Brigadier Currie, as he may properly be called, was declared by the minister to be the best qualified man in Canada. Unless the minister says he does not believe him, then let every hon. member in this house accept that report; and because we did get so much information in that report, let the minister extend the information and tell us, not in the refined version but in its original form, the details of the Kennedy report.
In this whole subject a very successful device has been employed. Either the document has the word "confidential" on it, a very easy word to write, or it is not in the public interest to disclose the document. This is a very easy device with which to suppress effective information. The fact is that one thing that has so lengthened debates in this house-
George Drew.

The distinguished hon. member opposite says "George Drew". I know the minister would prefer that the opposition remain silent and that we just meet here like the Soviet parliament, listen to what the

politburo tells us, and then go home; but we do not intend now or any other time to accept that interpretation.
We will stay for the summer, if you want.

We intend to fulfil our function as an opposition, in spite of the difficulty of obtaining information. But we do make it clear to the people of Canada who send us here that one of the things that have lengthened this parliament is the fruitless effort that has been made by the opposition to obtain the kind of information that, as members of parliament and in consideration of the rights of the people, we should have in discussing these vitally important subjects before us.
At what point, Mr.,Chairman, is the information going to become available? We made the proposal last year that this gentleman, whom the Minister of National Defence described as the best qualified in Canada, should extend his report to every branch of the Department of National Defence. Do not let any member of the government, and above all the minister, say to this house that this reflects on any member of the armed forces. The highest tribute we can pay to the members of the armed forces is to insist that they have the training, the equipment and, above all, the reserves behind them that they are entitled to have as young men and women who have accepted the heavy obligations they have assumed in the uniform of Canada.
What we argued last year, what we have argued this year, and what we will still contend, is that even if the Minister of National Defence is not prepared to appoint Mr. Currie to conduct such an inquiry, then he should appoint some other individual or group of individuals, with the same freedom Mr. Currie had, to examine the organization of the Department of National Defence, and of general defence organizations throughout Canada.
After all, is there a single member in the House of Commons who believes for one moment that the very substantial savings which resulted from the Currie report would ever have been made if that inquiry had not been conducted in that way? There is no hon. member in this House of Commons, including those on the other side of the house, who thinks for a moment that this would have been done. And yet, let hon. members recall this, and particularly those who were not in the house when that report was discussed, that the inquiry conducted by Mr. Currie and those associated with him dealt only with one segment of one part of one
Supply-National Defence branch of the service. It dealt with less than a twentieth of the army organization, alone. Now, if that much was found which called for substantial savings, and very sweeping reorganization such as was recommended in the Currie report, then surely there can be no hon. member who would suggest that tremendous savings would not be made by a similarly objective inquiry carried into the whole organization.
Do not suggest that anyone in proposing this is seeking scapegoats, any more than those members of parliament who support a Companies Act which calls for regular audit would suggest that there is something inherently dishonest in business when they make it an absolute requirement that every year there shall be an independent audit of the books and of the organization of a company. That is done as an ordinary and sensible and businesslike recommendation. There is no suggestion that there is any natural tendency to impropriety in the handling of business of that kind. With the very best of intentions and of business purpose, any rapidly expanding organization is bound to break out at the seams. Any expanding organization calls for examination and review.
That is what we have asked for, and I repeat that request now. We are coming toward the end of the session; but such an inquiry could be conducted under an appointment made by the government while the House of Commons is not sitting. Such inquiry would produce information which, if it were placed before members of the house, would make it possible for us to deal with this problem next year in a way that has not been possible previously at any time.
We have here a long series of items. It is not our intention to continue repetitive inquiries in regard to those items in the unavailing thought that by such inquiry we might finally break through this veil of secrecy which has been thrown around the real details in the Department of National Defence. Nothing will be served by that procedure. Nothing will be served by constant requests for the examination of this item and that. We admit right now, and without hesitation, that by the method the government has followed, and by the use of the guillotine, which has been employed over and over again by the full weight of the government majority to stop inquiry, to close the door to the receiving of information, and to withhold reports, we are not in a position to discuss this subject as we should discuss it. We know that perfectly well. But I have just offered a few examples of things that are known to me. I have offered a few

Supply-National Defence examples that are known to hon. members on the other side of the house, in their own constituencies, in regard to actual conditions of the reserve force in their constituencies.
I would hope that we might have the refreshing experience of seeing one or two, or more, members on the other side of the house getting up and explaining that in spite of the high quality of the officers, the N.C.O.'s and men, and in spite of their earnestness, the reserve units in their constituencies in many cases are not able to meet the opportunities presented to them.
They are too interested in the Senate and parliamentary jobs, and assistants, to do that.

Mr. Chairman, this talk about secrecy, this talk about confidential information is nothing but a farce. This talk about information which cannot be disclosed to the elected members of the people is nothing but an attempt to hide information which would simply whet the appetites of hon. members- and I hope hon. members on the other side of the house-for still more information.
Each one of those reports being withheld contains findings which explain where substantial savings could be made. Each one of them does. Let us have those reports. Let us have the Kennedy report. And, Mr. Chairman, unless the Minister of National Defence is prepared to say that Field Marshal Montgomery was exaggerating the gravity of the situation when he made his statement on May 24 last, appendix "A" to which I have put on the record, then let the Minister of National Defence now tell us that there will be an examination of the whole organization of the Department of National Defence, such as produced the savings about which he boasted following the Currie report. And then next year we would be able to come back here and really deal with these vitally important items, with knowledge of what lies behind them.
Let the public know today that the veil of secrecy thrown around the Department of National Defence by this government precludes the effectiveness of detailed questioning. Let us remember that we have a right to that information, because we are not dealing only with some two billions of dollars of the taxpayers' money: we are dealing with nothing less than national survival itself.

Mr. Chairman, I agree with some of the things the Leader of the Opposition said, when he referred to the personalities of two of our distinguished members. But there is a lot I do not agree with in what he said. I do not agree with his


statement that guns, armament, fleets and material things are the only things necessary to win a war.
And neither do I, Mr. Chairman.
Nobody else does.

What was it that beat Hitler? It was not because he had a great fleet of submarines, the best in the world; it was not because he had more aeroplanes than all the allies put together, perhaps twice over; it was not because he had big guns and arms and armament, the best in the world. What beat Hitler? It was not his lack of preparation. We have heard from the Leader of the Opposition-
Mr. Chairman, may I ask-
Sit down.
No; the hon. member has asked a question, and I can answer it in a few words if he wants it answered. I will answer it very quickly, if he wants it answered.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The Leader of the Opposition knows that the hon. member for Fort William can be interrupted only with his own consent, and if he does not sit down he does not indicate that.
That is quite true. I merely said if the hon. member is really asking a question I can answer it very quickly.
You have all the answers.

I will make myself pretty clear before I am through, I hope. I asked the question, and I am asking it of myself. What beat Hitler? One of the first things that beat Hitler was when he went out and murdered the Jews by the thousand for no other crime than that they were efficient and good businessmen, and that they believed in one God. "Thou shalt not kill." And he who breaks the Ten Commandments will be broken by them. Napoleon said, Talk not to me of Providence: Providence is on the side of heaviest battalions. But Providence was not on the side of heaviest battalions when he attacked Russia. When half a million of the flower of France were frozen to death in their saddles, Providence was on the side of the thin, clear, cool air of Russia. Providence was on the side of the snowflakes of Russia and not on the side of the well-equipped army of France.
The Leader of the Opposition said a good deal about information. If the Ministers of National Defence were not capable of keeping the information that should be kept they should not be there. What does Russia want to know? They want to get all the information that the Department of National Defence

has, and I do not think they should have it. I admit that we have only 15 million people in Canada, but when we have 113,000 in the armed forces, that is not too bad.
That is Liberal defence; that is not defence of Canada.

The hon. member can rise in his place in a moment or two. I am not through yet, but I shall soon be. What beat Hitler? Headquarters asked the Christian church in Canada all over for their co-operation, and after that co-operation what happened? You could see Hitler making his mistakes after Dunkirk. Why did they not wipe out the remnants of the British army in that area? They had enough aeroplanes, but they did not do it. What they did was to attack Russia, the second big mistake. The next mistake they made was when Japan was induced to make its attack on Pearl Harbor. You could see things coming along.
I can say, Mr. Chairman, that the Minister of National Defence has done a fine job in preparation. I have read the white paper. I have not gone on all the trips that we might have had, to see what the Department of National Defence is doing. We went to Petawawa, and to me it was a wonderful revelation to see what they were doing. We went out to the airfield in Ottawa and we saw what the aeroplanes were doing. The Minister of National Defence has done a splendid job. There comes a time in preparations when you cannot prepare any further and then the Man above comes in and He does His work.

I desire to say a few words on this matter. I do not expect to be very long, but I do want to add my contribution in stating that I fail to understand the reason why at the present time the elected members of this House of Commons, and thereby the true representatives of the people, are not taken more into the confidence of the minister and of the government as to the defence situation in this dominion at the present time, and as to the value that is being received for the expenditures of over half of our national budget.
I can remember when Canada was at war, Mr. Chairman, and there was an enemy on the western coast. The members of the legislature of British Columbia were very disturbed about the situation because they were almost in the dark as to what it was. Therefore, the members of the legislature of British Columbia raised their voices and demanded that they be taken into the confidence of the military authorities as to what was going on in British Columbia and as to what our position was.
Supply-National Defence
Now, Mr. Chairman, there we were at war. There was a demand, if you like to put it that way, or more politely a request, that the members of the legislature be taken into the military confidence. What happened? Within the matter of seven days Mr. Hart, as the premier of British Columbia, and I as the leader of the opposition in British Columbia, and representatives on the floor of the legislature, were called together by the general in charge of the Pacific command, and he sits right here on the floor of the house, General Pearkes. He can tell you that what I am saying is correct. We were taken into the confidence of the general in charge of the command. We were told what was going on; we were given a demonstration of what could be done. I can remember we said: In the event of an air attack, a bombing attack on Victoria, how soon can you have a scramble of air fighters so as to meet those bombers? We were given an actual demonstration right then and there. We were not told what someone in a certain office told him; we were given a demonstration, and we knew right to the second just how soon a bombing raid could be met. I am not going to go into details, but I am going to say this on my responsibility in this house. As a member of the legislature of British Columbia in time of war we knew the situation, we knew the number of troops, we knew the number of ships and sailors and aircraft and fighters, and so on.
In view of that experience, I must admit that I cannot understand why at this time the members of this House of Commons cannot be taken into the confidence of the government to a far greater extent than they are at the present time. If there is some reason why it cannot be done in the open, then I say at least it should be done in camera. I have been amazed that we cannot get information from the minister or from the government on our own affairs here in the realm of defence in Canada, and yet just a few days ago we could meet-yes, in camera it was- and we could get information on what is going on in Europe under the NATO troops, information of vital importance, of vital interest. If the commander in chief of the NATO forces could see fit to take the members of parliament at least in part into his confidence, then why cannot our own minister of defence in Canada take his own members of parliament, the members of parliament of Canada, into a far greater confidence than has been done hitherto?
I do want to say a word in particular about the reserve army, because honestly I will admit I should like to know a lot more than I do at the present time about that army. I have a great deal of pride in that body of

Supply-National Defence men. I had the honour of being a member of the reserve forces in the city of Vancouver for a number of years, and I think that it certainly redounds to their credit that they do their eight hours of work in the factory, in the shop or in the office and then turn out two or three times a week at night and week ends and give up their annual holidays so as to go to the training camps. I was not very high; I was only one of those two-pip miracles. However, I was a training officer and in the two or three years I was in the reserve army I got to know the problems we run up against. I know of things that went on that we just could not understand, things which just about sent the training officers out of their heads. We had such things as changes in orders, changes in rules, changes in equipment, and we never knew exactly where we stood. There may have been reasons for them but I know that was the situation then and I would like to know whether these problems have been met, and I want to know whether we can obtain the information which is contained in the Kennedy report.
I do not think I need add any more, and certainly there is little need to be emotional about this. I would say, however, that the reserve army must be efficient and in view of the key information given to the elected representatives of British Columbia in time of war I cannot understand the hesitancy of the Minister of National Defence in making more information available to us at this time.
It is all very well for the minister to take up that attitude here in Ottawa, but in a matter of a week or two when we return to our constituencies we are the ones who are going to have to answer the questions about this and we cannot do it unless we are given that information by the executive. I sincerely hope that after due deliberation and perhaps a little more serious thought the minister will consider taking the people's elected representatives a little bit more into his confidence than he has done up to now.

I think it seems obvious,
Mr. Chairman, that members of this committee find it difficult to discuss the subject of national defence in a vacuum of information. It also seems obvious that the reason for the extended discussion on this matter is due to a lack of specific knowledge of the affairs of the department. I know that I personally have tried on three occasions to scrutinize the items in the estimates so as to come to grips with some of the underlying difficulties. But I have found it almost impossible because we have been dependent upon the vague statements to which reference has already been made on numerous occasions


in this house. I have searched through the white paper and according to that white paper all is well in the department. I have examined the minister's statements and according to these statements everything is rosy in the defence garden.
Unfortunately that conclusion does not jibe with the reports I have received through personal contact with certain branches of the services, and also from the numerous letters which reach me particularly with regard to our reserve forces. This has been particularly true since the announcement of the completion of the Kennedy report. When queried for information, I find myself in the same position as other hon. members in this house, forced to say, "I am sorry but we have no information. We are merely members of parliament and apparently not to be taken into the confidence of the government in regard to these important matters."
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am rising to speak at this time because of a special interest in a subject with which I think it will be impossible to deal during the discussion on later items. I am especially concerned with the government's decision to deny these reports to members of parliament, because I am the victim of one of these refusals. I refer particularly to the Hendry report. I have been on the trail of this report for a long time and I have had to work on the basis of trial and error because there was no specific information available. In fact it was only indirectly that I learned such a report existed. During the pursuit there were times when I almost had it. Those most intimately connected with its preparation were of the opinion that there was no secrecy involved and that any revelations concerning it would not place our defence preparations in jeopardy.
At one time, when I thought I was going to receive this report, those whom I contacted said that as a precautionary measure they would have to consult the Department of National Defence. It was there that this cloak of secrecy descended upon what is a harmless and innocuous report in so far as military strategy, secret weapons and arms development are concerned.
If there is anything vital to the defence program of this country, civil defence as well as armed defence, it is the matter of comprehensive welfare planning. In this connection it is not only this matter of denying members of parliament access to reports which disturbs me. The shroud of secrecy around the department goes much further than that. During recent months, for example, I have been in touch with some of my

old air force buddies still active in the service. One particular incident would have been amusing if the implications behind it had not been so serious. We had not seen one another for a long time so we had lunch together in the parliamentary restaurant. This officer was ticked off for consorting with a member of the opposition. I think that is carrying the shroud of secrecy too far. It is this accumulation of frustration resulting from the denial of reports as well as other instances of police state tactics which bring me to my feet at the present time.
Then, there is the matter of our contacts with the reserve units. Some hon. members of this house maintain reserve contacts. I do not know whether my experience is exceptional, but I have found it very difficult to get into close contact with the work which is of the greatest interest to me and work for which my background, training and preparation in military matters best qualifies me to pursue. This seems to be particularly difficult if one happens to be a member of the House of Commons, which to my mind is the exact reverse of the principle which should prevail in a democratic society. My background happens to be that of an allweather night fighter pilot, but when I turn out for reserve training I am put on personnel work dealing with personnel problems which crop up fairly regularly under the present military scheme of things.
The only conclusion I can draw from this, Mr. Chairman, is that the government, in defence matters, is more afraid of the opposition than they are of any potential enemy. I have said this before and I repeat it now. I am quite sure that if there is any state interested in attacking this country, then they know far more about our military potential and preparation than do the members of the opposition in this House of Commons. That situation naturally arouses our suspicions. If we are sent here by our constituents to represent them in running the affairs of this country, then we must become suspicious when we are denied access to the details concerning a department which is one of the biggest spending departments of government, and which, in the present uneasy state of affairs existing in the world-and which state of affairs is likely to continue for some considerable time-has a great measure of responsibility for our security. I have come to the conclusion that an attitude of this kind can only suggest that the government is more afraid for the security and defence of the Liberal party than they are for the security and defence of the nation. That is not a particularly healthy attitude in view of the 83276-4031
Supply-National Defence emergency or the crisis, on the level of external affairs, that at this time confronts Canada and all the nations of the western world.
In the discussion this morning it has been pointed out that Canada's defence force is and always will be essentially a civilian force. That is something that has been so in more primitive, and earlier, experiences of military activity in this country. It certainly is much more true in the face of the kind of warfare confronting us in this twentieth century. The advent of the H-bomb and similar weapons of total destruction means that everyone, more or less, is in the front line. All we can hope to do in maintaining a defence force, a group of professionals, is to support a nucleus who, in the event of an emergency, would be able to bring into a state of rapid preparation and mobilization the much larger force that would be needed.
If we are going to maintain the interest of the public or if we are going to maintain the interest of the civilian soldier, the reservist, in defence matters, to me it seems logical to believe that we must take him into our confidence. It seems to me that the government must take the citizens into their confidence, must place all the facts before them, must present them repeatedly-and shock them if necessary-with the challenge of the urgency of the moment. That is why I have pursued this subject of welfare. I do not want to look at it in any narrow or restricted sense at all. But in a democracy where you have not the totalitarian or authoritarian machinery with which to do what should be done quickly in the face of a crisis, you have to depend upon high morale and esprit de corps among the citizenry generally. They must be inoculated with a deepseated conviction concerning their responsibilities in these matters. If we are going to be able to carry out our defence program successfully, it seems to me that such a happy state of affairs can arise only from the existence of a well-informed public.
From that standpoint alone I think it is unfortunate if not tragic-in view of the continuing emergency confronting us-that we as members in the first instance are denied access to those documents that have been referred to. Perhaps it is unfortunate that the Currie report, or what has sometimes been referred to as the bootleg copy of the Currie report, was revealed to the members of the House of Commons because, since the revelations that were made in that Currie report, the defence department has buried its head in the sand even deeper than before. I cannot imagine them denying access

Supply-National Defence to the members to such a harmless document as the Hendry report on welfare services had they not been, having regard to the implications of the Currie report, unduly disturbed for the security of the Liberal party.
If I needed to quote any example as to the proper attitude that should be taken in maintaining the necessary interest in defence matters in a democratic society, I think I need only refer to Sir Winston Churchill, the British Prime Minister. All during the twilight period before world war II he was the voice crying in the wilderness. Because he was not in tune or in step with the prevailing or predominating attitudes toward external affairs in the western world at that time, he was not very popular politically. He represented the "blood, sweat and tears" philosophy. Of course that philosophy, at any time, is not very sweet as far as the electorate is concerned. It does not help in the necessary process of obtaining votes. However, he was right. Because he was right, when the crisis eventually came he was called upon to assume responsibility. The story is well known to all the free peoples of the western world.
Like the hon. member for Vancouver East, I was greatly impressed with the frankness with which the problems of defence in relation to the present world situation were dealt with by General Gruenther. It was a straightforward and frank appraisal, as contrasted with the "gobbledygook", the circumvention that goes on in this chamber with regard to defence matters in relation to Canada which, in the matter of population, is a relatively small segment of the whole NATO defence program at the moment. I suppose it is inevitable that Canada remain ambivalent and vacillating with regard to these matters. I suppose that attitude is inevitable in view of our pre-war record, and in view of our postwar record for that matter because, after the war, we immediately indulged in wholesale rapid demobilization. Then along came Korea and we were forced to assume what has been referred to by the Minister of National Defence as "crash planning" in order to meet the immediate challenge of the outbreak of hostilities in Korea. But in this year 1954 I think the time has now long since passed when we should break away from crash planning and should begin to look into the future-the long haul and the long pull -with regard to defence matters.
I do not want to speak for too long on this matter. However, surveying briefly what has been accomplished in the field of defence
IMr. DinsdaleJ
at the expenditure of some $5 billion, may I say that the emphasis, as I review the situation, has been on supply and construction and it looks to me as though personnel problems have been minimized. I am just going to refer briefly to what has taken place in the air force and also to what has taken place in that closely related field of radar defences. Then finally I shall make some brief references to the situation so far as materiel supply is concerned.
The heart of our air force defence program has been the development of the all-weather fighter, the CF-100. That of course is logical in view of the challenge with which Canada would be confronted by any possible air attack. We have now arrived at the stage where a token force of CF-lOO's is operational. I would suggest that we cannot go very much further than the preparation of a token force so far as the all-weather fighter is concerned mainly because technological changes in aviation are taking place so quickly that a new type becomes obsolescent almost before it is ready for operational duty.
That is a difficulty that goes right back to world war II. From actual experience with a night fighter squadron, I remember that one of the biggest bugbears we had to face was the constant reconversion to new aircraft and the extensive retraining in the use of rapidly developing airborne radar equipment. We have arrived at the stage where we have a token all-weather fighter force. This does not solve the problems of reserve squadrons because it is very difficult for reserve squadrons to maintain the efficiency necessary to cope successfully and to keep themselves up to an operational level so far as the allweather jet fighters in service at the present time are concerned. I suggest that matter needs to be given serious consideration because if the reserves are the backbone of the defence of this country we are far from reaching the desirable state of preparedness that is mentioned so freely and glibly in the white paper report.
As to radar, I think the statement has been made in the house that we are now in a position to intercept nine out of ten enemy aircraft.
No such statement was made.

As I read the record that is the implication I got from the minister's statement. That statement has already been repudiated, and well it might be because no fighter-radar combination could possibly achieve that degree of success in coping with the difficulties involved in night operations, particularly bad weather operations. It is true that the two must be developed hand

in hand. All-weather fighters and the radar establishments are integral parts of the same system. Indeed, had it not been for the rapid development of radar or radio-location, as it was known in Britain, at the beginning of world war II it is doubtful whether the German luftwaffe could have been driven back during the crucial days of the battle of Britain. The secret of the operational use of radar was very carefully kept until the end of the war.
I remember that popular thinking during the war regarded members of night fighter units as individuals wearing mysterious dark goggles and eating great quantities of carrots in order to improve their vision at night. In my three years overseas I never saw any carrots. In fact, our staple vegetable diet was brussels sprouts which do not have any necessarily beneficial effects so far as night vision is concerned. It was due to the presence of a very efficient radar system that the battle of Britain was won which gave the allies an opportunity to prepare to meet the eventual onslaught of the nazi forces across Europe.
I mention that point merely to indicate the contrast today so far as this subject is concerned. We have very elaborate information on our radar establishments. In fact, Roundel, the official air force magazine, was even pinpointing these units for us a short time ago. Yet we are denied access to a report dealing with the broad subject of welfare for the troops as well as the problem of integration of military forces with the civilian population.
I am not going to elaborate on that theme any further. It seems to me that what we have achieved thus far is that we have spent large sums of money on material and equipment, and we have not yet come to grips with the real problem of any defence force in a democratic state, the problem of challenging the ordinary citizen so that he becomes keenly aware of his responsibilities in these matters, particularly in the face of the total war which threatens us at the present time.
It is almost one o'clock, Mr. Chairman, and before proceeding with one or two specific points on the subject of welfare I should like to call it one o'clock.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

When the committee rose at one o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I was just coming to the concluding portion of my remarks concerning the general problem of
Supply-National Defence welfare services as they relate themselves to the armed forces. The theme I was endeavouring to develop was that in defence matters as well as in any other public affairs in this country, there must be the closest possible co-ordination and co-operation between the government and the people of Canada.
I have just one further observation concerning the major emphasis that has been felt in defence planning in this country. Since* the Korean incident we have been straining every resource and every fibre in building, up the materiel demands of our defence-effort; constructing permanent buildings, developing new types of aircraft and so on almost ad infinitum. But I do feel we have been neglecting the most vital part of the whole structure, that is the problem of personnel. It is a fine thing to have the best housed, best clothed, and best paid defence force in the western sphere of influence, but that does not necessarily mean that we have the most efficient defence force.
It occurs to me that the Roman legionnaires, at the time when the Roman empire was most vulnerable, could boast of all those things. They had the best equipment, the best materiel and all the other physical factors going towards the preparation of a defensive force. The one thing they lacked was good morale, the esprit de corps, and certainly there was very little integration and co-ordination between the civilian population and the military elite.
It seems to me, from the limited opportunities I have had of looking into our defence program, there is a lack of close integration. Elaborate training programs are carried on to meet the demands of technological warfare, but not much is done by way of endeavouring to integrate the military training programs with the needs of the civilian population. That is just one method whereby there could be closer relationship. It has been customary in any war effort to which Canada has made a contribution to make use of the civilian resources, buildings and so forth, to the maximum in order to effect complete mobilization. I sometimes compare the lavish sums of money that are spent in this process that has been described as "crash planning" in our defence build-up, with some of the financially restricted educational programs in civilian circles. The educational institution with which I was once connected, for example, carries on its whole year's work on a budget of $200,000, merely a drop in the bucket when compared; with the lavish expenditures we find taking;

Supply-National Defence place in our defence planning. Yet that institution has made many outstanding contributions to the public life of this country. The student body has included such people as the premier of Saskatchewan, the premier of Manitoba and no less a personage than the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I am referring, of course, to Brandon college. I am raising that point to indicate that while heavy expenditure is necessary to meet the defence challenge of the moment, and we are spending billions, as the record indicates; let us not be entirely preoccupied with the urgency of the moment, a tendency of all governments. Let us look into the future and consider the commitments of long-term planning.
I feel that this is where the subject of welfare planning comes into the picture, Mr. Chairman. As I have indicated, I am not referring to the provision of recreation programs only, or providing canteens, which is basic to any military welfare program. I am concerned with the broader problem of bringing together the special needs of the military community and the special needs of the civilian population. So long as we are dependent on a civilian military force, these two aspects of our defence program will have to work as one.
In a letter from the defence minister last January refusing me access to the Hendry report, this report is described as a special report prepared for the confidential information of those concerned. I cannot conceive of any group who should be more concerned about this matter than the members of this house. Our whole problem of raising the morale and esprit de corps of the people of Canada to meet the challenge of the moment is of vital concern to all the people of this [DOT]country.
There has been a lot of discussion in the press concerning incidents that crop up in military camps from time to time. There has been resulting criticism laid at the door of inadequate welfare and recreation facilities. I am not going to harp on, or labour, that particular point, because those incidents will occur in any large military force where you have a group of men who are uprooted from their regular community ties. Special social problems and personal behaviour problems are bound to occur under such circumstances. These have to deal with the narrower welfare approach. Routine recreation programs are necessary, as are canteens. Those things are basic and almost axiomatic; we have to provide those services in the regular civilian community. There has been a tendency in recent years to increase the contribution the public bodies make towards
[Mr. Dlnsdale.l

welfare programs of this kind in order to offset the impact of commercialized recreation, which I feel sometimes should be spelled '"wreckreation", rather than in the traditional manner of "recreation".
A comprehensive welfare program that is going to deal with the larger problem must tie in the voluntary groups. Indeed, in any crisis it is usually the voluntary groups who carry the main burden of responsibility and, in turn, it is these voluntary groups who, by means of their close contact with the civilian population, are able to arouse the necessary enthusiasm and interest among the citizenry generally in order to have them make a worth-while contribution to a welfare program. Again, it is through the voluntary groups that the contact with the home can be made and maintained. At the moment the Department of National Defence, so far as I can gather, is moving forward in all these categories. The routine recreational program is being strengthened, canteens are being provided, and an attempt is being made to work more closely with the voluntary groups. I do understand however that, so far as home contacts are concerned, we are still pretty well dependent upon the Department of Veterans Affairs to investigate the home situation and to make its report. Unfortunately the difficulty there arises from the fact that, having examined the situation and having given their report, they have no service to provide. As we know, the Department of Veterans Affairs is restricted in what it can do. So the net result is that they suffer from paralysis of analysis. All they can do is outline the problem. They have no resources for assisting in the solution.
There is another matter connected with this subject of welfare suggesting the tendency to segregate civilian from military needs. Right across the country there has been a tendency to carry on a program of segregation between the military camps and the civilian population. I was not in on the preliminary post-war discussions of mobilization for defence planning in Canada, but it seems to me that to segregate military formations, and to isolate them in self-contained army, air force or even navy encampments, is working against the real needs of a comprehensive and all-out defence program which would tie in our civilian population so that, if a crisis ever came, they would be aware of the problem and fully alerted to the responsibilities relating thereto.
Summing up, I would say there are immediate plans that have to be made to meet what has been called the demands of creeping mobilization, which has been the defence

program up to the present time. We have been adjusting ourselves slowly to the needs of this creeping mobilization. The situation has improved slowly. I am sure that had we had access to reports such as the Hendry report, we might have been able to make complimentary remarks concerning what has been going on, because no doubt the report contains a thorough examination of the situation. But we are working in the dark. We can give our viewpoint and express our conclusions only from a very restricted background of knowledge. That is the handicap under which we are working at the present time.
In addition to immediate plans, there is the need for long-term plans for total mobilization, if that desperate situation should ever develop in this country. It seems to me that, so far as welfare needs are concerned, here is where we are weakest. There is no group engaged in comprehensive over-all planning. The chaos which would result from a lack of co-ordination and integration, and because the situation has been obscure, owing to the attitude of the defence department in trying to assure us that all is well, would produce a very difficult situation, if a major crisis ever developed.
In connection with all these matters I maintain that the House of Commons should be taken into the confidence of the cabinet and its advisers. If anyone is vitally interested in these matters, then surely it should be the elected representatives of the people. Defence planning must take in the whole of the population.
I hope that some discussion along these lines will take place when we are dealing with civil defence. There needs to be co-ordination and complete integration if we are going to be in a position to meet the defence challenge of the moment.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say only a word or two in the discussion of the first item of the estimates for the Department of National Defence, although I claim no expert knowledge in matters of national defence. I have never been a member of the armed forces. Apart from the occasional hunting trip I have never fired a gun, and I do not claim to be an expert on these matters. Nevertheless I think something should be said on one or two points.
I listened attentively this morning to the leader of the official opposition who, in many respects, seemed to be giving quite a speech. I did think however that in some respects it was a bit weak. Because I support the Leader of the Opposition in some of the
Supply-National Defence things he said, I would not want the minister or the government to gain the impression that I supported him 100 per cent. For instance, I saw no particular reason for bringing up the old story about the horses on the payroll.
I was here in the last parliament, of course-as I have been for a number of years. We all heard the story about the horses; and, frankly, I must confess I was pretty well satisfied with the Prime Minister's reply. I thought he replied conscientiously in the matter. Further, a committee of the house was set up and had every opportunity in the world to go into the subject. They had before them the man who was responsible for the Currie report. I had expected some fireworks in that committee, but there did not seem to be very much by way of an explosion at that time. I must confess that, after all the hullabaloo that went on about these things, I thought our Conservative friends fell down just a little bit in carrying out any vital investigation during the sittings of that committee.
For the Leader of the Opposition to bring in that matter this morning, after so long a time has passed by-for after all this was a matter that was brought up in a session previous to the last election-was rather small potatoes. I think it weakened his whole argument because I felt, well, now, surely he has something more important than that to bring up at this time. It is true, and I do agree with him, that since we have an expenditure of about $2 billion for defence, we have every right to know that it is efficiently spent; we have a right to know that we are getting a dollar's worth of efficiency and effectiveness for every dollar spent.
If there are any documents that might be regarded as secret, if those documents apply to such matters as defence strategy or some particular piece of equipment that it is not wise for the enemy to know about- and I doubt there is very much that they do not know about-if there is anything of that kind, I can quite understand how certain documents might be regarded as secret. But if those documents are involved with government policy, or the general conduct of the Department of National Defence, then I do not believe that any documents should be secret.
What I rose particularly to talk about was this. I wonder just how enthusiastic the people of Canada are in subscribing to the annual revenues of this country to the tune of $2 billion for defence. Are they enthusiastic in coming through with that much
