Supply-National Defence money for the carrying on of this department? I cannot answer that myself, but I do believe that you cannot go farther in defence expenditure or in anything else, as far as that goes, and have the support of the people, without carrying the people along with you, and letting them know what the score may be.
I am just wondering whether we have done a good job of really conditioning our people to what might be regarded as necessary in respect to our national defence budget. We use the term "national defence budget" but in reality it is a military budget. We use those terms because we do not like to have any connotation which might indicate that we are aggressive. But in reality it is a military budget, just as much a wartime budget as if we were in a war, although we are now living in peace and there are no particular shooting wars. Have our people been conditioned properly to understand even the potential powers of the enemy and the necessity of such vast expenditures for a small nation of 15 million people? I am inclined to think that instead of conditioning the people to withstand a formidable enemy, in many respects we have been conditioning the people to accept the enemy and accept them on their terms.
It seems to me that in the matter of public relations in this respect we have fallen down completely on the job. It seems to me that we have been playing cat and mouse with those who we know are our enemies, and more often than not we have been the mouse, and we have not gained many victories over the cat.
May I put it this way. Any gain geographically or in any other way that the Soviets have made has not been owing to any military successes. It has been owing to a type of propaganda, and yet they have gobbled up half the world without even firing a shot. I am not saying they have not aided and abetted other countries behind the iron curtain, but they themselves have been able to stay out of any military complications. They have done it by carrying on a real psychological warfare, both in the diplomatic field and in the field of propaganda throughout the world.
What are we doing psychologically to weaken them as they have been doing to weaken us? What are we doing psychologically to weaken the Soviets and those other powers behind the iron curtain? Well, they have certainly not overlooked the opportunity to weaken us within our borders. The object of their psychological warfare is their destruction of western democracy. This is all involved in a matter of defence. I should


like to know what we have actually been doing to weaken communistic dictatorships in the communist countries. We might boast that we have the atom bomb. So have they! We might boast that we have certain strategic bases and positions. So have they, to a very large extent; and, as far as I can understand it, they can match us man for man and gun for gun. But there is one place in which they cannot match us, and that is in the exposition of our way of life as compared with theirs.
I know what might be said. Well, we have to be careful because that would not be diplomatic protocol. All I would say to that is, how much do they care as to what is diplomatic protocol? They are out for the destruction of our way of life. I am going to suggest that the Department of National Defence take over the international shortwave service and really use it to engage in psychological war; for that is what they are doing continually. If it is not used for that purpose, to my mind it serves no purpose at all.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to take up much time of the house in speaking on the estimates for national defence. However, there are one or two things about which I think I should express an opinion in view of the speeches which have been made here today. One matter I would like to suggest the minister should take under consideration is with regard to the pay for reserve forces who are employed by the dominion government. When I was on the city council of Guelph in 1948 we decided that the employees of the city who went to military camps for training as members of the reserve army should have their pay made up by the city so that they would not lose any money. I supported that because I thought it was the proper thing to do, and I would urge our government to give such a scheme their consideration today.
I would not suggest that they treat the taxpayers' money lightly and just go ahead and pay wages to these men to the same extent as they receive in their civilian job, although there are provincial governments, for instance the one in Ontario, which do. I do not think our government should take such a free attitude with the taxpayers' money that they are prepared to pay anything. Indeed, if my suggestion is accepted I would suggest that a further restriction be incorporated. I think it would be helpful to our reserve army if we made up that proportion of the recruit's pay so that he would not lose any money while attending camp, but in order to qualify for that allowance the recruit must turn in a report from his O.C.

verifying that he had attended a certain percentage of the regular drills. This percentage could be set at 75 or 80 per cent. If a recruit did that, then I think the government would be justified in making his pay up so that it would not be any hardship for his family if he attended a reserve army camp for training.
As most hon. members are no doubt aware, I represent the dominion artillery city, Guelph, and as the Leader of the Opposition pointed out early this morning, artillery is a very important arm of the services. Of course, everyone knows that the engineers are the backbone of the army, but since I represent an artillery city I would concede that they take second place. I was-
What about the S.R.D.?

I will come to that in a moment. I was touched by the magnificence of the address made this morning by the Leader of the Opposition. I envy his masterful style, and the cadence of expression he can get into his voice, but I want to tell him it has been my experience that the men in the army we used to refer to as "barrack room lawyers" were not very much admired. They used to say that the barracks were no good, that the officers were no good, the grub was no good, and in fact everything connected with the army was no good; and it has been my experience that they exercised very little influence for good on the morale of the troops.
If we are trying to get boys to join the reserve army it is hardly fitting for the Leader of the Opposition to stand up here and say that on reserve army parades there are more officers present than men. I do not believe that would inspire one single person in the Dominion of Canada to join a reserve army unit. That type of propaganda has never been made in my hearing by his supporter, the hon. member for Simcoe North. I have listened to him on several occasions both inside and outside the house, and he has always claimed that the army training he received was something of which he was proud. He makes the kind of speeches that will inspire our boys to join the reserve army.
If the Leader of the Opposition is really interested in getting men to join our reserve forces, that is the sort of attitude he should take, and he should not suggest that we have an army of thieves, a reserve army comprised of people who will not take part in their parades, and that more officers are present than men. He should leave out all these arguments, of the type which are used by the barrack room lawyers to make out a very bad case for conditions in the army.

It would be far better if the Leader of the Opposition listened to the hon. member for Cape Breton South when that hon. member told us about his experiences and the good times that were had in the army. Everyone who has been in the army knows it is not all hard work. There is plenty of hard work but there are good times in the army too. There is good fellowship, great experiences, and good training. Those are the things that will attract recruits, not the sort of dissertation indulged in by barrack room lawyers, who always annoyed those charged with the responsibility of doing a job when we were overseas. I do not think any reasonable person either in the army or in civilian life would expect a training unit to have a full complement of guns on exercise. When the Leader of the Opposition mentions this fact he gives the impression there is not sufficient equipment for the troops who attend army reserve training camps to enable them to obtain a good training.
Neither there is.

That is not the case. Here again I must refer to my artillery friends, for the officer commanding that unit told me they had the very best of equipment, food, and conditions in camp. They did not come back and report to me that the food and conditions were bad and they were short of guns. In fact, they told me the absolute reverse of that, and the people who criticize and who are always complaining do very much to break down the morale of our troops. I do not like to hear it and I do not think it is a good thing for our country.
We have difficulties enough in inspiring in our people a belief that our country is worth fighting for and that it is necessary for a certain number of citizens to assume the responsibility of defending it. The socialists, who want to see everyone's service paid for, will never inspire anyone to join the army, and under their system it is impossible to get good troops. However, in a democracy there is every good reason to fight for one's country; that is the reason why people join our reserve army and fighting forces. It is certainly not for any of the other reasons which have been mentioned.

Mr. Chairman, I am taking part again in this debate owing to the completely unsatisfactory statement which the minister made on May 21. As reported at page 4992 of Hansard, in reference to the fact that I had mentioned armour, he said this:
This matter has already been dealt with in the house on April 15, 1953, on December 1, 1953; and on several other occasions we have gone over the same ground.
The implication conveyed by this sentence is that the subject of armour has been completely dealt with in the debates here in the house. The implication is that the minister has covered the ground fully and carefully with regard to armour. The actual fact is that no such thing has been done.
If you look at the first reference which he gave, Mr. Chairman, that of April 15, 1953, you will discover that we were then discussing the suggestion which had been put forward by the opposition for the employment of an
IMr. Hosking.]

armoured brigade in Europe instead of an infantry brigade, and that the minister simply dismissed the idea out of hand. His second reference is to December 1,	1953. His
reference is correct in this regard, namely that the matter was fully covered; but it was fully covered only by me. I made a speech on December 1. The minister did not do so. I dealt with the necessity for armour in the Canadian army and lamented the fact that the armoured corps was being sadly neglected. I appealed to the minister to put his mind to the problem of employing the armoured personnel carrier in order to save the lives of Canadian infantry soldiers. That was the speech of December 1. The minister had no part whatsoever in the discussion that day. He had spoken in the debate on the speech from the throne on November 26 and in the course of his remarks he did not once mention armour.
When I spoke on this matter last month, again I dwelt on the subject of the neglect of the armoured corps and I was ably supported by the hon member for Calgary North and others. I suggested to the minister that, if it was not possible to adopt our earlier suggestion of maintaining an armoured brigade in Europe and an armoured brigade at home, rotating the two, in order at least to get the army back into proper balance we should maintain an armoured brigade at home, and that that would require activating another armoured regiment, brigading it with the Royal Canadian Dragoons and the Lord Strathcona's Horse, setting up brigade headquarters and carrying out here in Canada armoured brigade training. The minister completely ignored this suggestion. He paid no attention whatsoever to it. The statement on May 21 refers to the impossibility of rotating the armoured regiments. Let me just read his statement so that you will see what it is:
I should like to point out that it is impossible to work our present armed forces, with their commitments in Korea and in Germany and the requirement of having a mobile striking force of airborne troops, and still have two armoured regiments rotating abroad. You just cannot figure out mathematically a way of using the same manpower to do that complicated operation. Once you train a man for armour, you do not want to use him in the infantry and vice versa.
Mr. Chairman, this is one of the typical statements of the Minister of National Defence. He has acquired a national reputation for statements of this nature which are allembracing, comprehensive and completely meaningless. He has completely evaded the issue. At no time have I suggested that an armoured regiment be maintained overseas and be rotated with the other armoured

regiments at home. I talked in terms of an armoured brigade. At no time have I suggested that you should train a man as an armoured corps man and then use him in the infantry or should train a man in the infantry and then use him in a tank. Only the minister could come forward with a suggestion of that nature. It has no meaning. It is confusing. It may confuse the general public. It may confuse those who have no knowledge of the army. However, it certainly has not confused anyone here on the opposition side. It beclouds the issue unnecessarily. What a suggestion to make! The minister has told us that we cannot do this because it involves training a man for armoured vehicle purposes and then sending him overseas and using him as an infantryman or of training a man as an infantryman and employing him in a tank. That is utter nonsense.
In completing his statement with regard to my request for greater use of armour, the minister said this:
Also, of course, an armoured brigade would cost about $100 million more than a corresponding infantry brigade.
That is the end of the quotation. There is no break-down made with regard to the number oi vehicles required or the number of men, nor is there given any estimate of the cost by regiment or anything of that nature. It is just one of those general statements. The minister says it will cost $100 million more for an armoured brigade than it would for an infantry brigade. Earlier the minister had said that the cost of the present infantry brigade in Europe, to maintain it there, was approximately $60 million a year. The implication then is that an armoured brigade similarly placed would cost $160 million. I suggest to the minister that he produce his figures to indicate how he arrives at this grand total. For one thing, based on the figures found in the handbook for war establishments published by the Department of National Defence, an armoured brigade would require 500 fewer men than an infantry brigade, and if you work out the cost of 500 men on an annual basis with their pay and allowances-the figure given to me last year was something in the neighbourhood of $7 per man per day, but it must be higher now-you would effect a saving on pay and allowances, even accepting that figure, of $1,500,000 a year as between an infantry brigade and an armoured brigade. That is without taking into account such matters as married quarters and schooling for children, because obviously there would be fewer married quarters required and fewer children to be educated if you had 500 fewer men overseas.
Supply-National Defence
Let us consider the question of equipment. An armoured brigade requires 232 tanks. Some of these tanks are used for different purposes, some are small and some are large; but for our discussion here I think it would be fair enough to consider that they might all be Centurion tanks, the gun tank that was the normal equipment of our armoured regiments. The cost of the Centurion tank is roughly $100,000. Two hundred and thirty-two, the equipment for a brigade, would give you a cost of $23 million. It is not a recurring annual cost. Tanks do not disintegrate and become unusable in just one year. They last for a very long time. The reserve army regiments of the armoured corps are using for training purposes tanks which must be at least ten years old. The minister may remember that in the year 1940 at Camp Borden the first Canadian armoured brigade used for training purposes tanks which had been manufactured by the United States in 1918. They served a useful purpose. They were still serviceable to a certain extent over twenty years later.
Therefore the expenditure of $23 million to equip a brigade fully with tanks is not an annual recurring expenditure. How then does the minister get the $100 million more for an armoured brigade than for an infantry brigade? Even though we make a generous allowance for other things, spare parts and so on, and take a figure of say $30 million, there is a discrepancy of $70 million for which the minister has to account. I hope he will give us an accounting rather than brush aside an armoured brigade on the implication that it is prohibitive in cost. It is not prohibitive in cost, and in any case it would not mean at this time an additional $30 million added to the national defence budget, because surely we have come close to the end of some of the stockpiling that is going on of soft goods and things of that nature and can divert to actual fighting vehicles some of the money which has been set aside for other matters.
The minister in his statement has, I think, confused the issue completely. I have maintained that the Canadian army is out of balance. Other nations are still maintaining their armoured formations-the United States, the United Kingdom. Canada has fallen behind. We have produced an infantry army with the supporting arms, artillery and engineers, and it is a good army for infantry work. But that is the type of army we had from 1914 to 1918. It is not a modem mobile force, and it is a modern mobile force that is the requirement at the present time.
But the minister refuses to consider this problem. He is content to let the armoured corps remain at the strength of just two

Supply-National Defence regiments, content to raise and equip infantry formations, and is not taking the precaution to see that those infantry formations are protected against loss of life. The experience of the last war showed very clearly that infantry can be protected against unnecessary loss of life, particularly in an advance. In the course of my remarks in the house during the last three years I have repeatedly referred to Canada's great discovery and invention, the armoured personnel carrier, which has been neglected by the Canadian army since the war. I cannot understand why that should be so. But I find that in the United Kingdom they are providing armoured personnel carriers for the protection of their infantry. In the United States they are doing the same thing. It is astonishing to turn to the issue of Life of June 7 of this year and find pictures and an article with regard to an armoured personnel carrier that has been devised and is in use in the United States army, and for which they are appropriating the sum of $50 million.
It is a very wise investment indeed, and I should like to read a sentence or two from the article to indicate what is involved. Appropriately enough, they are calling these vehicles "lifesavers", which is what they are. Here is the description:
The M-59 "lifesaver", a boxlike vehicle with tread to carry it over bad terrain and armour to ward off machine gun bullets is the United States army's latest and most promising attempt to adapt infantry to mechanized and atomic war. Carrying a squad of nine riflemen, it can keep up with tanks and take infantry across open ground which would be suicidal in foot attack. It also enables friendly artillery, firing ahead of infantry, to keep shelling until the last moments since shell fragments also bounce off the M-59. In atomic warfare, where mobility under fire is the key to ground tactics, the M-59 lifesaver would be invaluable. It has been called a "mechanized atomic foxhole", its armour providing protection against radiation and heat flash and its 30-m.p.h. speed permitting quick dispersion.
I think it is a rather sad reflection on the Department of National Defence that Canada, the country which produced the armoured personnel carrier, should now be last in the field, and that we have to turn to the United States and the United Kingdom to discover what is being done along this line. But that is necessary for infantry tactics on the battlefield if our purpose is to save the lives of infantrymen. I submit that the lives of infantrymen have been sacrificed needlessly in two or three wars in which Canada has been engaged, and that fact is known to all. But Canada discovered a means of saving the lives of infantrymen in the last war and should adopt that means now for the protection of our men.

Again I say that the minister has neglected to deal adequately with this particular matter. I went to some length, when I spoke on this subject last May, to point out that we were failing to train the high command properly if we did not provide armoured formations within a brigade so that they could become accustomed to using armour, artillery and infantry in conjunction; and until we do provide armoured formations in adequate number we will not train the high command properly. From that we will suffer serious results because it is essential that those who are placed in command of armies know how to use properly all arms of the services. Unless we provide an armoured brigade, train it on a brigade level and provide it for the training of divisional and corps commanders, there will be little effective training of those who will attain high command in our Canadian army.
You see what we have done, Mr. Chairman. Earlier this afternoon the hon. member for Macleod was asking if we were getting a dollar's worth for a dollar expended in national defence. I have intimated people would be satisfied if that were the case. I think we cannot get a dollar's worth for a dollar expended because we are out of balance so far as the Canadian army is concerned. We are producing an army in the 1914-18 pattern, and conditions of warfare have changed and are changing very quickly since the development of atomic weapons. Those people who are in command in Europe over our NATO forces are asking for mobility and more mobility. In a newspaper not long ago one of our own distinguished generals commented upon and stressed the necessity for mobility of troops in the field. What are we doing about it? You are not very mobile on your flat feet. You have to have tracked armoured vehicles, tanks and armoured personnel carriers, if you are going to make your infantry forces mobile and if you are going to protect them. We are not, therefore, keeping up with the times and the responsibility rests with the Minister of National Defence.
I think it is a pretence to suggest that our brigade in Europe, fine as it may be as an infantry brigade-I think it is one of the finest because it has so many veterans of the second world war and Korea in its ranks- is an effective fighting machine against the type of attack which may be launched against that brigade by the Russians. You have only to recall how the Germans swept through Europe in 1940, with a very small mobile armoured force, to realize the truth of my remarks. The Germans were opposed at that time by infantry forces similar to our infantry forces.

Infantry forces of that nature are ineffective against powerful armoured formations. You have to have tanks and a preponderance of artillery if you are going to resist armour. We have committed our infantry brigade over in Europe to a very great hazard. I am surprised the Minister of National Defence does not recognize that and does not take effective steps to put the brigade in better condition to resist attack.
I shall conclude these remarks, Mr. Chairman, with a reference to the white paper. The white paper lists three objectives of our defence policy, namely defence against direct attack on Canada; implementation of undertakings for collective security, and the buildup of our organization for total war. In my opinion, the minister has fallen far short of achieving any of these objectives. The second one, in my opinion, should be rewritten and instead of saying, "implementation of undertakings for collective security," which is an odd and general phrase that might mean anything, I think we should say, the provision of fully equipped and highly trained forces and formations of armour, artillery and infantry suitable for modern mobile warfare in order to implement any undertakings by Canada for collective security.
I do not intend to detain the committee very long.
Hear, hear.

Some hon. members say, "hear, hear", that is a good way to extend debate. First of all, I want to make a reference to the remarks made by the hon. member for Wellington South. He made some rather caustic comments about the principles of socialism, and then went on to say there was a good deal of happiness found in the army. That statement is quite correct, and I agree with it. Why is there a great deal of happiness found in the army? It is because of the sense of security provided by an assured income, permanent employment, good housing, clothing always provided and three good meals a day for certain. I must admit that so far as Canada is concerned, these things are provided in good quantity and quality. All the socialist wants to do is to provide the same sense of security to the whole population in Canada which many do not enjoy now.
The same is true of being in jail.

Mr. Chairman, is the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek suggesting that being in the army is like being in jail? I am amazed. How is that condition
Supply-National Defence obtained? It is the result of government organization and government action. From time to time we in this group are asking the same things for those people who do not enjoy similar security.
Strangely enough, I disagree with the hon. member's comments in one respect, but I support them wholeheartedly in another. The hon. member suggested we could use some of the members of the permanent forces for construction purposes, the building of roads and bridges. Speakers at a recent conference in Canada concerning our renewable natural resources suggested these men could be used for fire-fighting purposes. Here we are in Canada lagging in the building of the trans-Canada highway, lagging in the building of roads and bridges everywhere, and we have this great force of excellent men available who, no doubt under present conditions, will find themselves in the army for a number of years. I believe the hon. member's suggestion is an excellent one, and I support it.
These men would gain experience from useful employment that would be of great advantage to this country. I have had letters from men in the forces who tell me they get tired of digging a hole and filling it in again, of building a bridge and pulling it down, and of doing all those things that are necessary to train engineers, and pioneers over and over again. I feel the hon. member made a very good suggestion. We could perhaps rotate a proportion of our _armed forces and use them in construction of trans-Canada and other highways that are so necessary at the present time. At the same time they would be gaining experience that they have to gain in other less useful ways.
I was very pleased with the minister's reply to my brief comments in the debate when the estimates were before the committee on a previous occasion. He told the house there were no members of the defence forces who served in the second world war, and who committed offences, that were still in jail. I was very glad to hear that indeed. I wish to make another brief appeal with respect to officers and other ranks who were dismissed from the forces and who lost permanent pension rights and other rights as a result of military offences which, in some cases, would not be serious offences in civil life. In my opinion these men should receive at least equal consideration to those in the R.C.M.P. I will quote from a Canadian Press

Supply-National Defence dispatch in this respect. The dispatch is headed "Misconduct Mounties given Pension Break". It reads:
Seven members of the RCMP discharged since 1949 for inefficiency or misconduct will have their pensions restored in part under legislation introduced in Commons.
The bill changes an RCMP pension plan, in effect since 1949, to allow a partial pension to be paid to members of the force discharged for inefficiency or misconduct.
Justice Minister Garson informed the house that the measure will be made retroactive to cover seven members discharged for those reasons in the last five years.
He said the change is being made to put insurance plans in line with the former pension plan under which those discharged for inefficiency or misconduct were eligible for half-pension until the age of sixty-five and a two-thirds pension after that.
I feel that if the Minister of Justice can give former R.C.M.P. personnel a break in that respect our defence minister should give those men who are suffering from their misdemeanours under military law a break. Therefore I appeal for a reconsideration of their cases.
I want to mention another little matter that rather intrigued me. I am speaking as a sort of backwoodsman without any knowledge of the details of present military life. I was interested in a press dispatch in the Ottawa Citizen of June 16, 1954, headed "Not Permitted to take Salute". Then, it goes on to say:
The dispute centres around a plan that the mayor would take the salute of the Cameron Highlanders regiment in a ceremony at city hall square on July 1.
I want it to be understood that I am not taking the mayor's part or anything of that sort, but in my opinion there is a principle involved here.
The army has advised that the mayor cannot take the salute-that this honour is reserved to the Queen, her official representatives, the Minister of National Defence and senior army officials.
I did not know this privilege was so limited, because I have seen mayors take the salute before. Senator McGeer while mayor of Vancouver took the salute on one occasion in the city of Nelson from the armed forces present. My question is this: Upon what regulation is this ruling based? When the minister is replying I would like him to answer this question: Does this ruling preclude the Prime Minister of Canada or the premier of a province from taking the salute from a regiment? I cannot understand in a democratic country why the Prime Minister or a premier of a province would be denied taking the salute from a regiment of our armed forces, because of regulations. I get the very strong suspicion that this is a musty old tradition that has come down from the Victorian period, and
[Mr. Herridge.j

that some obscure and unknown official of the armed forces has dug it up from the dusty files to thwart the wishes of the present mayor of Ottawa.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Some people would like to give her a 21-gun salute.

As a matter of fact, I may not leave Ottawa until midnight July 1, because I want to see the ceremony.
I come now to my last point. We in Canada look upon our defence forces as a citizens army, whether these citizens are in the permanent force or the reserve army. At this point I wish to pay tribute to the members of the reserve army who give their evenings and summer holidays over to training in the reserve force. I think they should receive every encouragement. I know the two or three units in my district struggle along under considerable difficulty and, particularly in Nelson, with very little accommodation and equipment. But these few men at least carry on a very useful work, and I should be very pleased to hear what is going to be done in the future to improve the position of the reserve army, and support their efforts.
Canadian citizens who fought in the first and second world wars did so for the defence of this country, because they had a general understanding of and respect for democratic principles and democratic ideals-and that means a great deal in any army. They had faith and belief in certain principles, which gave weight to their blows against the enemy. And, because of that strength, engendered by such principles, a totalitarian dictatorship was defeated.
I wish to see our army maintained as a citizen army and I would hope it will continue to be composed of people who believe in democratic principles and in democratic ideals, and who are willing to defend this country because they believe in those ideals. I believe the hon. member for Macleod made reference to the same subject, that our army should be composed of persons of that kind.
However, I have been a little bit disturbed by reports I have received, and to which I am rather inclined to give some attention.
I would ask the minister three questions which I trust he will answer when he replies in this debate. Fi-rst, are German immigrants being brought into Canada who served in the armed forces of the Third Reich, who are not citizens of Canada, but who are being enlisted in the armed forces of this country? If so, in what numbers?
They are being enlisted now. And it is a good thing they are; they are good fighters.
The hon. member can make his speech later.
I am informing you.
I wish to say this, that if I depended upon the hon. member for Simeoe North for my information, I would be misinformed very often.
You would be more accurate than you are now; you would not make as many mistakes.

My second question is this: If so, were any of these men who have been enlisted in the armed forces of Canada awarded the iron cross or other decorations, personally, by Hitler, because of aggressive action against the British or Canadian troops?
My third question is this: Have any of these men asked permission of their commanding officers to wear these decorations on Canadian uniforms? That is all I have to say at the moment. I believe the hon. member for Simeoe North is ready to speak.

Yes, I am. I am not sure whether the Minister of National Defence got this preferred position near the closing hours of the session so that it would be run through in as few hours as possible. But in my opinion this is one department that should have had a full-scale discussion. It is one department of government that is spending many more millions of dollars than any other department.
One of the motives which prompted me to stand as a candidate for parliament was that I enlisted in the first war, and at the time I enlisted I had great faith in the government. I thought: Well, we have a good minister of national defence in Sam Hughes. He has all the information available from that great British war machine. But it was not very long before I realized the truth of the situation.
The British government had been forced into war by the kaiser, and there was never any group of people more unprepared to meet that war than the people of the British Empire. That war was not necessary; it was absolutely unnecessary. But we always sat back and said: Well, we will not believe the facts we see; we will not believe the kaiser has built an army so large that the only thing he can do is to start a war.
No, we were not prepared. Men were sent overseas with insufficient ammunition in their pouches to defend themselves. I served one whole winter, personally, in the trenches as second in command of a company. There was only our company commander, with myself, in those trenches during the entire
Supply-National Defence winter on our piece of front line. In March seven or eight officers came to reinforce the company.
Many situations are similar today. At the time of the last war I talked to the manager of the Hotchkiss company of France. This man was an Englishman. When France was taken by the Germans he paid a visit to Canada, and during that visit came to my home. I said to him, "Well, the French capitulated." Bear in mind that this chap was an Englishman. He said to me, "I do not blame them, at all."
Let us be frank about it. At that time the great braintrusters in England said to the French, "You build the Maginot line and you can hold the Germans there. We will be prepared to stop any German rush on the beaches."
What was the result of the preparations for defence? Well, the Germans came down through Holland and Belgium. They circled around the Maginot line and came in behind it on the beaches. This man was one who had aided Lloyd George tremendously in the first war in the production of munitions. He was not just some man who was shooting off his mouth concerning something he knew nothing about. This man just escaped from France with his life when the Germans came in. He told me there were only about 27 anti-aircraft guns in the whole of the British Isles when war broke out-or maybe it was 28.
Knowing these things to be true, and knowing from personal experience that we have never been prepared, I have always felt that as members of parliament, irrespective of politics, we should come to Ottawa and offer our little bit, for what it may be worth, as the representatives of the people in the constituencies of Canada. We should do this irrespective of politics, so that, with an open mind, the minister would be able to accept advice, even from opposition members, if it was worth while. Members of the Liberal party should realize what they owe to their constituents, not just during a war but before it starts, to make sure of one thing-that Canada is prepared, so far as she can go.
Do not bother so much about what the other fellow is doing. The Americans may be adequately prepared; the people of England may be, or they may not be. We have an obligation here in Canada, as a group of people sent to Ottawa, to look after the rights of the people and to prepare ourselves. We can aid very little when the minister hides behind the iron curtain as far as information regarding our armed forces is concerned. We as

Supply-National Defence members of parliament duly elected from every section of this country are big enough and ugly enough to take the cold facts whether we are adequately prepared according to conditions in the world today. We are either prepared or we are not prepared. We can take it on the end of the nose if we need greater taxation, greater expansion, greater sacrifices now before the war starts rather than months after it starts.
Down in Barrie we have an armoury that was built in 1910. It is not big enough for sea cadets or the flying corps cadets to train one-tenth as properly as they should train, to say nothing of men in the militia. We find this government building-what they call armouries in certain communities. In my opinion they are glorified bar rooms for leading citizens to consume liquor in for hours at a stretch.
Has the hon. gentleman any personal experience?

Yes, I have, and enjoyed it. I am not a hypocrite like some people I know but it was not built intentionally for my enjoyment or for the enjoyment of anybody else. It was built to train troops, or else take the name "armoury" away from it. Why do we not get down to facts? Why try to satisfy a handful of people in the militia in a small community by putting up a luxury building with beautiful furnishings, lovely drapes and a bar, and have the members of that particular section of the militia go out and solicit people to come in and have a drink of liquor in those places? They are now competing against the veterans' beer parlours. These are the facts. They are known to everybody. I have no objection to drinking liquor, not at all. I have drunk it on every occasion all my life, and I will continue to do so, if that is any answer to you.
Be careful.

That has nothing to do with the question of preparedness. We are not prepared in this country. If the minister is properly prepared for conditions which might arise he should be the proudest man in the Dominion of Canada, and he should come out and say, This is what we have; we defy any enemy. This is what we have in this country. We have adequate places in which to train people; we have adequate camps. We have no trouble with recruiting; we are proud of our army and the people of Canada are proud of the army. Young men are falling over themselves to belong to a group of Canadians of whom they should be justly


proud. Young men wearing the Queen's uniform have every right to stick their chests out and hold their heads high, and say: We are members of the armed forces.
We should have no difficulty with recruiting; but as long as the minister is going to permit senior officers to take an emblem off the caps of a certain branch of the forces- the hon. member from Newfoundland throws his head back, guffaws and laughs. That is symbolic of his party, Mr. Chairman. That is exactly what the minister has permitted in the air force. When the minister laughs about the removal of the crown from the caps, I say it is not helpful to this country. The crown is a symbol, and thank God most of the men and women of the country are very proud of it. But there are some who throw their heads back and grin when the crown is mentioned.
What about the time when your friends took it off the motor licence plate?
Two wrongs never made a right. You are now talking about a piece of tin plate on the back of a motor car. That has no comparison with Her Majesty's forces in the Royal Canadian Air Force of Canada.
A very poor answer.

Don't bring the crown on the cap badges down to the level of a licence on an automobile. That is about the size of your mentality. I ask the minister whether he has had sufficient time to obliterate the slur which was cast on Her Majesty the Queen of this empire by the abolition of that crown without her consent? This matter was brought up on a previous occasion and the minister said he would make a statement. I was interrupted by the Speaker of the house when I mentioned it' before and I was not permitted on that occasion to speak regarding the removal of that cap badge. Is it permanently removed? Was permission granted? If so, was permission granted by Her Majesty the Queen? What good reason can the minister give for taking off the crown? He should give a reason for taking "Rule, Britannia", the theme of the navy, out of the navy. It is just one thing after another, tearing down the traditions of the British Empire and everything that we have to fight for. The regiments of this country have become famous because they are affiliated with the famous British regiments who defended this empire before a Canadian soldier ever stood up in the Dominion of Canada. Go out to the Toronto exhibition,

at Fort York, and take a look at the little cemetery there, forty feet by forty feet, and read the names of the men in the regiments who defended muddy York in 1812. Every single one is a British regiment.
We have men who joined regiments and fought in the South African war, the first big war, and in the second war, who were proud to wear the kilt, who were proud to wear the riflemen's uniform when there was tradition behind them. You take tradition out of the army and you have no army. You have a machine which cannot stand up against enthusiasm and esprit de corps. I say this to the minister. It is not too late to give back to these men the crown, the symbol of the Queen of this empire. Put it back on the cap badges. If it was too heavy for some of the fragile young women to wear in the service, what are we running, a military establishment, a flying corps or what?
I hold in my hand a big file of protests. There are letters and telegrams from all over Canada protesting the action of a senior officer of the R.C.A.F. in taking the crown off the cap badges of our air force. We are the only air force in the commonwealth that took the crown off. I think it is despicable, but it is in keeping with many actions of the minister in obliterating the things that we hold dear, the tradition of the great British Isles and the regiments that we have been affiliated with and which built up the great Canadian armies of the past, that have fought for these things and that have stood for this type of character that we have in Canada. Do not keep on taking these traditions away from them. Give them back if you possibly can.

If there is no further general debate I should like to pay hon. members opposite the courtesy of a reply. With regard to what the hon. member for Simcoe North said, I have nothing to add to what was said in the house with regard to the badge on some of the caps of the R.C.A.F. This matter was explained at that time. I have nothing to add to it. If it becomes desirable in the view of the services and of the department to make a change, then the change will be made and announced in due course.
It is of course ridiculous to say that any slur was cast on the Queen. I would like to add this. I have not interfered in any way with the traditions of the armed forces, and have done everything possible during the time that I have had to do with them to build up in them a feeling of affection for
Supply-National Defence and pride in their own country. It may be recalled that the ships of the Royal Canadian Navy carried maple leaves on their funnels during the war. Soon after I came into office I found that when the ships were being repainted the maple leaf was being painted out. As soon as I found that out I told them to paint the maple leaf back on and keep it on, and that has since happened.
I found officers and men in certain components of the armed forces no longer wearing the name of the country on their shoulders. When I found this out I directed that all officers and men of the services were always to wear "Canada" or "Canadian" either on their shoulders or shoulder badges if the name was not clearly written on some other insignia they were wearing. I can add that they are just as proud of their country as I hope all hon. members are. They have shown their devotion to their Queen and country by their service at home and abroad. They also showed that in the part they took and took magnificently in the reception of the Queen, then Princess, during the royal tour of Canada, and in the splendid ceremonies of the coronation abroad and at home they were second to none in their loyalty to the Queen and in their pride in their country.
No one mentioned loyalty to the Queen. I was talking about cap badges.

Now, Mr. Chairman, the Leader of the Opposition referred to a matter that I will certainly not deal with at this time beyond saying that the answer to the question he raised can be found at page 893 of Hansard for January 12, 1953, where it will be found that the position is precisely as it is stated to be.
Other hon. members requested information and I repeat what I have said before on many occasions, namely that I do not think any parliament in the British commonwealth has ever had so much information about defence in all its aspects as this parliament has had over the past several years. This charge today was pinned on a refusal to table two reports, one of which was referred to as the Hendry report and the other a report on the reserve army. It was suggested that there was nothing secret in these reports. Whether or not there is anything secret in these reports can really only be ascertained by those who have seen them. But the point here is not whether there is anything secret in the reports but whether the reports were designed for the information of the officers of the armed services, the officials of the department, or members of the government
6384	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence in order that they might decide, on the basis of that information and advice, what action they should take.
It is a fundamental rule of our parliamentary democracy, as practised at Westminster and here right down through the years, that members of the government are entitled to have frank and full information from those reporting to them, and they are entitled to ask whom they want for advice. They are entitled to treat that advice as confidential for two reasons. There is no reason why they should disclose the basis of their action. The second reason is that the people who give them that advice are entitled to have its source treated as confidential because they are not here to speak for themselves. On the basis of that advice the government makes its decision, announces it to parliament, and is responsible to parliament for that action, the policy adopted, and answers for any of the civil servants or officers involved. That is our system and in order to enable it to work it seems to me it is essential that members of the government, like members of the armed forces and officials in government departments, should be able to get advice, information, and assistance on a confidential basis. The thing is just as simple as that.
Now, sir, there are a few other points some of which I think might more properly be dealt with as we come to the details of the estimates, but I would like to refer here to the remarks made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre with regard to armour. As he pointed out, this is a favourite subject of his. He has brought it forward on at least three occasions and he does not appear to be satisfied with the answers I have given. I do not need to tell him that I do not pretend to be an expert . in armour. In the first world war, in which I took a small part for a short time, I saw some tanks in the distance and they were mostly bogged down and stayed bogged down. That was my only personal experience of that operation. But in this we must take the advice of responsible officers of the department who have the advantage of conferring with the officers of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, and we must work out with our allies in that organization the type of balanced force which will enable our country to make its particular contribution in the most economical and effective way it can and at the place where it is most needed. The hon. member disclaimed knowledge of there being rotation of armoured regiments in Europe and he said that we required an armoured brigade group. But that makes it just about three times as impossible. An


armoured brigade group is a difficult thing far us to maintain abroad in peacetime. It is difficult because you have to have tanks in Germany; you have to service them in England; and then you require very nearly the equivalent number of tanks in Canada where almost inevitably they will never be used in war but must be available for training purposes. It is also difficult because of the very much larger number of men who would be involved, and of course there would be an impossible mathematical problem involved in rotation. I will just say a word about each of these.
With regard to the number of men, we are talking here not of a brigade, as I understand they were organized during the second world war, but of a brigade group, that is, something which might operate in a fairly independent way and which would have to have all the supporting services that an infantry brigade group has at the present time. Then it would have to have special services appropriate to the maintenance of tanks, as well as regiments of tanks. The number of men, I am told, who would be involved in such a formation in Europe would be 6,899, and the number of men involved in an infantry brigade group is 5,933. Now, the expenses to which the hon. member referred were not the cost of maintaining either an infantry brigade group or an armoured brigade group in Europe for a year. That was the one-time cost of equipping it and the cost of maintaining it for a year.
In the case of an independent armoured brigade group the one-time cost was $120,800,000 and the cost of an infantry brigade was $45,525,000, whereas the estimated annual recurring cost of an armoured brigade was $39,600,000 and an infantry brigade $29,762,000, so that the differential is rather less than the $100,000,000 to which I referred. Now let me state the reason why it is mathematically impossible for us to do what is suggested with an army of about the size of the present one. At the present time, we have to have three infantry battalions in Korea. They are rotated as units each year. We have to have three infantry battalions as part of the mobile striking force, and that operation has to be carried on continuously. Then we have three infantry battalions overseas in Germany as part of the first infantry brigade there. So that in those formations, in the first Canadian infantry brigade in Korea we have three battalions, three in the mobile striking force and three overseas in Germany. That is nine battalions of infantry to carry out rotation annually for units to Korea and once every two years for units to Germany, and to do

this on a basis which ensures that in between service abroad the unit will have at least eighteen months in Canada, requires that we have six more infantry battalions, or a total of fifteen infantry battalions. Also that number of battalions will enable us, at the end of the Korean war, to constitute an infantry division at full strength with some reinforcements in addition to the mobile striking force. However, if we put into Europe an armoured brigade group of three regiments, then we cannot interchange those regiments with infantry regiments. I would say you would have to have at least five armoured regiments in Canada to do the job. That would mean seven or eight armoured regiments and three airborne infantry battalions in the mobile striking force which would not be interchangeable with the regiments in Germany. Then you would have to have four and a half or five infantry battalions to rotate with the infantry battalions in Korea. In other words, you would require a larger number of major formations; you would not have the same interchangeability and you would have this greatly increased expenditure.
There is another reason and that is, of course, that in the event of a war I think everyone would contemplate that we would be expected to have at least the equivalent of a division in Europe in D-plus the time of transportation. In order to supply the tanks of the infantry division in D-plus the time of transportation we must have the tanks already in Europe. We are building up mobilization stores of heavy equipment for that purpose there. This will bring home to hon. members just how complex is this business of building up forces in peacetime, with the enormous quantities of expensive and heavy equipment required, on another continent 3,000 miles away. No other country I know of feels it necessary to build up mobilization stores to meet the challenge of an emergency in a country abroad.
The hon. member for Kootenay West referred to Germans enlisting in the armed forces of Canada. We have taken into the armed forces a very small number of German immigrants. Each case is considered on its own merits. It is only done on the specific personal permission of the chief of staff of the service concerned. There is just as much screening as possible. I know of none of them having an iron cross for any reason.
Will the minister look into the matter?

Yes. If such a man were foolish enough to ask an officer if he might wear the iron cross, I think the officer would
Supply-National Defence speedily tell him "No", in extremely emphatic terms. It is almost unthinkable that anyone should have the silliness to ask the question.
I think I have covered most of the points raised by hon. members. If there are any that I have not covered, I shall be only too happy to be reminded now or else I can deal with them when the details are before us for consideration.
There was one series of observations made, I think, by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin when the defence estimates were before us on May 20 and 21. He said he had been told that the troops in Korea had been furnished with quonset huts shortly in advance of and probably on account of the Prime Minister's visit and that the broadcasting station had been out of order and was only put into order before the Prime Minister's visit. May I say that the quonset huts referred to were ordered for the whole commonwealth division about eight months before the Prime Minister's visit and the last huts were delivered some months before his visit. There is nothing in that. The radio station was brought into operation about Christmas, 1953. I am informed that it has been out of operation for less than an hour and this was for technical reasons but that otherwise it has been in operation and that there is nothing the matter with it.
I also want to assure the hon. member for Kootenay West that there is nothing in the rather amusing story he told about coffee on the minister's pants. There is also nothing in the account he appears to have got that a general notice or order was posted with regard to the carriage of coffee. Some person thought it was desirable to cut down this kind of transportation around the building- and I believe it is desirable-and he posted this up for his own staff.
I hope there is nothing in the remarks of the hon. member for Brandon to the effect that some officer was ticked off for talking to a member of the opposition. I have never heard of such a thing. I cannot imagine any officer acting this way. I do not know of any more delightful thing than to talk to members of the opposition. I hope the officers of the armed forces talk to them still more, so that thereby they would be able to make most interesting and valuable contributions to our debates and would feel that our officers were good at their jobs.

I should like to ask the minister this question. Is it necessary to obtain Her Majesty's consent to the wearing of the crown by any regiment, before the crown can at any time be put on any part of the uniform?

Supply-National Defence
That has been the case for some years past, but I understand it was not always the case.
I have a supplementary question. When the crown is once up, is it necessary to ask Her Majesty's permission to take the crown down?
Certainly not.
I should like to ask the minister one question-

I should perhaps make the situation clear to the hon. member because I know he is keenly interested in it. The reason why permission is asked of Her Majesty for the use of the crown is so that the sovereign and those personally advising her may have complete control over the conditions in which the crown is used.
That is what I would think.

For instance, over the size and the shape of the crown. For example, since the present Queen became queen there has been a direction that the crown used should be a different type of crown from the one used previously. That will be gradually replaced. But there is no suggestion, no order and no regulation to the effect that when you do not use the crown, you must ask her consent.
But when you use the crown and you have had that permission granted, the minister says her consent is not necessary-
That is right.
-and that the crown can be taken down by the wish of any senior officer in the armed forces.
The crown is not taken down. There was no crown taken down here. What was done was that a new badge was adopted without a crown for a certain limited use.
I call that "taking down".
The minister did not answer my question with relation to the regulation with respect to saluting. Do the regulations preclude the prime minister of Canada taking the salute from any regiment?

No. The regulations were revised quite substantially some years ago. They are the same in all commonwealth countries. They generally provide for a long list of persons being given military honours. There is a general catch-all for them, but mayors of municipalities are not included. I should make it plain that the mayor of Ottawa never complained to me or raised with me or anyone in the department the question of receiving the salute. What has obscured

the situation, I think, is that the arrangements for the ceremony to take place on July 1 provided that a unit of the Canadian reserve army would be present, that His Excellency the Governor General would be present, and that the unit would naturally give military honours to His Excellency the Governor General. It is completely unthinkable under military practice and tradition that either before or after the Governor General receives military honours the same unit on the same parade should give military honours to anyone else.
But the regulations would not prevent the Prime Minister receiving the salute?

Oh, no, but not on that same occasion. On the other hand, military honours are, generally speaking, given to people who have to do with military things, and of course to members of the royal family because they are members of the royal family. As a matter of courtesy the practice has grown up in recent years of prime ministers and similar people receiving military honours. That is a rather recent development that has come about in the last fifty or sixty years.
Who drafts the regulations?
They are passed by the governor in council.
For each country?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. In order to make for an orderly discussion, is it now the desire of the committee that I call the headings in the blue book?

May I take a minute to comment on the minister's statement and to say that I recognize the hopelessness of attempting to debate the question of an armoured corps with the minister. Our minds are certainly not at one with regard to the matter. I am not the least bit impressed with his advisers, and I regret that in the figures he has now placed on Hansard he has used the basis of an independent armoured brigade group which was not the subject I was talking about. I was talking about an armoured brigade, and naturally his figures are different from mine. Consequently he makes the picture appear much blacker, much more prohibitive in cost because he is talking about a different thing.
But, as I say, I recognize the hopelessness of continuing a discussion along these lines. I further regret that the minister has not dealt with the question of the maintenance build-up of the armoured corps in Canada and with the introduction of the armoured personnel carrier to save the lives of our infantry overseas.

I beg the hon. member's pardon. With respect to the armoured personnel carrier, I should tell him that we are by no means satisfied with the carriers so far developed in any country. With support from the British and United States armies, we are initiating a development program to see if we cannot develop a more satisfactory infantry carrier than has yet been devised, and that work is under way. I think the account in Life of what they have in the United States is rather glowing.
With regard to the other point, if the hon. member would not like us to have an armoured brigade group abroad then I assume he would be prepared to have Canada take the consequences and have the supporting services for our armour that he would propose to have abroad supplied for us by the British or American forces. I am sure they would not do it.

With respect to the minister saying that I would not wish to have an armoured brigade group overseas, may I say that I have not said anything of that nature whatsoever. But when for the purpose of argument I discuss an armoured brigade and give figures with respect to an armoured brigade I think the minister, if he is refuting my charges with regard to the number of men and the cost, should use a somewhat comparable formation and not an armoured brigade group.
That formation would be totally unacceptable to the Canadian government, the Canadian parliament and the Canadian people because it would not be a selfsupporting independent Canadian unit.

I should like to ask of the minister a question which I do not think comes properly under any particular item. I wish to raise the question of Canadian morale, and I should like the minister to follow my reasoning closely in order to see if it seems sound. If I have got the right idea concerning our preparations for war, we are arming with the ultimate purpose of meeting and beating communism. Is that correct? We are looking to an ultimate showdown with the communist conspiracy which rules Russia.

That is not our object. Our object is to try to avoid another war by showing the communists that they cannot win, and to maintain the strength of our economies during that period. That means a lot more than military preparedness. We look forward to the time when the communists may be persuaded by peaceful means to change their attitude so that we can live in the world together without the necessity of
Supply-National Defence having these armed camps on each side by which the communists are deterred from war through their fear that they will not win and through which we hope to achieve our desire for peace.

I agree utterly with the minister's general ideal, but while we have been looking forward to this idyllic situation he dreams of, we have lost something like 700 million people to communism. It seems to me the conclusion must be obvious that the Russians have no such idea as that of settling down to live with us on this planet. They have made declarations time and again that capitalism and communism cannot live together. Surely we are not stupid enough to be impossible of teaching in these matters!
If that is the case, then let me ask one other question. I think the minister would agree that, in our hope, which is perfectly righteous and with which I completely agree, that ultimately we can bring Russia to reason, we should be preparing, in case of need, to do everything in our power to defeat Russia. That is correct, is it not? The minister is aiming at that purpose. If we have to fight, he intends that we shall be able to meet the foe and defeat him. I think the minister has no reservations to make on that statement.
If this is the case, everything that takes place in Canada which tends to weaken the Canadian morale to fight communism, is working diametrically against the purpose of the minister. Would that be correct? I assume the minister's omission to reply is tantamount to acquiescence in what I say. Has the minister given thought and study, as part of the over-all problem of making ready this nation to meet and defeat the communist conspiracy, to what is going on in Canada tending to weaken the Canadian morale to fight against communism? Has he taken any measures?
To clarify, may I illustrate? In dealing with the C.B.C. the other day I referred to Bill Boss. Bill Boss has been writing articles which have appeared in so many of the newspapers of Canada that I am tempted to suppose they have appeared in all of them. Almost every one of these articles has tended to make people believe that communism was not so bad after all, and that possibly it just was not worth while taking serious measures to get ready to fight communism. Has the minister given any attention to articles like those written by Bill Boss?

Certainly in my quality as a member of the government, a citizen of Canada and a member of parliament I give consideration to all such things. As Minister of National Defence, however, that does not

I would suggest to the members of the committee that, in accordance with the understanding we have had and now that the hon. member has, I think, made his point, we should go ahead with consideration of the main headings of the estimates.

That would be fine, but there are two or three other matters that have to be taken up, too. I suggested something the other night upon which I still have not had an opportunity of elaborating, and upon which I intend to elaborate to the bitter end. It is that the C.B.C. is indoctrinating people in Canada with communism, and because of that-

speechtext: Order. May I point out to the hon. member that we are now discussing the estimates of the Minister of National Defence, and he has nothing whatever to do with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. If the hon. member wishes to continue, I would ask him to direct his remarks specifically to the Department of National Defence.

What I am having to say, Mr. Chairman, is specifically connected with defence in Canada, whether or not it has to do with the Department of National Defence. No one with any sense of reality will question that it has to do with the defence of Canada; that must be quite obvious.
I do not propose to follow this matter to any great extent today, but I do suggest that unless the minister, somehow or other, is, by the cabinet, given some means whereby he can co-ordinate the efforts of all the departments of government in the general direction of total preparation for total war against the communist conspiracy, then his efforts are being defeated. Now, that must be serious. If we are spending $2 billion per year of the taxpayers' money that we can ill afford, if we are spending that to prepare to defeat the enemy, and then we are allowing our efforts to be neutralized through the back door and through the basement windows, and a half dozen other means, where is the consistency in our procedure?
I would say with all deference, Mr. Chairman, that certainly we must look upon this whole matter of preparedness as a whole matter. We have the Department of Defence Production, and certainly that enters directly into the general over-all preparedness of Canada; certainly our finance department is working in that direction and many other departments must be co-operating. I just wanted to know whether the minister was looking into this communist propaganda matter at all.


May I suggest to him, in all seriousness, that there has been no more steady supporter of the Minister of National Defence than I. He knows that. Certainly, no member of the opposition has stood more earnestly behind him than I have. I say to him that I believe he means business, that he really intends to defeat the enemy if he has to. May I, as one of the most sympathetic of all opposition members, tell the minister he had better look to all these matters, such as that of indoctrinating the Canadian people with communism, and he should see that something adequate is done to offset the stream of communist propaganda that is pouring into this nation from four or five different sources. Otherwise, we are just wasting our time in preparing an army.
All we have to do is take one simple illustration. We had this year a proposal-though it was not, I grant, seriously brought down by the dominion government-implying quite definitely that we should recognize red China. It was fairly well understood. Now anyone knows that recognition of red China would be taken as a definite step forward by Russia. Russia knows that, whether or not we do. Every one of such little steps plays an important part in the over-all picture. I believe I have made quite clear what my meaning is. I hope I do not have to raise this matter again, but if I have to do so, I certainly will.

The hon. member did ask me about this when we were discussing the estimates on May 20 and May 21 and I prepared an answer for him which I omitted to give just a few minutes ago.
