speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall we take departmental administration, as the item is found on page 287 setting out the details?
Departmental administration.

It is not our proposal to carry out a long series of unrelated questions on these various items under the different headings which you will call. You will recall that the Leader of the Opposition pointed out this morning that in the past we had not achieved much success in getting information by that procedure, nor had we earlier in this session, for the same reason, asked that a committee be set up under defence expenditures. There will be some questions which we will feel are pertinent, and about which we must ask for further information.
Under this first heading of departmental administration I note there is an increase of $550,000 for civilian personnel. When we recall that this is at the end of a three-year program during which there has been a build-up of defence services going on, one might at least have expected a levelling off of expenditures in other than what might be termed the actual fighting services. I am surprised to see that there is this increase in expenditure for civilian personnel. Nor can it be passed off by the suggestion that it is due entirely to the introduction of the five-day week. I noticed that there was an increase from 277 to 362 civilian clerks, and it is quite obvious that increase far exceeds the number which would be necessary to compensate for the introduction of the five-day week.
I noticed that the second item following the item covering the salary of the deputy minister covers a special adviser to the Department of National Defence. I imagine that is the special adviser on civilian personnel. Quite obviously he is imbued with the idea of increasing the number of civilian personnel which are included in the department. Then we have been told several times that the peak has been reached in so far as defence construction is concerned.
I am surprised to find that there is for the first time a real estate appraiser being appointed for the Department of National Defence. Could the minister enlighten us as to why it is so necessary to increase the strength of civilian personnel there? Then, again, I notice an increase in accountants from 14 to 31. I am referring to civilian accountants. We do recall that there was some criticism a few months ago of the accounting system in the army, when it was disclosed that there were no less than eight different accounting systems. One can understand that there must necessarily be some
Supply-National Defence difference in the system in the various services, and even in the arms of those services. But is this an attempt to straighten out the accounting system by doubling the number of accountants this year?

Answering the first question put by the hon. member, the adviser on civilian personnel ceased to be associated with the department on March 31, 1954. In any event he had nothing to do with the establishment specifically, and certainly was in no sense an empire builder.
Then why do you need the item for $13,500, if he is going to cease his duties?
He came in after the book was published last year and went out after it was published this year.
So you do not need the money?

That is correct. But as the hon. member knows, these details, after all, make up a total approximating two billions of dollars, and they are put here for the convenience of hon. members.
Then, with regard to the increase in staff: the number of civilian staff proposed to be increased amounts to 49, of which 10 are for the staff of the associate minister, formerly paid by the Department of Justice; 2 are for the deputy minister's branch. These are for new positions in the United Kingdom on account of our increasing activities there; 34 are in the directorate of civilian personnel, and 3 in the chief auditor's branch. The total is 49, representing an increase of $136,210. Then $200,000 is provided for the increase in civil service salary rates.
What about the real estate appraiser? Can we dispense with him, too?
No.
I notice that the salary is $7,200.
This is a reclassification. The same man is doing the same work under a reclassification.
Has there been any revision in the accounting system which would justify doubling the number of accountants?
Yes, the number of accountants on the chief auditor's staff is being increased. That has been sought for some three years, and it is in order to have a more effective check.

Mr. Chairman, as I have when other estimates were introduced, I want to protest on this occasion about the
6390	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence way in which these estimates are presented to us. I have never been able to find out whether it is the responsibility of this department or that of the Department of National Revenue for the way in which these estimates are presented to us.
Let me give an illustration. We have here for the Department of National Defence 36 pages of details. Something more than 30 pages of these are concerned with details pertaining to civil employees. We are told exactly how many charwomen are employed in the three services, and what pay they receive. We are told how many office boys are employed, and the pay they receive. We are told how many messengers are employed and how many typists, and whether they are of grade 1, grade 2 or grade 3, and their pay.
For the army, for instance, we have 8 pages devoted to an itemized statement of civilian employees, and we are told that the total civil salaries and wages enumerated on those 8 pages amount to $40 million. Then the next item which deals with pay and allowances of the army amounts to $128 million, and it is dismissed with only three words. In other words, for an expenditure of $128 million there are only three words of explanation, but there are 8 pages of details for expenditures of $40 million.
I find that all the major items are detailed in the same way. For instance, the amount for clothing and personal equipment comes to over $12 million.
So far as the air force is concerned, 5 pages are devoted to enumerating expenditures on civil salaries amounting to $31 million, but there are only three words for an expenditure on pay and allowances amounting to $120 million. There are about five words for an expenditure of $107 million for the construction of buildings and works, and only three words for an expenditure of $305 million for aircraft and engines.
And so on, all down the line. One expenditure of $30 million is given only one word-"ships". I do not know how these estimates originated, or what purpose is served in giving us all this detail about civilian employees, right down to the last charwoman, and then disposing of the spending of hundreds of millions of dollars for construction, shipbuilding, aircraft, pay and allowances without any detail whatsoever, with the exception of two or three words.
I suggest someone could give some consideration to giving us estimates in a form in which they would be more useful and beneficial to members of the House of Commons than they are in their present form.


Then, I have one other matter I wish to bring to the minister's attention-and there will be others when we reach other items. I refer to the regulations formulated by somebody in the defence department with reference to the deduction of income tax from the pay of men and women in the forces. The administration of the income tax legislation rests with the Department of National Revenue, but that department says the regulations were drawn up by and presented to it by the Department of National Defence.
The regulations were designed for the convenience of collecting income tax from members of the forces. If a man remains in the forces, and as long as he remains in the forces, the regulations seem to work very satisfactorily. My complaint is that if a man is discharged from the forces at any time during the year he is given no statement of what his income was for that part of the year, nor of the taxes he paid for that part of the year. It is a closed book. He goes back into civilian life for a part of the year. He may get married in the latter part of the year. Were he a civilian he would be entitled to marriage status, but he is not permitted to take his whole year's income. That half or the part of his year's income that was earned in the services is a closed book. He starts over as though he were a different individual altogether. It seems to me as though it would be feasible for anyone who is discharged at any time during the year to be given, as is a private civilian, a statement of his earnings for that part of the year that he was in the forces, and a statement of his deductions so that he may incorporate them when he comes to make up his income tax for the year. And if he has paid more taxes than he should have paid, he would then be able to get a refund on the same basis as the civilian taxpayer. As it is, he cannot. I have given some study to this and I find that the only ones who profit by ihis practice are the higher paid officers. They may stand to profit by closing up that part of the year in which they were in the services, and starting over again as civilians. The ones who lose in every instance are the privates and the non-commissioned officers and those in the lower ranks. They are the only ones who stand to lose by this regulation. I suggest to the minister that consideration be given to finding ways and means whereby any man being discharged from the forces during the half of the year be given the statement of his income and the taxes paid for that part of the year so that if he desires to do so he can incorporate it and make a return for his entire year's earnings.

With respect to the first point raised by the hon. member, I understand that the Department of National Defence, until some years ago, did not give all the details of the civil administration staff as they do at the present time. They now do because it was desired to have this department use the same form of set-up in the estimates as do the other departments.
With regard to the second point in respect of the income tax statements and deductions, I understand that this department worked out the existing income tax regulations in conjunction with the Department of National Revenue, but I shall certainly be glad to look into the observation the hon. member has made. I am not aware that it is so. I am not aware that people who leave the services are not in a position to deal with their income statements and their income tax as in other cases of severance.

Included in the details we are looking at on page 287 is an item listed as "Director of bureau of current affairs." I presume it is that bureau that is responsible for the production of the very interesting series of booklets entitled "Current Affairs for the Canadian Forces." Particularly is that the case when the booklet deals with some other country or something entirely apart from Canada. On the whole, I would say a very useful bit of educational work is being done through this series of booklets. In fact, I find them useful to file away. They contain in very brief form very worth while and helpful information. I felt, however, that this one which I hold in my hand, which is volume 6, No. 3, February 1, 1954, did not quite measure up to the standards of other booklets in terms of objectivity. It is entitled "The Canadian Budget." I do not know who wrote it, but it is well set up, in the sense that it is broken down into four general aspects of the problem. The first chapter of the booklet is entitled "What is the budget and why is it important?" The second chapter is entitled "What do you get for your taxes?" The third chapter is entitled "How do you pay for federal services?" The fourth and final chapter is entitled "The budget before parliament."
The first three chapters measure up to the standards of objectivity pretty well,
Supply-National Defence except that I notice interesting comments as to the fairness of the present tax set-up in Canada, with which all hon. members in the House of Commons, and with which all Canadian citizens might not fully agree. However, I was prepared to forgive what I felt to be that lack of fairness, but as I got to chapter 4, which was entitled "The budget before parliament", I thought that this would be a chapter in which it would surely be admitted that the parliament of Canada is not a one-party affair. Thence, concluding his remarks, he summarized the tax changes and moved a series of resolutions to amend the various tax acts.
The general debate which followed this budget speech took place upon the minister's motion to go into committee.

Inspection services.

Mr. Chairman, this is one of the subheadings which looks extremely encouraging. The total expenditure is down by about $1,100,000 and the number of employees by about 250. It appears as though some real effort has been made in the inspection services to institute some form of economy, and it is one of the few special items in the entire defence department in which this appears to have been done. I hope that this indeed is the case and that the reduction is a real reduction and has not been accomplished merely by transferring all these people to other departments and thereby building up the expenses under another heading. I wonder if the minister would just comment on that because not only have the number of employees been reduced but all the major items, including professional and special services, travelling and removal expenses-in the latter case a reduction of $500,000-appear to have been cut down. Could the minister tell us whether this has been a real saving?

Yes, I can give the hon. member that assurance. The inspection services, which are now at their post-war peak load, handle contracts amounting to $1,092 million, and with a greater continuity of work and better training it has been possible for about the same number of men to do the job.

I am very glad to hear that, Mr. Chairman, and I would think that what has been accomplished in this particular branch might very well be accomplished in a lot of other administrative branches of national defence, and of the three services as well which are covered by the general

Royal Canadian Navy-Active force and general.

Mr. Chairman, during the debate on this topic in May I made some observations in connection with destroyer-escort vessels and the delay there had been in the production of the first of that type of vessel. I also dealt with the very considerable increase in the estimated cost. Speaking during 1951 the minister intimated that the cost of the vessels would be in the neighbourhood of $8 million. I understand that the cost of that vessel has now increased very materially and they have now become extremely expensive. On May 21 the minister indicated that plans were under way for the construction of a ship which would be very much less expensive, easier to build, and which would carry out the same sort of task as that for which the destroyer-escort vessels were to be built. I would like to know what percentage of the $93 million devoted to ships will be included for the completion of the 14 destroyer-escort vessels.
I wish to raise the point again as to whether it is really necessary to go ahead with the completion of these very expensive vessels. I know there is value at certain times in the desire of the armed services to try and get a superlative weapon, and here no doubt we are getting, or are laying plans to get the very best escort vessel in the world. But it is also the most expensive vessel of any of the navies of the world, and I wonder whether we should go on with this particular type if we can get a cheaper vessel which will do the same work.
As I explained on May 20, we are going to need many, many more escort vessels than was first appreciated owing to the increased range and manoeuvrability of the modem torpedo. Again, on May 20 I called to the attention of the minister the fact that the Royal Navy of the United Kingdom is now concentrating its efforts on helicopters for anti-submarine operation, and that these helicopters are being equipped with dipping asdic which will enable them to report on the presence of submarines. There was a short article recently dispatched from Portsmouth, England, in which it was stated that in the exercise which will be carried out this summer by the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, naval squadrons in the Mediterranean will operate with helicopters fitted

with these dipping asdics for the location of submerged hostile submarines. Of course, the great advantage of the helicopter is that it is not vulnerable to the submarine, whereas the escort vessel, no matter how expensive, is still vulnerable to submarine.
The same article goes on to tell about a new device for locating submarines which will be attached to Fairey Gannets. I think this device is called a sonobuoy and the Fairey Gannets are to replace the Avenger in the Royal Navy. My questions are these. How much of the money allocated for the construction of ships is still earmarked for the completion of the 14 destroyer-escort vessels? Can the minister give us any information regarding these newer and cheaper escort vessels, plans for which he said on May 21 were being considered?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member on several occasions has referred to our shipbuilding and conversion program and perhaps I should say a few words about it now. This program upon which we embarked in 1951 involved the construction of 35 major vessels of five different types, ranging from destroyer-escorts to gate vessels, and 41 auxiliary craft of eight different types. The conversion and rearmament program covered 40 major vessels of six different types, ranging from "Tribal" class destroyers to "Bangors". In a good many instances this conversion was a fairly thorough job. For example, the work on H.M.C.S. Algonquin, which was completed in March 1953, took about one and a quarter million shipfitting man-hours.
It is a major operation to convert these "Tribal" class destroyers into modern escort vessels. This is a sizeable program and must be viewed in relation to Canada's shipbuilding and refitting abilities at that time. Moreover the program had to be fitted into the operation of three ships in the Korean war in which eight destroyers engaged, and that involved a good deal of work and refitting and also a good deal of deployment of especially experienced personnel.
With regard to the new anti-submarine escort vessels, I should draw the attention of the committee again to the fact that our major role at sea in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization is anti-submarine work. That is recognized by us all. In fact, that function and coastal defence are our only roles. Our fleet is being built up, renovated, trained and manned for this purpose. Included in the submarine threat to which the Leader of the Opposition and others have referred is, of course, the fact that the Russians have a number of high-speed, long-range submarines. The threat is much greater today than 83276-4044
Supply-National Defence it was at any time in the first or second world wars; that is, the power of the enemy to employ high-speed submarines at long range, for long periods of time, is greater than it ever was in either war.
The number of long-range high-speed submarines the Soviet union has cannot be disclosed. It is still, I am glad to say, relatively small. Our anti-submarine escort vessel is designed as a ship-and it is one of the few ships designed for that purpose-to be able to hunt those high-speed submarines. On that account it must have the very expensive characteristics of great speed, lack of vibration, low noise level, non-magnetic features and the like as well as a very full set of electronic and electrical equipment. It is an extremely complicated and advanced ship. We designed it after co-operation and consultation with the British navy and with expert assistance from civilian firms.
Delays were caused by a number of factors, including the extremely complicated nature of the ship. In the second place, I think was the fact that we rather underestimated the amount of electronic and electrical work of a new character and the great demand that would be made on engineers in those professions, both in the navy and in civilian firms. Then too we had complicated problems of engineering, engine design and the like. However, it was announced that the first of these ships would be launched in 1951, and it was launched in 1951. The first of them to be completed should be completed next year, rather more than a year behind schedule. That is the target, but really the targets were the best guess we could make, in the light of lack of any experience in building a ship of this kind.
The hon. member has referred to the expense of the ship. It has cost a great deal more than was estimated. That fact is partly owing to the increased costs and partly owing to the fact that this equipment is so special and so new and that it takes a great deal of time to fit it into the ship. He spoke about the possibility of dropping the thing now. These are really our front line antisubmarine vessels. It would be an appalling waste to stop them now. We do not propose to build any more of them. These add greatly to our ability to discharge our role under SACLANT in convoying across the south Atlantic. They are counted in with our forces at least at a later stage and we propose to go through with the project. We do not know yet whether they will prove to be as successful as we expect but, from indications, we are very hopeful.
With regard to the construction of another anti-submarine ship of lesser cost, we are

Supply-National Defence proceeding with designs and specifications for such a ship and they ought to be completed next year. We have no intention of entering upon the construction of any such ships until the designs are thoroughly completed, the specifications are drawn up and everything possible done to ready the work. However, it is not yet decided whether or not to proceed with the construction of ships of this new class.
The hon. member referred to helicopters. We have a number of helicopters in the navy. We are forming a group of anti-submarine helicopters this summer-we hope to get delivery of the new helicopters probably in July-and it will form the first anti-submarine helicopter group.
As to sonobuoys, we have been working closely with the British and Americans on this matter. Our new anti-submarine aircraft, the S-2F, like the "Avenger", is designed to use the sonobuoy. I can tell the hon. member that just last week there was a conference here in Ottawa of the representatives of the Royal Navy, the United States navy and the Canadian navy, under our auspices, working on standardization in this field.

I am not critical of the policy or of the advice that the minister received in 1951. I admit quite frankly that these destroyer-escort vessels seemed to be the answer to the submarine menace in 1951. But since then we have advanced considerably. Not only have we advanced but, as I said before, the range and the manoeuvrability of the torpedoes are matters in which tremendous strides have also been made. While it was a sound policy to start on the building of these destroyer-escort vessels in those days, I now question the advisability of continuing with the construction of this particular type of vessel. We shall have the pilot model commissioned in the near future, but the other vessels are far from being completed. While it may be an appalling waste, as the minister said a few moments ago, to stop construction of this particular type of vessel, if the policy under which these vessels were constructed is now proved to be out of date, I suggest it is going to be an even greater and more appalling waste if we continue to develop all these fourteen vessels only to find, before they are launched -and certainly before they are commissioned-that, because of the advance in the trend in anti-submarine methods, they are obsolete. I know that these trends and changes take place. All too frequently the design of an aircraft, a ship or a gun proves to be out of date before that particular weapon is produced. I do not think anybody as to blame for that. But if it becomes clear
IMr. Claxton.]

that a type of vessel, aircraft or gun is not going to be able to play the role that it was intended it should play when it was first designed several years ago I think it is highly questionable whether it is advisable to continue with the construction of vessels of that type or other things which are not nearing completion at the present time.

I can assure the hon. member that his premise has no foundation whatever. These vessels are not out of date. They are not obsolete. They are not obsolescent except in the sense that every article of military equipment in the long run becomes obsolete. These are the last word. They are being equipped with the most modern and advanced electronic submarine detection devices. They are equipped with the most modern anti-submarine weapons and guns for anti-aircraft work as well as anti-submarine work. It is still fundamental in our concept of anti-submarine warfare that it should be fought by surface vessels and aircraft working together in teams. This is the leading element in this important part of the team. I should also add that both the British and the Americans are proceeding on the same assumption, that we need surface vessels for this operation and that it is a team operation.
They are also proceeding with the construction of ships along these lines. I do not think they are quite as far advanced and I do not think their ships will have quite the performance that ours have. That is our hope, but from the reports I have received we will have the leading vessel of this type at the time necessary to do the job.

My question involves the navy, army and air force, but perhaps the minister might answer it at this point. Some of my medical friends advise me that with a medical service provided for each of the three services during the war we had a good deal of overlapping. It was difficult to get one set-up at that time but it was their hope that in peacetime it might be possible to have one central organization to provide medical services for all the armed services. However, I note from the telephone directory that we have a medical director general for the navy, a director general of medical services for the army and a director of medical services for the air force. Would the minister indicate what progress is being made with a view to bringing these services together?
In a place like Halifax, for example, an excellent naval hospital was built during the war. It hardly seems necessary that similar

hospitals should be available for the army and the air force. With such a shortage of medical doctors in the country I would think we could have a better medical service with fewer personnel if these services were combined. My understanding is that that was achieved some time ago in connection with the dental services. Could the minister indicate the number of medical officers we now have for the navy, army and air force and also what progress is being made with respect to combining the services?

I have not the figures of the medical personnel gathered together for the three services, but I can give that to the hon. member later. As to the elimination of duplication, that has been our aim since the reorganization began in 1946 and 1947. At times we have considered amalgamating the three medical services but on further reconsideration it did not seem that any great economy would be effected, and that a great deal would be lost in the way of tradition, pride of service and the like. However, we have eliminated all duplication that has been found. For example, the naval hospital at H.M.C.S. Stadacona in Halifax looks after army and air force personnel. Similarly, the air force hospital at Rockcliffe looks after navy and army personnel. The army hospital at Winnipeg looks after personnel of all three services. In this triservice operation as between the services there is no paper work, payments backwards and forwards, forms and so on.
All three services have common medical practices. They have a single medical stores which is run by the army and a single dental service which is operated by the army. To further effect co-ordination we have recently set up a civilian committee called the armed forces medical council with Dr. J. A. Mac-Farlane, dean of the faculty of medicine of the University of Toronto, as chairman. He devotes a great deal of his time to this matter. The other members are Dr. G. E. Hall, president of Western Ontario University, Dr. Mathieu Samson of Quebec and Laval University and Dr. W. C. Mackenzie of Edmonton. They are a very outstanding group. They have made a report on this and other subjects and are now carrying it through with the full co-operation of the armed forces. Acting as full-time secretary of this council is Brigadier Crawford, who is deputy director general of medical services of the army.
One of the main objectives of this activity is to eliminate duplication. We now think we are getting to the place where we will have enough doctors for the three services. We are still short, but with the' recruits from
Supply-National Defence abroad, whom we are continuing to get from the British Isles, and others brought in through university plans we should be able in time to overtake this deficiency, although it is still considerable.

I should like to refer to the matter of seaward defences. We learn from the white paper that installations have been made at Halifax and also that plans are going ahead at St. John's, Newfoundland and Esquimalt. I believe that Sydney also comes under present plans. I am interested in the position of Saint John, New Brunswick, so far as seaward defence plans are concerned. We in Saint John have always felt that we were in a fairly strategic position. We have a drydock there, and it is the largest manufacturing city in the maritimes. It has also been understood that if any sort of concerted attack were to be made on the maritimes it would be natural that the enemy forces would come to Saint John. Perhaps they would cut off Nova Scotia at the neck of land between the two provinces. I am interested in hearing from the minister whether the plans of the first and second wars have been changed in the light of present warfare, or are we still to be included in these necessary defences on the Atlantic coast?

Seaward defences are being constructed at the places we consider to be the most vulnerable. I should point out that even if you have seaward defences fully constructed it takes some hours to put in the installation. The nets, booms and buoys deteriorate rapidly if left in sea water. The state of readiness in any event is relative. We are getting equipment. At Saint John equipment will be made available out of funds that are provided in these estimates, but it is not our present intention to make a permanent installation there for the reason I have stated. In addition, we have finished the program of construction of gate vessels.
May I ask the minister if he does not think that Saint" John is just as important as Sydney or St. John's, Newfoundland?
It is not nearly as exposed.

Will the minister comment on my remark that Saint John is in a vulnerable position due to the fact that an enemy could cut off Nova Scotia at the neck. That has always been our impression. There were submarines in the bay of Fundy in the last war, and I never heard of any actually creating any danger to Halifax harbour.

Sydney is designed for seaward defence now because that is where we have our whole reserve fleet in storage.

Supply-National Defence There are now something like twenty odd vessels. I am informed there will be a total of twenty-nine. It also will be our secondary base on the Atlantic for naval operations; so that it requires special treatment and will be regarded as particularly liable to attack; both for those reasons and on account of its location. Saint John does not fall within that category and the question of vulnerability is a relative one. We have to do the most vulnerable things first.
May I ask the minister if he does not think Saint John will be of increasing importance because it will be a seaport for the new army camp?
Yes, I quite agree.
May I ask that serious consideration be given this matter of Saint John because we feel we are being overlooked in this respect?
Yes.

Earlier this year the Department of Public Works called for tenders for the construction of a new naval dock in Esquimalt harbour. The newspapers at the time said that this was connected with the seaward defence of Esquimalt harbour. At Easter the tenders were all returned to the various engineering firms that had submitted tenders. Is it the intention of the department to go ahead with the construction of this new wharf? If so, what was the reason for suddenly cancelling the tenders and returning them to the firms concerned?

The jetty at Esquimalt to which the hon. member refers was undertaken as part of our seaward defence, and was designed and to be constructed by the Department of Public Works as our agent. The designs were completed and tenders called, but further studies of the harbour and the nature of the bottom of the harbour led to some doubt as to whether the present design would be suitable. Some further investigations were made and it was decided to redesign, in part at least, this jetty. The jetty will be built as proposed, but it will be delayed for some time until these designs have been drawn to the satisfaction of the Department of Public Works and ourselves.

I want to ask a question under this heading in connection with the supply of naval fuel. I put a question on the order paper the other day, and was surprised upon seeing the answer to find that bunker fuel and diesel oil fuel was being supplied from foreign crude oil, and then it was being delivered direct to Esquimalt by tankers coming from California. While I imagine that the source


from which this oil is obtained may be a question to be answered by the Minister of Defence Production, I should like to know what is to' be the future of H.M.C.S. Dundurn, which is a Canadian naval tanker on the Pacific coast. Are we going to allow that tanker to remain idle in Esquimalt harbour or what is its future?
If we are having oil delivered from foreign sources instead of from Canadian sources in Vancouver where the Dundurn would be able to move the fuel from Vancouver to Esquimalt, I wonder what is the future for that vessel. I intend to ask the Minister of Defence Production about the source of supply. It seems an extraordinary thing that we should build a pipe line from Alberta to Vancouver, and then have the government turn around and buy this oil direct from California.

As regards the source of the fuel oil for naval vessels in Esquimalt, I understand we did not specify the source, but merely gave the specifications and the Department of Defence Production made the purchase.
With regard to the Dundurn, I understand that she is used in the harbour for fuelling the larger ships instead of sending them to the jetty. She is not generally used to transport oil from Vancouver or other sources. I understand if oil is purchased from Vancouver, it is delivered by the tanker of the company which sells the oil.
Is the future of the Dundurn assured then?
Yes, she will continue as at present.

It seems to me extremely regrettable, after this pipe line was built from Alberta to the Pacific coast with defence as one objective, that the government buys oil from foreign sources. The pipe line was built to obviate the long and hazardous route which this oil would follow from the Middle East. Just after the pipe line had been in operation a short time the Department of National Defence starts buying oil from foreign sources, thus increasing the difficulty this pipe line has been meeting in any event due to a tanker war. This war has made it possible to deliver Middle Eastern oil at a cost slightly below that delivered from Alberta. The situation is not going to continue very long, I understand, but I say it is regrettable and it is not in the interests of Canada generally, including defence policy, to use these other sources which would not

be available in time of war. We should patronize our home industry and particularly this pipe line.

No. Under this particular heading I note that the total number of employees has increased. The cost of these employees has increased some $4-5 million. I would have thought that the same thing could have been done in this branch of the department as was done in the inspection branch. The number of these civilian employees might have been reduced or at any rate might have been held to the same level instead of being increased by a little more than 12 per cent over last year. I am not going to go into the numerous cases in which those increases have taken place, but I should like to call attention to one or two instances that I believe are completely unjustified.
According to the details on page 294 the total number of clerks of various classes is going to be increased and this year will be 1,651 compared with 1,335 for last year or an increase of 316 clerks. Now, surely all that indicates is a great multiplication of the paper work. This is the very thing we have been complaining about for so long and the minister agreed that it should be cut down. Here we find one of the surest means of increasing it, a very large increase in the number of clerks. It is extremely difficult for me to see how an increase of that sort is jusified.
Then the only other item I will mention is mess men. The number is increased from 44 to 130. I presume these are the men who wait on the troops at dinner and things of that sort. It is difficult also to understand why there should be an increase from 44 to 130, three times as many mess boys in one year. From those two examples, and the general 12 per cent increase in personnel, it does not appear that any effort has been made to economize so far as civilian personnel are concerned. The total increase in personnel in the navy is not going to be very great and it does not seem to me to justify anything like this large increase in the number of civilian and administrative personnel.

As is obvious, I suggest, from information given the house thus far, the navy is increasing the number of ships and the number of servicing stations necessary to service those ships. This increase of personnel, amounting, roughly, to a thousand-

Is the associate minister referring to civilian personnel?
Naval personnel.
But I am not talking about naval personnel; I am talking about civilians. The increase is over 1,200.
I was going to give information as to the civilians.
Under the naval branch?

Yes. The increase in civilian personnel which will be required during the present year is made up of approximately 200 people who are now manning the principal stores depot at Montreal, which was recently put into operation for all naval supplies; over 100 who will be required in the maintenance of ships in inactive reserve at Sydney-security, fire and various servicing activities; something over 100 in Ottawa, at headquarters, to meet the needs of the increasing expansion and about 300 each on the east coast and a similar number on the west coast in the dockyards, stores departments, armament depots, and in the magazines which either have been or are being constructed and put into operation to serve the fleet, as it increases in number.

The minister has not met my criticism, I am sorry to say. I do not want to take up more time, but I would refer to it in this way: A department store, for example, may have 500 employees and is doing $5 million worth of business. If the number of customers increases, and the value of the business also increases, we will say to $7 million or something like that, they do not have to have a very great increase in the number of clerks in the store. In other words once you have your basic set-up in an organization you can handle quite a bit more business without any great increase in staff.
In other words, my general criticism is that the number of personnel is increasing every year. If this happened in only one year it would be a different matter; but it is going up, up, up, up every year. Here we have another increase from last year, when it had already built up to 10,000 people.
Furthermore, what the minister has said does not explain this increase. For instance, a quarter of the total increase is made up of about 300 clerks. What he said does not meet my general criticism and does not explain why there should be this great increase in the number of clerks, people who handle paper.

Well, I mentioned a moment ago that the navy is increasing quite rapidly. Naturally once a ship is in commission we must take care of its contracts and all its day to day activities. There is office work in connection with that, and also more work in the servicing departments-armament depots, ammunition stores, etc. Naturally the staff will increase slightly each year until we reach a fixed position in the navy. 1 suggest that is obvious. First of all we must have a substantial nucleus to serve the navy generally, and then we have all these specific services to meet the needs of ships individually and collectively as they become more numerous on our east and west coasts.

The fact that the number is increasing like this-and there can be no doubt about it-indicates that there is not proper control being exercised and no real effort being made to hold down these administrative expenses. I am very concerned about this matter, and have been for some time. We have been told what was accomplished in the inspection branch, in spite of the fact that the work of that branch, as the minister said, is now at its peak. In spite of that, the number of people employed has been greatly reduced. I am only too glad to give credit to the department for having accomplished this. I have already complimented them upon it, and I will do it again. But having been able to accomplish this in the inspection branch when things were at a peak, I cannot see any reason at all for this very large increase in civilian employees generally of the navy. And I refer particularly to this terrific increase in the number of clerks.

I might say that it has always been the practice of the navy to operate all their shore establishments with civilians. In connection with the big naval stores depot at La Salle, brought into service not many months ago, I might mention there are 400 civilians employed there, and probably only six or eight naval personnel. It is the practice of the navy to operate their shore establishments to a great extent with civilians. As the requirements become greater and as the fleet grows this will be reflected in the increased number of civilian employees.

Why is it necessary to have 300 more clerks? This general talk about building up the navy does not answer my question at all; it does not get to the nub of the matter. Why is it necessary to have an increase of 316 clerks? That is about 25 per cent in one year.
Depots consist mostly of clerks for servicing and accounting.
But the depots have been there right along.

No, some of them have been enlarged and some have just been built. At least one armament depot has just come into use. I am trying to say to my hon. friend that these servicing establishments on both coasts, and in various parts of the country- at least some of them-are just coming into commission now. Some have had to be enlarged.

Mr. Chairman, I have a couple of questions, and they apply equally to all three services. Perhaps the minister in replying could answer with that in mind, and save duplication. My first question relates to automatic punch card machines which are used for personnel records. Are they owned by the department, or are they rented? If they are rented, are they all rented from the same source? If so, what is the rental?
Subject to some exceptions, I believe generally they are rented, and obtained from three sources: International Business Machines, National Cash Register and Burroughs.

Then in connection with travelling and removal expenses in the case of postings overseas to Europe: I have had complaints from servicemen going to Europe that there is a wide discrepancy in the standard of accommodation supplied to various personnel of equal rank in equal circumstances. What standards are required of the shipping companies, or whoever supplies this accommodation, when troops are being posted either to or from Europe?

The question of transportation is almost entirely army and air force, which we have not reached yet. We shall get it for you and answer it later. The entitlement for all three services is on a uniform basis. While standards are laid down uniformly, inevitably the type of accommodation, and sometimes transportation, depends on availability. If we were to wait until the wives and children all got the same they might be disappointed in not getting there. Therefore it is sometimes better to take poorer accommodation in order to get them together just as soon as possible. It is largely a question of availability.
I presume some minimum standards are required.
Yes.

At the bottom of page 298 there is an item "Major procurement of equipment". Ships, aircraft, engines and so

on are mentioned. Aircraft and engines are up from roughly $1,500,000 to $23,500,000 in round figures. Can the minister put something on the record with regard to the replacement program of naval aircraft?

This is a very fair proportion of the total cost of getting new suit of aircraft for the Magnificent's successor, H.M.C.S. Bonaventure. We are replacing the Avengers with the S-2F aircraft and we are replacing Sea Furies by jet Banshees. Most of these have been purchased. We are also buying a considerable number of helicopters. That accounts for the cost.

In the case of removal and travelling expenses for civilians, I notice the item is down considerably from $750,000 to $498,000. My question is not with regard to the amount. I take it that civilians are generally speaking locally employed. What are the circumstances under which it is necessary to post civilians who are employed in the service from one area to another, and therefore require removal expenses?

Transportation allowances are provided for civilians employed in outlying districts, and also some provision is made for transportation of children of service personnel to schools. But generally speaking what the hon. member says is correct. There are no large movements of civilian personnel from place to place, but there is a considerable removal of supervisory personnel. Some of the naval magazines and depots are not close to major centres. One thinks of some of the wireless stations, Renous, depots in New Brunswick, and there are three ammunition dumps or depots in British Columbia. This also includes a considerable amount for reallocation of personnel consequent on the establishment of the new naval depot at La Salle, near Montreal.

The general picture presented here is somewhat interesting. The total amount to be expended this year is just $5 million more than the amount that was expended last year, and, as I pointed out before, this is the same amount as the increase in the cost of civilian personnel this year amounts to Apart from this increase in the cost of civilian personnel there will be no increase by and large as far as the cost of the navy is concerned. We find an item of $23,500,000 this year; whereas last year it was only $14 million for aircraft and engines which my colleague has just been talking about; which means that some $22 million at least has been pared off the other items. I notice it has come chiefly off the other items which are important as far as a fighting navy is concerned; that is, the 83276-405
Supply-National Defence things that they fight with. For example, signal and wireless equipment are down nearly $7 million. Armament equipment, guns and so forth are down $4 million. The ships are down $1 million. Then we find that ammunition and bombs are down nearly $8,500,000. Therefore, some of the other items which are not fighting items, you might say, are up. It would appear that the items for the navy this year, that is, items of fighting equipment such as bombs, ammunition, guns and so forth are all down really very materially. Can the minister explain why that is? It is all right to build up all these big civilian staffs, and so on, but when it actually comes to the navy doing the work for which we maintain it, the important things for them to have are ships, guns, planes, ammunition and so forth, to run them. As I say, it appears from this that these are the very things by and large in which there has been quite a large reduction. Non-essential items have gone up.

It is explained to me that in the case of those items of fighting equipment that the hon. member mentions, the changes are owing to different changes in the time of placing and getting delivery of contracts. We have got ammunition; we need lots of it. We have got electronics; we need lots of that. I am only mentioning these as illustrations. The hon. member did not mention clothing and personnel equipment which is down from $7 million to $2,500,000. That is because we were able to get quite a considerable proportion of these so-called "soft" things, and they are on hand. There is no particular significance in this except I should tell the hon. member that the navy and the other two services work out, through their chiefs of staffs, with the deputy minister and others the proportion of the defence dollar that is allotted to them, and then they have to divide that year's money so as best to carry out the program and keep that phase together. Therefore next year it may be that some of this no doubt will be up again.
Just one comment-

The committee resumed at seven o'clock. The Chairman: When the committee rose at six o'clock we were discussing the item
6400	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence under the Royal Canadian Navy-active force and general. Is this discussion concluded?

No, Mr. Chairman, I had just risen in order to make a brief comment on what the minister said in reply to the very brief observation I had made that the total cost for the navy is up by some $5 million and that that is accounted for almost entirely by the increase in civilian personnel. I asked why it was that there had been considerable reductions in the fighting equipment for the navy.
Without going into the minister's reply I would like to comment that I think this is a good example of the fact that the expenditure of more money does not necessarily mean we are getting more defence. In spite of the fact that we are spending more money under this particular heading the actual amount being spent for ships, guns, and other things which make the navy an effective fighting force is being reduced, and unfortunately I believe that has been the situation for quite a number of years in most of the branches of the department. One of the chief arguments we have advanced here over the last four or five years was that that was what was actually happening, and that the very large sums of money which have been spent have not produced for us the fighting force to which we are entitled for the large amount of money expended.

I would like to get some idea from the minister as to what kind of machinery exists between the defence purchasing department and the Department of National Defence. Defence purchasing in Canada means quite a lot of employment in Canada, and I would like to give a case in point. There is a large naval base at Sydney, Nova Scotia, and in that area about one mile from the base there is a large wire and nail mill. At the present time there is a bad unemployment problem there. Last November I found that large shipments of nails brought from Hamilton, Ontario, were being used at that naval base at a time when nails were being manufactured in that area and when half the men in that factory were unemployed. I was just wondering where the economy is obtained by purchasing nails for the Department of National Defence in Hamilton, Ontario, and shipping them 1,400 miles for use in a spot where there is a nail mill in operation working half time.
I would like the Minister of National Defence or the associate minister to give me an explanation about this because it is pretty poor planning. It may be bad salesmanship on the part of the company which manufactures these nails, but if it is I would like to know. I know for a fact that many
[The Chairman.]

kegs of these nails come from Hamilton because I not only looked at them myself but I took one of the covers with me in order to make sure I would have the evidence if I was questioned. If this is the kind of way in which materials are purchased, without regard to employment conditions in the area, and regardless of the fact that you can obtain the materials cheaper and at the same time assist that area in the matter of employment, then I think there is poor planning somewhere between the Department of National Defence and the defence purchasing department.
I wonder if the hon. member could tell me whether the nails he mentioned were obtained from a contractor or were being used by the navy.

I do not know for certain. The base is a naval base and it is under the Department of National Defence. I do not know whether a contractor purchased these nails but in any case that contract would be let by the Department of National Defence and I think there should be some understanding when letting these contracts that the materials that are available in the area in which the work is being carried on should be given first priority, other things being equal. I thought it looked pretty bad to see a nail mill working half time while a project which was under national defence was using nails they had dragged 1,400 miles across the country which would bear the additional burden of freight. I think it adds up to poor salesmanship somewhere.

It is my understanding that as regards the procurement of goods for the Department of National Defence by the Department of Defence Production we prepare a specification for the required goods and we make what is called a contract demand on the Department of Defence Production. That department is then charged with the responsibility of procuring these materials, having regard to the specification, price, delivery terms, and so on. Procurement of the goods having been completed, we then inspect them, accept them and pay for them. Under those circumstances I presume there are a number of considerations which actuate my colleague, the Minister of Defence Production, in securing the goods for which we have made a contract demand. The only variation there might be with regard to this particular case, and of course I am not aware of all the facts, is that we might have sent nails to our own naval base from some of our stores at some point or other for use by the navy. That might have happened, but generally speaking

I think the procedure is as I have outlined it, subject to anything my colleague might say on the matter.
When the estimates tor the Department of Defence Production come up I hope I will be able to get a run-down answer to this question.

Mr. Chairman, it is very difficult for a layman to venture into the field of questioning military expenditures, but I think even a layman is entitled to ask a question about civilian expenditure. I am coming back to the matter the hon. member for Calgary North has already ventilated and to be found in the details at page 298. I note there is between $4 million and $5 million apparently additional on the civilian part of the staff. That seems to me a lot of money. We think it is a lot of money in Greenwood. I would like to ask the minister what steps are taken to satisfy the department that those men are needed.
I heard of one industrialist who approached his staff with a very crude and simple test. He divided his staff into those that produced and those that did not produce. The only producers in his mind were the people who produced the things that you could handle. He regarded all his office staff as non-producers and he was accordingly critical of them. In the same way it seems to me that as laymen we are entitled to be extremely inquisitive and curious about the civilian staff. This businessman I speak of is reported to have been made the head of a certain company and to have begun by firing all the clerical staff and then taking them back one by one as they were proved to be needed. That is a crude illustration of what I have in mind. In any event it is a crude illustration of the feeling one has in surveying a military establishment, with all the civilians that are in it.
Even those of us whose experience of war is not as recent as it might be can remember the scornful way in which we used to talk of the paper war and speak of all the people who never got outside of the office and who were on lines of communication. Now in peacetime I suppose you not only have those people but you have out-and-out civilians.
I want to ask the minister this question. I have raised it before. It is not new. In some departments recourse has been had to people whose business is organizing efficiency. I should like to ask the minister whether any recourse has been had to efficiency experts in this instance? They have been used in certain departments. At one time when I raised this question I was told that 83276-405J
Supply-National Defence such assistance was not used in large organizations in civilian life but only in small ones. That statement is manifestly wrong. Actually they are used more in larger undertakings than in smaller ones. I should like to ask the minister whether, if that is something that has not been done, it will be done. It seems to me that the onus is absolutely on the department, when they come along with between $4 million and $5 million for additional civilian assistance, to explain why. If any other department came in here with $4 million additional for clerical assistance, I think we would be absolutely outraged. I realize that the military establishment is huge. It may be that if we knew all about it we would be satisfied. But that item of nearly $5 million raises a big question in my mind.

Mr. Chairman, I would repeat first just briefly what I observed when this matter was raised by the hon. member for Calgary North. First, the naval establishment ashore is primarily and almost entirely civilian. As the navy grows and the shore establishment grows, naturally the civilian component of the shore establishment increases. I am informed that when a branch which has been established or which has increased its facilities wishes to have new personnel to meet that need, that branch makes an application to the naval complement committee at headquarters who as specialists review the applications carefully. If it is approved by the naval complement committee-and only to that extent because the committee has powers and facilities to investigate and if necessary to reduce the numbers required-the requirement then goes to the civil service commission. The commission also has its own methods of investigation and of satisfying itself as to the need. When the application has survived those two reviews-if it has; I refer to the need of the branch as set forth in the requirement-it goes to treasury board. From my experience serving on treasury board that body is not in any sense a rubber stamp. It also has its own methods of investigation both here and at other places. It is only when treasury board has approved the setting up of an additional civilian position or a number of positions to meet an established need in a certain place that those positions are filled.

I am still left with this basic question. The minister has mentioned this naval committee. As I understand it, these additional requirements are first of all endorsed and approved by what the minister
6402	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence called a naval committee. What would be the personnel of that committee? Is it composed of naval officers?
It is a joint committee composed of navy officers and civilians in the department.

No one has more respect than I have for naval officers but I do not imagine that naval officers have spent much of their time in being trained for office management. At any rate I would hope that they have not. I would hope that sea duties are what they have been trained in. It is therefore all very well for the minister to say that this matter goes to two or three bodies, each of which scrutinizes it, including the civil service commission and the treasury board. I know the treasury board is always held up as being a most formidable body, and I have no doubt that it is. Nevertheless, if the thing gets a bad start-if you have the original recommendation made without the thorough scrutiny which I am asking for, if indeed it is not being made now-if you get it started without a proper scrutiny, it seems to me that from then on everyone else is beaten. They are not going to send down and make an entirely new investigation of the duties. Surely the civil service commission is not going to do it all over again and treasury board is not going to do it all over again. I am not quite sure whether the minister is differing with me or whether he is going to say that they do that, but I still feel uneasy and that somehow or other this matter is not getting the scrutiny that it should get.

I might just point out to the hon. member that it has just been brought to my attention that very recently, as a result of a survey by the naval complement committee, over 80 applications were turned down. I think this committee is a thoroughgoing and rigorous committee. Any application must pass that committee before it even goes to the civil service commission, much less the treasury board. I am informed that the naval complement committee is extremely strict and looks into the situation most thoroughly.

I have one final question, or at least I hope it is final. The minister said that the increased staff on shore had to take care of increased personnel and increased units afloat, if I understood him correctly. Can he indicate what, in the last year, has been the increase of the service personnel as distinct from the administrative? When I say "service" I mean really "service".
As between March 31, 1953, to March 31, 1954, in the naval strength there was an increase of practically 1,500.
What percentage is that? I do not want the total. What would that be in percentage?
From 15,546 on March 31, 1953, to 16,955 on March 31, 1954.
What is the civilian increase?
The civilian increase was nearly 1,200.
That is naval personnel.
