I have several questions to ask but I will start with an easy one so that we will get into the army picture. My first question concerns the size of our force in Korea compared with the size of our force in northwest Europe. In view of the minister's statement this afternoon with respect to brigade groups, could we have the picture clearly as to those two forces? I understand that in Korea we have an infantry brigade incorporated within the commonwealth division. In Europe we have an infantry brigade group able to operate independently. In the words of the minister, I think he said at one time it was almost a small division. My question is what is the difference in the number of personnel as between these two formations?
My second question is this. Has the infantry brigade incorporated within the commonwealth division in Korea been able to function to the satisfaction of that division and the Department of National Defence? Then I come to my third question, and I do not want to labour this point. If the infantry brigade incorporated within the commonwealth division has been found a satisfactory answer to some of our commitments abroad, could not an armoured brigade incorporated within a British armoured division perhaps be the answer to this problem of the armoured corps?

In answer to the hon. member's questions, I can say that the British have two armoured divisions in Germany and they have none in Korea. In Korea we have operated exceedingly happily with the commonwealth division. It has worked out very well. They were all infantry with a component of armour. But in Europe the British formations are organized as divisions, and it would be very difficult indeed to integrate an armoured brigade group into one of their divisions. I am advised it could not be done, that it would have to be an extra unit and it would have to have the extra supporting services that I referred to before.
Are the figures available with regard to the difference in size of these forces?
They are very much the same.

My other question has to do with the rifle. Some time earlier in the house I asked a number of questions concerning the adoption by Canada of the Belgian rifle, which has been adopted as the standard infantry weapon for the United Kingdom. The minister's reply to this question indicated that tests were being conducted in Canada of

Supply-National Defence the FN rifle, and that if they were satisfactory an announcement would be made in due course. Is the minister prepared to give us a full statement now with regard to this question of the rifle?

Yes, to bring the house up to date I may say that the Belgian FN rifle has been adopted by the British army, and they are obtaining some quantities for further trial and testing. We have not yet decided to adopt the rifle. We are subjecting it to further tests. We have placed an order for a number that are being delivered to us. Simultaneously the United States have had some FN rifles which they have subjected to Arctic trials, and trials under northern conditions. As a consequence of this, I think some modifications will have to be made.
In the meanwhile our role in the picture is that we are, through Canadian Arsenals Limited, arriving at engineering designs and production designs and specifications for the production of the rifle according to the standards that have been agreed upon by the British, Canadian and United States teams. This work is being pushed by the Department of Defence Production through Canadian Arsenals Limited. If it were decided to go ahead with the production of the rifle, there will be no delay in connection with the work. In that connection work is being pressed forward in the production of drawings, designs and engineering specifications. We are getting rifles from Belgium for that purpose. My colleague the Minister of Defence Production has had officers in Belgium working with Canadian army officers and with Fabrique Nationale, the original producer of this rifle. The work is progressing satisfactorily.
How soon it will be possible to announce the final results, I do not know because it will depend on the tests. We have been very anxious in this not to get too far ahead of any country in the decision to adopt the rifle. We have been very anxious indeed that Great Britain, the United States, France, Belgium and ourselves should adopt the rifle as standard, and we have done everything possible to that end. The discussions started really in 1946 in what is called the A.B.C. committee, composed of United States, Britain and Canada and in April 1951 these considerations seemed to be getting nowhere, when the British announced their intention to go ahead with their own rifle, the EM. I made an appeal, which I think has been reported to this house, to the then minister of defence in Britain and the secretary of defence in the United States, that we should meet once more
IMr. Churchill.]
at the ministerial level with very high ranking officers and have another look at the matter.
I am glad to say the meeting took place in Washington on the first and second of August, 1951. Since then we have been working progressively towards a solution of that very desirable objective, the adoption of a common rifle. In the meantime, however, we have agreed on a common round; that was announced by me at the meeting we had in Paris of the North Atlantic council in December. This work is also proceeding. The experts met in Quebec and Ottawa, and arrived at the final specifications for the round. Those were agreed to and the round has now been agreed upon. While it has been a long struggle, I am happy to say we are making considerable progress. I believe we will arrive, not only at a uniform round but also a uniform rifle.

There are some circumstances in regard to the question of the rifle which I think need clarification. There was a debate in the British House of Commons some time ago in connection with the decision there to adopt the Belgian FN rifle, whereas earlier the British government of that period until 1951 had decided the British EM2 rifle was the most satisfactory weapon. The adoption of a rifle is an important matter. The Lee Enfield rifle, which has been the standard rifle for over 50 years now, is an indication of the length of life that may be expected of a rifle used in the army. When the time comes to adopt a new type of rifle, the greatest care is necessary to ensure that it is the most satisfactory.
After the conclusion of the second world war the British, as I understand from reading accounts, asked for a new rifle which would be automatic or semi-automatic and which would be, if possible, shorter and lighter than the Lee Enfield. From that point inquiries have been made and studies made in order to arrive at the type of rifle that would be most suitable for modern requirements. Modern requirements seem to point to the use of a rifle which is automatic, shorter and lighter. The result at the moment is that the Belgian FN rifle does not meet all these requirements. In some respects it does not seem to be the equal of the British EM2 rifle.
My concern about this was aroused by reading certain accounts as to Canada's position in the matter. I believe Canada's position is quite clear with regard to the standardization of the round, now standardized at -30. I think there could be no dispute

about that at all, and that is a major advancement. The NATO countries have agreed to use the same type of ammunition. Our record does not seem to me to be quite so clear with regard to the rifle. We appear to have adopted a negative attitude in so far as that was concerned.
I notice reports from the British House of Commons regarding the Canadian stand on the rifle, and accounts in the press, which seemed to indicate that if our representatives had taken a definite stand the British EM2 rifle would have been selected. For example in the House of Commons at Westminster on February 1, 1954, during the debate on the adoption of the rifle, Canada came into the picture on several occasions. The discussion is found at page 55 of the British Hansard for that date. The subject was mentioned by the prime minister and then Mr. Shinwell had this to say:
The position of the United States was as the right hon. gentleman has stated, the position of France was that she had no opinion at all, and the position of Canada was as stated by the then, and, I think, present minister of defence, Mr. Brooke Claxton, that he was quite unconcerned about the size of the round or the type of rifle as long as Canada had the opportunity of producing whatever rifle or whatever round was decided upon.
And then at page 93 Mr. Shinwell, in answer to some further point in the debate, has this to say:
Where does standardization come in? The French have not expressed their willingness to accept it. What about Canada? The prime minister talked about Canada and X said in an interjection that X had had discussions with Brooke Claxton, the minister of defence. He said to me, "I am not going to take sides. What we are concerned about is who is going to produce the rifle and the round."
Then at page 97 Mr. Head, speaking for the government, said this:
The point is that Canada has stated that for her government to manufacture a rifle which has been turned down by the United States would be a course which they could not accept.
That seems to indicate that the Canadian position has been that of a person on the sidelines, and in a measure unconcerned with regard to the type of rifle which might be placed in the hands of Canadian troops. It would indicate that rightly, and naturally, Canada was interested in the standardization process, and still more interested in the matter of production-and not without reason, because the British look to the American continent for the production of rifles.
Nevertheless I think Canada's position is a bit weak in this, when we seem not to have put forward our own view with regard to the type of rifle that would be most useful and suitable for our infantry. And that is the point that bothers me. Why could we not
Supply-National Defence determine and make our choice among the various types of rifles that are available- the Belgian FN, the British EM2, the modifications of the Garand that are being carried on in the United States, and perhaps others. Canadians are as familiar as any soldiers in the world with the type of rifle that would be most suitable for modern warfare. I discussed with a brigade commander who had a long and honourable career in the second world war in northwestern Europe and he told me that at one stage during the course of the conflict he was attempting to get his entire infantry component of the brigade equipped with a carbine, or a Sten gun, or a Thompson submachine gun, rather than the Lee Enfield rifle. The reason was that, in the type of attack they were carrying on, with so much night action, the shorter weapon, and the automatic weapon, was what was desirable. He failed to achieve his object. I asked him what would be his suggestion at the present time, and he said, "By all means something that is short and light and automatic".
Now, it is the opinion of fighting troops that that is essential in this matter. Too frequently, in such experiences as I have had, decisions are made by people who have not actually used weapons in the field. What I wonder is whether we have made a complete study of the rifle we have adopted now, which might well be the weapon in the hands of our forces for the next fifty years; because we cannot change from year to year the production of a standard weapon such as a rifle. You have to produce them in great numbers.
I tried to find out earlier if we had made comparative tests between the Belgian rifle and the British rifle, both adapted to use the common .30 round. However I did not get a complete answer to that question. Apparently we had observers at various try-outs of rifles. But some of those try-outs -and this is where the difficulty comes in- some of those trials which took place in the United States and Britain were between the British rifle using the .280 and the Belgian rifle using the .30. Now that they both use the same round, comparative tests should be conducted to determine which of the two is more satisfactory.
Or perhaps some other rifle would be much more satisfactory. I have been saying that Canada has played a strange part in this matter of the standardization of the rifle. She has taken a rather negative attitude, and that negative attitude may have been the decisive factor.
6408	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence I have a newspaper report here which appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune of February 25. It is a dispatch from London to the Canadian Press referring to the estimates submitted in the British House of Commons, and is in these words:
Because the FN was the type of rifle favoured by the Canadians and is also being ordered for trials by Americans, it was decided that its adoption was the wisest course in view of the greatly increased prospects of North American production. Neither Canada nor the United States would favour the adoption of the British EM2.
So Canada has weighed the balance in this matter. And the British, whether they have preferred their own EM2 rifle because of its design and weight and other important factors, would have preferred their own rifle if it could be produced in this country. Yet we are obliged, so far as I can find out from these records, to favour the Belgian rifle because the United States rejected the British EM2 and Canada played no active part in the deliberations. I think it would have been better for Canada to have played a much more active part in this than simply to have stood on the sidelines-not interested in the rifle, but interested only in the production thereof.
I do not think that is good enough. I believe Canadian military people have sufficient experience to determine the best rifle for Canadian use, without having to adopt something that is produced by some other country. And Canada might very well have come up with some other idea. The standardization of the rifle is important; but more important is the standardization of the round, which has been achieved. And it might well be that, for Canadian purposes, something different is desirable. Are we facing up to the realities of this, or are we simply going to wait and see what the United States does?
Now, let me point out that according to a report published in the Gazette of May 10, 1954 bearing a New York dateline and written by Hanson W. Baldwin of the New York Times service, it states, under the heading "Standard Rifle Far Off":
Belgium's rifle is lighter than the M-l-
An American model.
-and fires in bursts at a rate of about 700 rounds a minute. But the FN, in later tests, did not meet trials in severe cold in Canada as well as the M-l and T-44; there were more malfunctions and some breakages.
Well, that seems to cast some doubt on this rifle, which for some reason or other has had to be adopted by Britain, and has been rejected by the United States.
What does the hon. member mean "rejected by the United States"?

I am quoting from what I read in the British Hansard and from those reports. The minister has corrected me. The United States is still continuing tests with regard to the Belgian rifle. In so far as these reports are concerned, the United States has been reluctant to accept it. The Winnipeg Free Press of February 25 commented in an editorial on the Belgian rifle and had this to say dealing with remarks made in the United Kingdom. I quote:
Judging by Sir Winston's words, the attitude of the Canadian government was decisive. He might have been tempted to take a chance if Canada had favoured the British rifle. But without either Canada or the United States he was adamant.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the situation. I think it is a confused one with regard to the question of the type of rifle that might be adopted for the Canadian army in the future. We are in between the two larger powers, the United Kingdom and the United States, and we seem to have sided in a negative way with the United States which, according to the gentlemen in the United Kingdom, has affected their decision with regard to the type of rifle that has been selected.
I would have felt happier about it if Canadian tests had been conducted with both these rifles or others, and if a full disclosure of all these operations with regard to the rifle had been made to us earlier and if a full understanding of this problem had been presented. At the moment it seems to me to be a bit confused, and the attitude of Canada does not seem to me to be as creditable as it might have been had we taken a more positive stand with regard to this particular matter.

If the hon. member is confused I am not surprised because he has indicated that confusion throughout his whole speech. He has referred to a matter which has been the subject of discussion and a released statement, which is well known. Yet he attempts at this time to confuse this committee and to confuse this most important issue.
The point that Canada made throughout was that it was vitally important, in the interests of our common defence in NATO and as between Britain, United States and Canada particularly, that we should agree on a round and on a rifle. If anyone takes issue with the part that Canada played in aiming at that objective, then I take issue with him and so does every Canadian and so does every American, and so does everyone who lives in the British commonwealth and in the NATO countries. That was a desirable aim, and we aimed at that right

through. We found that the British were not going to adopt an American or other rifle. They felt in April, 1951 for reasons of their own that they should adopt the EM rifle and they so announced. Then I felt that in the interests of combined action and union between the three countries, but particularly in the interests of Canada, which is a surplus producer of arms, we should try again to see if we could not arrive at an agreement. Is that sitting back on the fence or of taking a backward position?
I sent a telegram-and I have the permission of the British war office and also of the secretary of defence to produce it-that in the interests of our unity we must agree on a round and on a rifle. If we could not agree on that, then what sense was there in NATO at all? This was fundamental. If we could not agree on a common hand weapon, then our whole alliance would be subject to very grave criticism. Anyway, in consequence of the Canadian intervention, we had this meeting at Washington. They suggested that it should be held at Ottawa. I suggested that it should be held at Washington. The United States was represented by the Hon. Frank Pace, former secretary of the army, and by General Joe Collins, the chief of the general staff. Britain was represented by the minister of defence, the Hon. Mr. Shinwell, accompanied by lieutenant-general, as he then was, now General Whiteley. France was represented by His Excellency Jules Moch, accompanied by a high ranking French officer. I was accompanied by Lieutenant General Simonds. We met during two days. We heard the experts describe their rifles. We received the reports again. It became perfectly evident that there had not been as full an interchange of information at various levels as there should have been. In consequence of those two-day discussions it was decided that we should have a fresh look.
In answer' to the hon. member, may I say that this meeting took place on the initiative of Canada. At the end of the meeting the secretary of the army of the United States said that he was grateful to the Canadian minister and to the Canadian team for the part they played in initiating this discussion and bringing them together. Then at our suggestion the discussion was transferred to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization's standing group. They agreed to a team of four on which we were represented by Major General Graham. That team brought in a report. Further studies were continued, and the result was an agreement on the round was announced at Paris, in December.
Supply-National Defence
When I was asked whether I would announce this agreement, it was done because the initiative was taken by Canada and followed up by Canadian generals and Canadian technicians in bringing the various groups together. The fact that I was asked to announce that agreement, and also to propose to the North Atlantic council that we should agree on this round as the standard round, has indicated that Canada was taking no backward part.
Then we came on to the rifle. If the British have adopted the FN rifle it is because the British chose to adopt the FN rifle. We do not influence the British. They make their own decisions. When that decision was announced and discussed in the house in the debate to which my hon. friend referred, some statements were made that seemed to me to have just about as little understanding of the real issues involved as those made in the speech we have just listened to from the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. I did not say, as quoted, that we were not concerned about what rifle or what round. How could I say that? Who in Heaven's name would ever say that? What I said was that what we were concerned with was that we should get agreement between the British, the Americans, the other countries and ourselves, and I said we would help to get that agreement. I said also that we were more interested in this than probably any other country of our size, because other countries would look to us as sources of supply, not only in the event of an emergency but in the event of the continuation of a cold war. They would expect us to supply them with rifles of one type or another, and it was of tremendous importance, in their interests, in the interests of the French, the British and everyone else, that whatever rifle was adopted would be one which would be adopted for common use and also if possible for common production in the United States, in Canada and in other countries.
We have been and we are still working towards that end. The record is totally against the view advanced by the hon. member. We have been constantly pressing to achieve an agreement on the rifle and I still hope that that agreement will be achieved. If there was anything wrong with the FN why did the British adopt it? If there is anything that requires to be corrected in this rifle on account of these Arctic trials then these corrections are and can be made and I hope they are being made successfully. If, on the other hand, it turns out that the FN is not the ideal rifle then it is still the best rifle that has yet been produced and it can be further developed. We are in the position

Supply-National Defence where we have not decided to take the FN because we want to see the results of the trials and we want to have user trials. We then want to go into production on whatever rifle we decide to produce.
All things considered I think it would be very desirable that we go into production on the FN rifle even if the United States does not choose that rifle, because it is a very good rifle and it is very desirable that the British should have an alternative source of supply outside of the United Kingdom. As everyone knows we supplied them with many hundreds of thousands of small arms during the war and with many billions of rounds of small arms ammunition. It is of vital importance that as far as possible we should work together. We have succeeded, in company with our allies and partners, in getting an agreement on a round. That is a great achievement and we now hope to succeed in getting an agreement on the rifle.

The minister thinks I am confused about this matter but I am not the least bit confused. I know what I am talking about in regard to the rifle and the round, and the confusion has arisen from the lack of information as supplied by the Department of National Defence. The minister confused the issue a little more just recently by discussing at great length the standardization of the round, for which I gave him full credit in my introductory remarks. The standardization of the round was made following that conference in 1951, and at that conference the British rifle, which was under consideration, was using -280 ammunition and the Belgian rifle was using -30. Canada came down in favour of the -30 ammunition and the NATO countries followed suit. We have standardized on the round and to that there is no objection.
But now the issue has advanced one stage further and it was with that further development that I was dealing. The issue has gone from that to the type of rifle to be adopted for the Canadian army. You can have a standardized round and a dozen different makes of rifles and machine guns all using that type of ammunition, and if you have the same ammunition for the NATO forces it might be better to have the same rifle. Nevertheless, if you have different makes and model of rifle each using the same type of ammunition you are on very sound ground indeed, and there is no confusion in my mind in that regard. There is no dispute on that point. We have standardized on the round.
But when it comes to the choice of rifle the evidence from the British Hansard


indicates that Canada's attitude was decisive with regard to the British having to adopt the Belgian FN rifle and

That simply is not true
either in regard to the British Hansard or in regard to the Canadian attitude. It has been shown to be completely untrue in the British Hansard, and all we have there are unproven statements.
Well, I deserve thanks from the minister for giving him the opportunity to correct the British Hansard which has put him in a very bad light.

I am correcting the hon.
member's interpretation of British Hansard.

It is not my interpretation. I have read the words of Mr. Shinwell and Mr. Head, and I shall not read them again^ as some hon. members here are suggesting. The words are there and I am not interpreting them. I am simply stating what I saw there and the press reports interpret them in much the same fashion. But let me give the words of the minister himself in order to see whether the issue has not been confused by the Department of National Defence. On March 3, 1954, I received an answer to a question which I placed on the order paper. Here was my question:
1.	Did the Minister of National Defence or any representative of his department recommend the adoption of or indicate a preference for the Belgian FN rifle at any conference of NATO countries on the subject of the standardization of weapons?
2.	If so, when and at what conference?
Here is the answer, Mr. Chairman.
1 and 2. Discussion at NATO meetings took place on the round but not on the rifle and the answer to this question is consequently "No".
I was trying to get information when I put that question on the order paper and that was the answer I received. In other words, we decided on the round but we made no commitments on the rifle. Now the minister is asserting that the situation is the opposite.
The answer is precisely as declared there. There is no commitment on the rifle.

But the minister said the rifle was discussed at this conference and apparently it was just the round. Who is providing the confusion? That is the situation, Mr. Chairman, and I think our position could be made clear if Canada took a somewhat more positive stand with regard to this very important-

May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? When the British have refused to adopt their own EM2 rifle would he ask

us to adopt that rifle when neither the British, the United States, the Belgians, the French, nor ourselves have adopted any one of the United States types? Would he not agree that the right course was for us to wait and see the result of the user trials?

Obviously, Mr. Chairman, the right course is to depend on the user trials which, I would hope, would be conducted by Canadians on all of these rifles firing the standard round. I hope we are not depending on other countries to make user trials and that these trials will be conducted under such conditions that we will be absolutely certain the proper rifle has been selected. We have a record in Canada of adopting a rifle which proved to be ineffective under battle conditions, and battle conditions involve mud and difficult weather conditions under which some rifles will not operate. Is there not a chance that unless we ourselves determine that this Belgian rifle is the most effective that we might make the mistake of adopting a rifle which would not stand up under difficult conditions? And what about the statement I read from that New York report to the effect that this rifle has not stood up under some of the Arctic trials? Are we trying out other rifles under the same conditions; is every country giving them the same test, and is Canada undertaking these tests?
I can assure the hon. member that we will make our decision on the basis of tests and trials by Canadians as well as by others working in this partnership.

During this debate and in speaking in previous debates the minister has always expressed a high degree of satisfaction with the condition of the Canadian army. I refer particularly to the organization, the adequacy of equipment and so forth. I think we are all agreed on the high calibre, on the whole, of the officers and men in the Canadian army, and that all wish to pay tribute to them whenever the opportunity presents itself. However, in view of these numerous statements by the minister which are echoed by the people on his side of the house -the ones who have spoken in this debate today-I should like to devote some time to an exercise which was held last year, called Buffalo IV and which was heralded widely in the press as the largest peacetime exercise in the history of the Canadian army.
These exercises or schemes are put on, of course, to give training to the troops and also as a test of their efficiency from various points of view as for example, their efficiency as subunits, as units, as formations, the efficiency of the various officers in exercising
Supply-National Defence command, tests of weapons and so on. As I say, this exercise which was heralded as the largest army exercise in peacetime as far as Canada was concerned was held last year in August.
There was a great deal of laudatory comment put out by the P.R.O.'s and so on. However, there attended at this exercise a reporter for the Calgary Herald by the name of Jim Senter who wrote four articles which were published in the Herald-I do not know what other papers they may have been in-giving his impressions of the exercise. I may say that I think he is particularly well qualified to give his impressions of this exercise. He went overseas. He happened to be in the same unit that I was in. He became an N.C.O., subsequently was put up for a commission and later served as a commissioned officer in the artillery. The particular article that I will start with, quote from fairly briefly and comment on is headed "Manoeuvres Reveal Weaknesses in Army; Many Improvements Considered Urgent to make Army Effective Defence Force". The article then goes on to say:
Exercise Buffalo IV, the biggest peacetime workout of the Canadian army, has passed into history and, with its passing, five basic weaknesses of the army stand revealed.
These weaknesses are to be found in the armoured corps,-
My friend the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has spoken about this matter at some length today and previously.
-the artillery,-
About which the Leader of the Opposition had something to say.
-the signal corps, the supply services, such as the Royal Canadian Army Service Corps, and the reserve army.
Basically, these are shortages of men and equipment but there is more to it than that.
There is the lack of proper training, units employed out of context, improper thinking, units that don't exist that should exist and units that have failed to be expanded in proportion to the increasing needs of the Canadian army.
The article then goes on and elaborates on those various points. I am not going to take up the time of the committee to go into all those matters. The point I want to make is that the rosy picture painted by the minister, particularly as to the situation in the Canadian army, is just not borne out by the exercises which have been held and by the facts, as far as competent observers who had the opportunity to look at them have reported. The organization of the army generally, as has been stressed by my friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, is wrong, in my opinion. Certainly the equipment is not adequate and in many cases it is

Supply-National Defence much out of date. This article goes on- it is talking about the armour to begin with-to say this:
The Strathconas-
The Strathconas are the armoured regiment in the west and are an exceptionally fine regiment. I have the honour of belonging to their mess as an honorary member and I have had the opportunity to observe them at their exercises at Sarcee and they are extremely fortunate to have a training ground right at their back door. I think they are in a high state of efficiency. The article continues:
-who supplied the armour for Buffalo IV, could provide only half their full strength for the exercise. One of their squadrons is now in Korea and the second is just now coming oil leave, having only recently returned from Korea.
This left two squadrons for the exercise and, of these two, one-"C" squadron, the first Canadian armoured unit to go to Korea-had to act in what is a new role for the Canadian army: heavy gun tanks . . .
The role of the heavy gun tanks is strictly defensive. It calls for a 65-ton tank mounting a gun ranging in size from 120 to 185 millimeters. Present thinking seems to favour the high velocity 120-mm.
Such a tank mounting such a gun certainly does not exist in Canada, and it is doubtful if a good version of such a weapon is to be found anywhere in the western world. "C" squadron had to use the obsolescent Sherman tank mounting a 76-mm. gun to simulate the role.
In their heavy gun tank role, the tanks were responsible for the divisional anti-tank defence-
I should like to stress that statement, that they were responsible for the divisional antitank defence. To continue:
-and provide depth and greater hitting power to the anti-tank screen provided by the infantry antitank platoons and the field artillery.
They are sited so that the enemy tanks in the offensive-
And so on. We do not need to go into that. To continue:
Though this role is new to the armour, it is not new to the Canadian army. In the second great war it was performed by anti-tank regiments using towed and self-propelled guns under the command of the artillery.
Aside from the fact that equipment for the heavy gun tank role does not exist . . . the biggest lesson learned here was that normal tank squadron and troop administration methods aren't enough.
I should like to follow up a bit this matter of anti-tank defence. It happens to have been the particular arm of the artillery in which I served for most of the war. Hence I have a certain amount of knowledge of it. About two or three years ago apparently a decision was taken-though it was extremely difficult to get the minister to admit it-that the anti-tank role would be taken on in future by the armoured corps and there would cease to be artillery antitank units. However nothing firm really has
[Mr. Harkness.l
happened about the matter since so that for the past two years or more the anti-tank regiments in the artillery-and those are the reserve anti-tank regiments, of course, because there are no permanent force ones- have been sitting there. They had their anti-tank weapons taken away from them. Some were given 25-pounder guns, some were given other guns. They are just sort of marking time not knowing what they would do.
In the meantime, nothing was done in the matter of building up anti-tank forces amongst the armour. The total result is, as is indicated here, that even the permanent force armoured regiment have had no training in anti-tank war. In spite of the fact that anti-tank defence was demonstrated during the last war as being one of the most important elements in the modern army, we have absolutely no anti-tank elements in our army at the present time. It was the lack of sufficient anti-tank weapons which enabled the German break-through of armour to take place in the overrunning of France in the early part of the war. It was the existence of a screen of German anti-tank guns which prevented our own armour from breaking through the German defence when we attempted it to begin with outside of Caen.
First the British army and then the Canadian army were foiled to a large extent by a screen of anti-tank guns. In spite of all the lessons of the necessity of anti-tank guns, particularly self-propelled anti-tank guns, the Canadian army has absolutely none now. The two regular force armoured regiments have had no training in the role, and as is indicated here this test showed that their troop organization and so forth was not of a kind that would enable them to carry out that role successfully. I will read further. He elaborates on that.
Who is "he"?

I indicated that. This
gentleman is Jim Senter who is either with the brigade in Europe or has just returned from there.

A newspaper reporter, a
reporter for the Calgary Herald'!

Yes. As he says here, this does establish that normal tank squadron and troop administration methods are not enough to enable them to carry out this difficult role. He continues:
Normally, a troop commander has his tanks close together and he can handle them and fire them from the turret of his command vehicle. In the heavy gun role, the tanks are widely deployed, dug

in and lying doggo. For better efficiency in fighting his tanks and in the administration and supply of the needs of his men, guns and vehicles, it is better that the troop and squadron commanders operate from a separate small headquarters of their own, leaving their command vehicles to be fought by a non-commissioned officer. These were lessons learned by the anti-tank regiments during the last war, and, for some reason, not passed on to the armour for the proper handling of their new role. Why has the armoured corps not been expanded to proportionate size with the rest of the army and why are the heavy gun tanks not available?
Those are two unanswered questions and two questions which of course I think the minister should answer. I should like to say a little more about the present anti-tank role which the armoured forces have taken on. As the result of some five years' experience during the last war I found it was a very difficult matter to train officers and men to deploy and handle anti-tank guns properly. Even after the long period of training we had in England a considerable number of guns were always badly placed. As a result some of course were lost and others would not have been effective if a tank attack had been made through their positions. It is a branch of army work which people just cannot walk out and do. It takes a lot of training and, as is indicated in this article, you need an administrative set-up within the troop and within the regiment so that the troop commander can control the placing of his guns and the squadron commander can control the deployment and fighting of his troops.
The way the armour is organized at the present time they just cannot do it. The squadrons which are with the troops in Korea and Europe at the present time have apparently been given this role and they are not able to carry it out because they are not organized properly for the purpose and they have not been trained for it. I repeat that we are really left without any anti-tank defence. In other words, from that point of view we have not a modern army at all or anything like it.
So much for that subject. There has been a good deal of talk about whether there is or is not sufficient equipment. Certainly there is no anti-tank equipment. That is one thing we are definitely short of. Here is another article about the same exercise which is headed, "Reserve Army Gunners Find Weapon Shortage". I wish to deal with this now because it also concerns the regular forces. That happens to be the heading of the article but it deals with the regular force gunners as well as those of the reserve force. The dispatch is from Wainwright and reads as follows:
Perhaps the most shocking disclosure to come out of the Canadian army's recently completed
Supply-National Defence exercise Buffalo IV held at Wainwright military camp, is the ragtailed state of the divisional artillery . . . Two regiments of artillery were deployed for the manoeuvre and, for lack of better names, were known as-
We do not need to go into that. The two regiments were made up of detachments from four of the reserve force units. This was their summer camp. I continue:
In all, reservists contributed by these four regiments totalled twenty-eight officers and seventy-two other ranks-
The total war strength of course of these four regiments would have been approximately 3,200 men all told. However they were only able to muster for this exercise 28 officers and 72 other ranks, and this constituted summer training. I continue:
Added to the reservists was a parachute battery from Canada's airborne brigade, "Z" battery. R.C.H.A.-
That was formerly an anti-tank battery but it is now converted to a parachute battery.
-which, normally, uses 4*2 in. mortars, and regular army gunners from the 119th and 129th light antiaircraft batteries, Victoria. The anti-aircraft gunners were given a two to three week conversion course from ack-ack to field artillery before proceeding to Wainwright for the exercise.
In other words, in order to hold this exercise in the western command and to put out in token form two field regiments to represent the divisional artillery-of course they would not because there would be three field regiments which would be backed up by a medium regiment-they had to bring in this regular force parachute battery and detachments from two ack-ack batteries on the Pacific coast.
This afternoon the hon. member for Wellington South said that there was plenty of equipment, that these people in the artillery units were all right and so forth. This article gives some idea of the number of people they can get out for summer camp. I will go on to something about equipment. He continues:
Cutting echelon groups to a minimum and eliminating wagon lines, cooks and tradesmen wherever possible, this left more than enough gunners and specialists to man, control and fire the some twenty-three 25-pounder field guns provided.
Why there were 23 provided I do not know. Twenty-four is the number for one regiment, not two regiments. I presume the reason there were 23 was that was all they could dig up in the western command to take out on the exercise. He continues:
It comes as something of a shock when it is realized that, of these twenty-three guns, only eight could be fired in a live shoot.

Supply-National Defence
Mark you, there are 23 guns on the exercise representing the divisional artillery, one gun short of the number there should have been for one field regiment, and of these 23 guns only eight could be fired. The others were there really as dummies on which people could do gun drill. Only eight could be fired in a live shoot. He continues:
The remaining fifteen had to stand idle in their gun positions. For the most part, these guns had not been calibrated. "They want reserve army men to come to camp and they can't even give us enough guns when we get here", said one reserve officer with considerable bitterness. I know a lot of reserve army gunners who won't be here next year."
As we have continually pointed out in the house time after time, there is one of the reasons why more people do not go to summer camp and do not turn out for the reserve forces. It is all right for the minister and the member for Wellington South to say that there is all kinds of equipment for these reserve force units, but when you discover what actually happened in this biggest exercise ever held in peacetime by the Canadian army you find that they only had eight guns that would fire for the entire divisional artillery. Naturally men are going to be disgusted. That kills their morale and they say "the heck with it, we will not come back." That is the kind of thing that kills morale and points up the terrible situation that exists. We ask that it be corrected. The article continues:
In some cases, three guns had to simulate a battery. During live firing, which occurred on only one day of the whole exercise, and that toward the end, gun crews had to line up and wait their turns at the guns.
Now, that was a fine exercise, was it not? Here is the biggest exercise ever held in Canada in peacetime and these gun detachments had to be brought from wherever their guns were and lined up one behind the other to take a turn at firing a few rounds of ammunition. That is extremely realistic training. It is certainly the type of training that is going to encourage people to join or stay in our reserve forces.
There was bad feeling over this among members of the reserve army as they felt they should have been given preference over the regular gunners in the firing practice. As it was, the reservists claim, it was the other way around.
In other words, instead of giving the reserves, who were out there for summer training practice, an opportunity to fire live ammunition, it was given chiefly to the regular army gunners. Perhaps that was the only practice they had, too; I do not know. It was felt the regular army had priority. I
[Mr. Harkness.l

shall not go on with the rest of this article, but I should like to read one or two more sentences:
What makes all this so depressing is the thought that the gunner representation on "Buffalo IV" represented the artillery resources of western command, the largest and probably the most important command in Canada.
I cannot resist reading the final paragraph:
In spite of everything, however, the gunners were reasonably well on their toes. And, as this reporter wandered about through the exercise area, the gunners were the only people who met him with levelled rifles and demanded to see his credentials.
In other words, the gunners are always on the job in spite of the difficulties imposed by this government or any other.
Did they have rifles or broomsticks?

They had rifles, but probably they would not fire.
The Calgary Herald commented on this editorial-
I think "editorial" is the right word.
I am glad the minister says it is right.

I said that I think "editorial" is the right word for this so-called report. I was referring to this so-called report of what happened and the hon. member said this "editorial" and I agree with you that it seems to be editorializing.
The reporter was giving his impression, and if the minister had been listening when I started he would have heard what this reporter's qualifications were.
I asked, and the hon. member told me.

I outlined the whole thing at some length before that, and just told the minister his name. The editorial is from the Calgary Herald and it speaks of this exercise in these words:
It was designed to test a division in a defensive role . . .
The first, and biggest, thing wrong with the whole operation was that there was no division to test, defensively or otherwise . . .
Operation Buffalo IV was supposed to be a western command exercise. Scraping the bottom of the barrel in both the regular and reserve army, western command fielded about one half a division. To make the exercise possible, other commands had had to be called in to help. The signals system alone required 900 men. The combined resources produced about 300. Food had to delivered by trucks in the field because there were neither sufficient men nor vehicles to provide a proper field ration and feeding system . . .

It is a waste of words to say again that this is a shocking condition to find in Canada's army in these times. It is past the shocking stage. It is enough to make anybody's hair stand straight on end, whether it is regarded from the standpoint of national safety or from the mundane angle of $2 billion a year being spent on a travesty of defence like this.
As I say, that shows the picture presented by a competent reporter with a military background, and without any axe to grind, except he is still a member of the reserve forces and so far as I know desires to improve the reserve and regular forces of this country. As the editorial says, it is indeed a shocking picture.
While I am on my feet, I should like to just indicate some of the things this same reporter found in the Canadian brigade in Germany, from where he has just returned and upon which he wrote another series of articles. I have one here which appeared in the Calgary Herald of Friday, June 4, and it is headed "Equipment Shortages Plague Canadian Troops in Germany". The heading, of course, was put on by the newspaper but the dateline is Soest, Germany. We have been told by the minister that we have all kinds of equipment, and so forth; no difficulties along this line; everything is rosy and everything is of the best. I am not going to read all this article, but I am going to read about a few of the shortages this reporter found and for which there seems to be absolutely no excuse. Here is a quotation from one of the men who said:
We can send 80 jet fighters to the Netherlands, but we do not even have shoe laces or stoppers for our own water bottles.
Then, the article goes on:
The shortages are to be found in transport, weapons and clothing, and much of the equipment at present possessed by the brigade is old, worn out and obsolescent.
And the thing which makes the Canadian soldier so angry is that this is supposed to be a show brigade. They are the only true NATO troops in the area, but they still have the worst equipment.
To be found close by are both the British and the Belgians. Both are occupation formations, operate under reparations and have the power of requisition. The Canadians, however, are NATO troops and, as such, pay their own way out of Canadian funds.
Yet, the British equipment is something out of this world-a dream to behold-and the Belgian units all have brand new transports and the finest weapons. But Canada's stuff is old and worn out and any large scale move means a widespread dotting of broken down Canadian tanks and trucks.
Just to look at the question of military transport, an item of vital importance to any military formation:
Military transport for the Canadian brigade totals approximately 1,800 vehicles of every kind for all units. In addition to these, extensive use is made of the German Volkswagen as "runabouts" within the brigade area.
Supply-National Defence
"It would take 200 three-ton trucks to carry all the spare parts used by military vehicles since the brigade came overseas last fall" said one officer who was in a position to know . . .
Everywhere within the Canadian brigade area in Germany today, transport is critically short in supply. "It's not that there is anything wrong with our maintenance, it's just that the breakdowns occur more rapidly than the repair services can fix them", another officer added.
"The vehicles are just old and worn out. They were not new when they came over here and they have travelled all over Europe, from Normandy at D-day to Berlin. We put in a new engine today and the vehicle is running fine. Tomorrow the rear end drops out."
And, as they look at their broken down vehicles, spread over the autobahns and by-roads of Europe, the Canadian soldier sums it up nicely. "It's embarrassing", they say.
The article says that weapons are another item of great concern, and talks about rifles. It reads as follows:
The rifles, for example, are worn and pitted, and, in many cases, have been re-blued over the rust. Bren guns, too, are badly worn and, in the case of one unit, out of approximately 80 Bren guns provided for in establishment, only ten could fire when first taken over by the unit.
Then the article goes on to deal with various other items of equipment. I am not going to take any more of the time of the committee to read this. There is a report by a responsible and competent observer, concerning what he saw in the early part of this month when visiting our brigade in Germany. The truth of the matter is that I believe we have had a situation with regard to this brigade in Germany misrepresented to us. I cannot say anything else. Quite evidently, the brigade has old equipment. It has rifles which, in many cases, probably if safe to fire at least are not going to be accurate because they are pitted and rusted.
