Supply-National Defence I said at the beginning, I think there is nothing wrong with the commanders, the officers or the men; I think they are absolutely splendid.
Everything is right except the shoe laces.
But according to this report -and I have confidence in it-the equipment those people have been supplied with is not up to scratch.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Have you no confidence in General Gruenther's report?

General Gruenther said
nothing about equipment. He never mentioned equipment. He said the brigade was a fine brigade.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: He spoke of the brigade as an operational brigade, and that includes equipment.
I have no doubt they are fine men. But it is made clear from this report; and I challenge the minister to deny the accuracy of this report-
I do accept the challenge, and I deny it.
All they do is challenge.
Why don't you prove it?

The minister challenges it. Are not those vehicles the same vehicles that we went to France with, in the invasion of the continent, during the last war, or that we went into Italy with, the year before that, in 1943?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: No.
Are they not the same vehicles? I challenge the minister.
No.

What vehicles are they, then? I am asking the minister:	What
vehicles are they, then?
It is not in the public interest to tell!
Let the minister tell us what vehicles they are.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Sit down, and let him have a chance.

Now, look, Mr. Chairman, the minister dare not say that they are not the same vehicles. He dare not say it, because they are the same vehicles. He started out to say it. I asked what vehicles they were, and he is not able to tell me. They may be vehicles which were used in England during the war; but they are either vehicles we used in England during the last


war, or the vehicles we left in France and Italy, one or the other. And if the minister wishes to say something, I will sit down.

Yes. I am afraid I cannot dig up the vehicle number of every motor vehicle in the armed forces. We have 31,000 of them. I will tell my hon. friend that the vehicles that went abroad with the 27th brigade to Europe were either new or as good as new-completely rebuilt motor vehicles. They were as good as could be found anywhere for any purpose at that time, and they went abroad in perfect condition.
When?

They may have had some use, but they were well maintained. We have some motor vehicles of new types we have been producing, and we have proposed to issue them as the old ones wear out. Of course that is natural enough. Why should it not be?
Good old rebuilts! The old rebuilts with the Canadian army!
Would you like us to throw away every motor vehicle?
Would you buy a secondhand car? You know you would not.

We have to rebuild and rebuild. And we rebuild them just as well as they can be rebuilt. And if they were not rebuilt my hon. friend opposite would be the first to complain about our throwing away two-year-old models.

Mr. Chairman, I think it is quite apparent that these vehicles are vehicles which were produced during the war, and which were used during the war. There may be a few of them that were not used at all, as the minister says, but they were vehicles produced during the war, and they were vehicles for the most part used during the war. Whether they were used in Canada or in England or in Italy or in France does not matter. The fact is that now they are worn out. They have had all that wear, and they have been repaired and repaired and repaired. And I am glad they have been repaired. But apparently they have reached the stage where it is not economical to repair them any more.
It is all very well for the minister to say, "We will keep on repairing them, to save money". But if you have ever had a fleet of trucks, and in that fleet you have a truck with a great number of miles on it, you know it is not economical to repair it any more. You are just throwing money away. You are far better off to get rid of it and get a new one. And I think, from what I can

make out, that that is the situation with regard to these vehicles with the brigade in Europe at the present time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Never mind the expense!
We could save money, but not by attempting to repair worn-out trucks.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: What about worn-out arguments?
Or this worn-out government.
Your argument is as worn-out as the trucks, and has as many holes in it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Don't go away mad.

So far as the other shortages are concerned, I have not the slightest doubt that they existed. The minister does not seem to know at the present time whether they existed or not. I would think it would be up to him to see if that is the situation; and I will be interested to see if it is correct. He should try to find that out, instead of getting up as he did a while ago and making the blunt assertion that none of this is correct. Here is an observer, a competent man with considerable background. There is absolutely no doubt that he is not the type who would send in an utterly false report about these things he saw. He is giving a news report on it. And if the minister followed the reasonable procedure he would find out to what extent this is old and worn-out equipment, and to what extent proper equipment is supplied to these troops.

I do not know how far I need to go in following Mr. Senter in his trip around the world. But it does indicate how difficult it is to answer the reports of a reporter as quoted by a member. There used to be a pretty good rule that you could not read newspaper reports in the house, because they are not evidence.
Now, with regard to what he said about this exercise-I was not there and I have never seen the report to which reference is made, and to which the hon. member referred. It must have escaped me. But I can tell him I am informed that this exercise was not the biggest exercise ever held in peacetime.
That is how it was advertised in all the papers.
I am not responsible for the papers.
Your P.R.O.'s are, though.

Not at all. He says that there was no divisional artillery. This was a brigade exercise, with only three battalions who were to go to Korea. They are in Korea, and so
Supply-National Defence far as I know they are doing excellently. They were the three battalions of the R.C.R.'s, the P.P.C.L.I.'s-no, the Black Watch and the Second Queens-
Who else, tell me?

And the Fourth Guards. These are very good battalions. They had a brigade exercise, but for the purpose of holding the exercise within the framework of a division they asked some reserve units to come in to form up the framework of a division. Any hon. member who served in any armed force in any war knows that you have exercises at the divisional level with sometimes no more than 150 officers present. That sometimes is done.
Then, the kind of remarks the hon. member has made about equipment-I just do not understand them, because we have no end of 25-pounder guns. We have given away probably a thousand. We have a surplus still, and they are available at command headquarters, as is all other equipment, for use by the reserves, as they can be used to advantage by them. It is not distributed to units beyond their capacity to use, store and maintain it, and that makes sense too, and that is because the reserve forces want it that way.
With regard to this business of equipment of the brigade overseas, I think the senior member for Halifax made a very good intervention, but the hon. member for Calgary North said that I should have made an inquiry and got a report. But I got a report of all this as soon as I saw the Senter piece. But I should like to refer to this against the background of the previous Senter piece:
Canadians draw Soviet interest as commonwealth exercises open.
That is the first part of it.
Canadians beat "desert rats", dominion's brigade in Germany excels in week-long commonwealth army exercises.
That was the second article:
Calgary units star in "War".
Canadian infantry put on good show against crack British in German scheme.
That was the third article. It was in this latter one that he dealt with equipment. Perhaps I will agree with the hon. member when he says that this was a good job and a very authentic and reliable reporter with regard to the first three articles, but when he comes to the fourth I must only assume that he has picked out bits and pieces of the kind of talk that you get around if you look for that kind of talk. This again is significant. I have the word of the chief of the general staff that any shortages that developed would be of a temporary nature only, and

Supply-National Defence would represent only the time necessary to call on reserves on the continent or in the United Kingdom.
Then a very big thing was made of the shortages of shoe laces. Well, now, shoe laces are not a very important element in fighting, but still it is a very important element in veracity, and I took this one up, too, and I had a signal sent across to the other side asking: "How many shoe laces have you got?" That is the kind of thing we are led into by this kind of talk, and I think it is a waste of public money. However, I found out that I have here from Brigadier Anderson in West Germany, a very fine officer commanding the brigade, information that we have a total of 5,206 pairs of shoe laces in the brigade, and I assure the hon. gentleman that there is no shortage.
The point is, when did they get them, after this article was written?

They could not get them after.
The hon. member made some remarks about anti-tank activities. Our troops are trained in anti-tank activities, whether they are armour, artillery or infantry, and that is about the biggest single item, the biggest single aspect of the field training that they have to do. How he can say they are not trained in anti-tank activities, I do not know, because he must have known. I have been at exercises at Wainwright and Petawawa and he must have been; I have seen them in Germany and seen them constantly in films that have been taken-there is a major field of continuous anti-tank activities. We try to have the latest types of training work, the latest type of dropping is practised, and they use the best kind of equipment.

On the basis of some five or six years experience of this, I can assure the minister that his remarks that everybody is trained in anti-tank activities and so forth merely indicate his complete lack of comprehension in regard to the role of these antitank guns and the methods of handling them, deploying them and everything else. When he says the infantry, the armour and everybody else are trained in the matter of antitank defence, he is talking about the medium anti-tank defence of a particular area where the platoon is or the company or anything else along that line. The very fact that he made that statement shows that he knows absolutely nothing of what I was talking about, just absolutely nothing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Do you know?

I do not know what the hon. member is talking about.
[Mr. Claxton.l

The minister's remarks
prove that he does not know, or he would not have made the remarks he did.

He talks about heavy antitank guns. We have anti-tank guns as a part of the tank equipment in the Centurions, and they occupy today an anti-tank role. That is their role. If he is talking about something heavier than that-
No, I am not talking about that. They are not organized to carry out the role. That is what I was saying, they cannot do it.
They are doing it steadily.

They cannot do it
effectively.
They are doing it steadily.
Mr. Chairman, he says they are doing it steadily. It is indicated in this article that an organized tank troop, tank squadrons cannot carry out that role effectively; it just cannot be done.

I have a subject here in which the minister is thoroughly informed, but he should give some information to the committee on this. This is the last topic I propose raising, and I shall be as brief as possible. A major decision was made in regard to the units within the Canadian army some time last year, and the Regiment of Canadian Guards was organized in October. On November 26, when the minister spoke in the House of Commons and gave a review of the situation in so far as national defence is concerned, he did not mention this major decision, nor did he mention it on May 20 when he spoke in this particular debate, and I wondered at his reticence in regard to this matter.
Why should we not be informed when a new departure is entered upon, a new active regiment is formed? I put some questions on the order paper to elicit information. The minister will recall that subsequently I asked him about the order of seniority of the regiments. There are not very many of them but at the moment he could not recall what it was, and yet a major decision to create the Regiment of Canadian Guards was made some time last year and this new regiment was named first in the seniority list. That is a complete departure in recent times from the army tradition, and some explanation should be forthcoming.
Well, the only way we have of getting information here is by questions on the order paper or by asking the minister. I did what I could. I asked him to name the infantry regiments in the Canadian army, when they

were formed and to give their battle honours. Of course the committee will recall the astonishing information which came as a result of these questions. The answer as to the infantry regiments is as follows, and I think their names should be recorded.
What is the date of that?

March 10, 1954. My question was:
What are the infantry regiments of the Canadian active army?
The answer was:-
The following are the infantry regiments of the Canadian army, active force:	(a) The Regiment
of Canadian Guards; (b) The Royal Canadian Regiment; (c) Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry; (d) Royal 22e Regiment; (e) The Queen's Own Rifles of Canada; (f) The Black Watch (Royal Highland Regiment) of Canada.
Then I asked for the dates when these regiments were originally formed. The answer was:
Their dates of original formation are: (a) October 16, 1953;
That is the Regiment of Canadian Guards. The Royal Canadian Regiment, December 21, 1883; Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, August 10, 1914; Royal 22e, October 22, 1914; Queen's Own, April 26, 1860; the Black Watch, January 1, 1862. My third question was:
What are the battle honours of each regiment?
The answer to that I will not read in full but part of the answer reads:
(a) The Regiment of Canadian Guards: none.
So here we are faced with this situation. The first regiment in seniority of the infantry regiments in the Canadian army is the Regiment of Canadian Guards, organized in October, 1953, carrying no battle honours. If you look at these other famous regiments you will see that their battle honours run from 20 to 27 and that is not counting the battle honours which will be accorded them after the second world war and for Korea. The older regiments have a great tradition behind them. I shall not dwell on the statement on the value and importance of tradition made this afternoon by the hon. member for Simcoe North in very fine terms. It is important, as he pointed out. Here we have a new regiment the first of the line and the senior regiment of the Canadian army with no tradition behind it.
Shame.

I wonder why the minister in organizing this new regiment did not bring behind it some of the other regiments which have an honourable history in the Canadian
Supply-National Defence army. He could have incorporated the foot-guards, the horseguards, or the Canadian Grenadier Guards. These names are not unfamiliar within the army. Why were they not made a part of this regiment and their battle honours carried over so that men serving in this new regiment would have something behind them which would serve as an inspiration?
I shall not read a newspaper report, Mr. Chairman, but I would like to refer to an advertisement which has been put in the newspapers and which is the responsibility of the Department of National Defence. It reads:
Applications now being accepted for the new
Regiment of Canadian Guards.
And then listen to the sentences which follow:	"Second to none on the -parade
ground." That seems to be the first matter of importance.
Never fought and were never defeated.
I wonder if this is a great inducement-
Quack! Quack!
Listen to the crows.

Then it goes on to say:
Incorporating the colour and smartness of military tradition at its finest, the Canadian guards ranks first among the army's regular infantry regiments.
Further on it says:
Right now there is a requirement for young men who would like to share in the colourful dress and ceremonial activities of the new Canadian guards.
Chocolate soldiers.

I was a bit shocked in 1946, Mr. Chairman, when I returned from overseas to see advertisements appearing in our newspapers and carried on buses urging young men to join the forces and offering them security. I think that was a remarkable statement to be put out, to urge young men of 18 and 19 to enter the services in search of security. Fortunately those advertisements disappeared and were replaced by others which made a different appeal to the young and active members of the population. This advertisement for the Canadian guards is reverting to that type of thing which appeared in 1946, and which places the emphasis in the wrong direction.
I do not know whether the men who are in the Regiment of Canadian Guards have been drafted or in what manner it has been formed but I hope the minister will give us a complete statement. My sympathy goes to those men who will be attempting to do their duty as they see it and who have back of
6418	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence them no tradition. It could have been arranged that they had something back of them in the way of tradition. But instead of that the emphasis is put on the parade ground and on ceremonial drill. In this century during which we have had war for most of the time we have no time for that type of emphasis. There is a place for ceremonial drill, for fine trappings and for good appearance for men in the armed services, but surely the emphasis should be on other matters. The emphasis must be on fighting quality and the men who enter the armed services must be prepared to risk their lives, and they will risk their lives if back of them they have a tradition within their regiment to look up to and which will comfort them in time of peril. Let me just quote from Field Marshal Sir William Slim, former chief of the imperial staff:
One vital element In army life is pride of regiment which is still the foundation of the British soldier's stubborn valour.
Pride in regiment is an important thing.
I am not unaware that regiments formed in time of war and placed on active service can very quickly acquire esprit de corps and build up a tradition such as was done by the Royal 22nd and the Princess Patricia's in the first world war. I have known regiments in both world wars, hastily formed and put into action which soon developed a fine esprit de corps and a magnificent tradition. But it is only on the battlefield that that can be developed and it seems to me to be rather a mistake to organize now, out of the blue, a regiment such as this and giving it the rather famous name of the Canadian guards with the implication that it is-and I believe it is to be-affiliated with the guards of Great Britain. That famous name is being used and yet behind this regiment there is nothing in the way of tradition. It will be difficult for the officers and men serving in the Canadian guards when they come in contact with some other regiment just to rest on their laurels as being a great parade ground regiment or a regiment expert on ceremonial duties. They have no tradition behind them of service on the battlefield and I think they are being placed in an awkward position. My sympathies go out to the officers and men who are at present serving in that regiment.
There is still time for the minister to do something about it. He can make the necessary arrangements to incorporate in that regiment some of these others regiments in Canadian history which have an honourable record. I do not know why the minister should not explain to the house at an early date when decisions such as this are taken so as to avoid misrepresentation, if you like, 

and misunderstanding, and to avoid criticism. We would gladly have heard him on November 26 with regard to this major decision, but not a word was said and we were dependent on the press and advertisements in the newspapers for information of this nature.
I hope the minister will tell us the purpose behind this and what he proposes to do to give this regiment something more than is implied in the advertisement to which I referred. It cannot compete properly with these other famous regiments, with their great tradition behind them, on such a slim basis as that. It has been named the senior regiment in the Canadian infantry and these other regiments with a much longer service have been overlooked. I hope that it is not intended to be just an imitation of the guards of England who are held in the highest respect among fighting men throughout the world. I hope it is not that. We do not want in this country an imitation of something elsewhere. We have our own products.
But as I say, the word "Guards" has been used in the Canadian army for many long years by those other regiments that I have mentioned and we could quite properly use it if we incorporate them in this formation in some way. But at the moment the impression abroad is that this is some new regiment designed to be second to none on the parade ground, designed to be first in executing ceremonial drill, with no fighting tradition behind it and not being prepared for battle. I think that the wrong type of suggestion is being made to our young men to join that regiment. I would not have taken this time on this subject, Mr. Chairman, had the Minister of National Defence earlier in the year taken the house into his confidence in this matter and given us the information which we deserve to have.

I think I should answer the hon. member, Mr. Chairman. He says he did not get any information. A release was issued in my name announcing this decision. I should say it would be in October, 1953. The regiment came into existence. They started work. Then the hon. member asked a question which was answered on March 10, 1954 giving him the information. But then all this kind of thing that he has just said was raised by another hon. member on May 21, 1954, as reported at page 4974 of Hansard. It is all there. Why he should be so greatly concerned about the matter, I do not know.
I can tell him that the regiment of guards is going great guns. It is derived from some famous units of the Canadian army. The first regiment of the guards is derived from

the third battalion of the R.C.R.'s. The second regiment is derived from the third battalion of the P.P.C.L.I. The third regiment is derived from the first infantry battalion which is in turn derived from five famous units of the reserve forces. The fourth guards battalion is derived from the second Canadian infantry battalion and is now on service in Korea.
As far as I know the question has been raised-and I think I am right-only by the hon. member for Peel, I think it was, and this hon. member who has raised the question tonight. I have not had a single word of complaint from either the old battalions or the new. They are getting along well. They are working well. They are doing their job. They are good Canadians. They are going to be good soldiers. They have a fine background of tradition through their origin. By what other name you could call them to suit the Canadian scene at that particular moment, I do not know.

Mr. Chairman, when you take an unknown regiment and put it'at the top of the list of Canadian regiments and put last the famous Queen's Own regiment of the city of Toronto and the little black devils of Winnipeg, I think some comment should be made. The minister said today he was talking about many well known Canadian regiments. Let me remind the minister that those regiments were Canadian in Canada before he was ever thought of as a Canadian.
Louder.

The Liberal crows from Toronto are not men enough to get up on their feet and defend the great and famous Queen's Own Rifles of Toronto. My greatgrandfather fought in that regiment for twenty years, or rather served in that regiment for twenty years. I had the great honour and privilege of serving with the black devils of Winnipeg.
Bragging.

That is not bragging. Let us have the facts truthfully about it and they will learn something if they try it. I resent the fact-not only with respect to my regiment but with respect to the Queen's Own in which my great-grandfather served-that we bring up a new regiment or a new name, try to put tradition behind that regiment and call it the first regiment of Canada.
The hon. member is helping a lot.

They threw the torch for you to carry, you Canadians. The men who died in Flanders fields threw the torch to
Supply-National Defence you. When we have a Minister of National Defence who throws that torch in the gutter-
Oh, oh.
Do not "oh, oh" me. You will not stop me from telling the truth.
This is all nonsense.
Oh, do not be so ridiculous.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

They handed on the torch for it to be carried by the veterans in the first war and the veterans in the second war. Let me say this to you men in the house tonight who served as soldiers in the first and the second war. You are letting the torch down as long as you let a man like the one we have today, as the head of our Department of National Defence, lower the name of the men who died and the regiments for which they fought, and put them down at the very bottom of the list as far as the standing of Canadian regiments goes. It is something that is on their conscience, as it should be. You men belong to a different party from that to which I belong, and sit on the opposite side of the house. I am not talking for a political purpose. I am talking about a disgrace that has been brought on the name of famous regiments in this country who protected this country so that we tonight can sit in parliament.
Woof!

It is time you learned something about the traditions of Canada rather than talk about things you do not appreciate. You know nothing about Canada's traditions or how the soldiers died and bled on the battlefield.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: I know more about it than you do.
Then why do you not voice your truthful opinion instead of being a rubber stamp for the government?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Why do you not?

You never heard a shot fired in your life. You never fought and never were wounded. That is your record. Yet you have had more to say than any man in the Liberal party. We expected more than that from you. I am fighting for these men who gave their lives in defence of this country and so made it possible for you to sit in parliament and drag their famous names down to the lowest standing among the Canadian regiments. We have a Minister of National Defence who forms a guards regiment out of a hodgepodge of other regiments which nobody knows very well and he puts down at the bottom of the list the

Supply-National Defence famous rifle regiments of Canada, the Queen's Own of Toronto and the little black devils of Winnipeg, famous regiments of this country who fought a hundred years ago in defence of this country, from famous regiments of the old country, the Black Watch-
Oh, oh.

You do not like it, you men of the Liberal party. Shame on you. You have not the gumption to stand up and even defend the dead soldiers. You sit here and you let the Minister of National Defence take all their traditions from you. You are afraid to stand up and be men, every one of you.
Oh, oh.

There comes a time in every man's life when he has got enough and says, "So far I will go and no further". But here we find a man who takes the "Rule, Britannia" out of the navy, the crown off the royal flying corps badges and forms a new regiment, calls it the guards and tries to justify his stand by saying, "We have put in one common cauldron some Canadian regiments". But he has by-passed regiments that are now in the permanent forces of Canada and has put the famous rifle regiments at the bottom of the list of Canadian regiments. The Minister of National Defence, supported by you Liberals, you Canadians, has done it.
Oh, oh.
All right. It will never be said that Julian Ferguson would ever be so subservient to any party that he would sink into that kind of mire, thank God.

I
object strongly to the attack by the hon. member for Simcoe North on the senior member for Halifax whose father is now lying in Flanders fields and has lain there since world war I.

The father handed on a torch which he should now be carrying. I am not standing on my father's glory. I am standing on the glory of the men who died, including his father for whom I have every regard.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Not only his father. Don't you try to defend him, Mister.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we pass on to the reserve force?

Before we deal with the question of the reserve force I should like to say that the units of the reserve forces have contributed to the various units of the active forces. There has been a good deal of


difficulty in raising the units for the new active forces, and in order not to emphasize too much the decision which had to be made as to the order of seniority of the various units of the forces I think a fair effort was made by the personnel of the defence department to try to give credit to the many units which have a long record in the Canadian army. Rather than single out two or three units in order to perpetuate them in the active force, the decision was made to create this new regiment of guards. I do not quite know how a different decision could have been reached had the desire been to give credit to the great many units of the reserve army. I am not going to say any more about that matter. Coming to the question of the reserve army-
May I interrupt the hon. member for a moment? I have one question respecting the active army. May I ask it now, or will it be understood that I can ask it later?
All right.
What forces of the Canadian army are stationed in the Yukon? What is their role, what is their equipment and what is the estimated cost of maintaining them for a year?

There are two sets of activities centred in the Yukon. The first is the part played mostly by the Royal Canadian Engineers in the maintenance and Qperation of the northwest highway system. The second is the operation of the Northwest Territories and Yukon telegraph system. The first has been carried on since the highway was handed over to the Royal Canadian Engineers in 1946, I believe. While we do not keep the accounts segregated that way any longer, my recollection is that the cost of maintenance and operation of the highway system is about $6 million a year. That would cover about 1,200 miles and it covers a good deal of replacement of capital installations such as bridges, culverts and the like on a more permanent basis. We are doing a steady program of replacement.
The Northwest Territories and Yukon telegraph system supplies all the telecommunication services, civilian and military, in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. Speaking again from memory, I believe there are twenty-one stations in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. They carry all the military traffic, all the government service and most of the commercial. My recollection would be that the amount of revenue they take from handling commercial traffic varies but averages approximately $500,000 a year.

They handle a good many hundred thousand messages for the armed forces, weather stations and other government services, so that these are two very considerable operations, one by the engineers and the other by the signals.

Would I be correct in summarizing what the minister has said in this way, that the units there are purely technical, engineers and signals, and that their duties are to maintain roads and communications? That tells the whole story of the troops located there, does it?
Yes, if the hon. member is talking about the army only. There are of course some elements of Canadian Rangers and some reserve force elements, but I am talking about the active force army.

I think the figure the minister gave for the road was for the upkeep on the road. Is that intended to cover also the cost of these units or can he segregate the cost of these units? That is the figure I seek, not the maintenance of the road but the expense of the units themselves.

Pay and allowances for the Northwest Territories and Yukon road system for 1953-54 amounted to $572,000, and for 1954-55 they are $581,000. A total of seven officers and 178 men are engaged in this operation. With respect to the northwest telegraph system the cash estimate was less than I said because it does not include some capital expenditures. This is just pay and allowances. For 1953-54 the pay and allowances were $1,215,000, and for 1954-55, $1,550,000. There is a total of 60 officers, 400 men and 322 civilians.
Would the minister give us the rank of the commanding officer?
Brigadier.

What is the relationship of this to the Department of Public Works? There was a report that the Department of Public Works had taken over the highway and there seemed to be some misunderstanding about it.

The Department of National Defence and the Department of Public Works are considering whether or not it would be a good thing for the Department of Public Works to take over this operation. We have had it in defence for the last eight years. It has now become stabilized, and more and more it is becoming essentially a civilian operation. We feel that it might be more economical and practical for it to be taken over by the Department of Public Works. Discussions are going on towards that end. No details have been arrived at, but I think
Supply-National Defence it is moving along in the direction of the Department of Public Works taking it over.
A few minutes ago I understood the minister to say that the third battalion of the guards regiment was formed by five reserve units. Would he give us the names of those reserve units?

I think there is a matter I should like to mention upon which the minister and I can agree more readily than the other matters I have mentioned. I refer to some complaints I have in regard to mail. I understand that so far as mail to Korea is concerned, there have been no complaints. Practically everyone has been well satisfied

Supply-National Defence with it in recent months. There was some delay, but in recent months I believe the situation has been improved.
There have been, however, some complaints in connection with mail to Europe. I understand that the Canadian army postal corps looks after the mail for both the army and the air force in Europe. I understand they do an extremely good job of it and there is no complaint from that point of view. I understand, however, that the mail sometimes comes later than some people feel is necessary because of the fact that all the mail going to Europe has to go via T.C.A. even though there are R.C.A.F. planes going over. Although it would provide better service the mail cannot go via R.C.A.F. because it would mean competition with T.C.A. When the minister replies, I should like him to comment on that. I ask him if that is indeed the case, and if it is the case, I would ask him if he could not get that corrected so the service would be improved.
Another complaint I have received concerns the price of mail. The complaint in this regard is that Canadian rates are much higher than those of the British or United States servicemen alongside of whom the Canadians are serving. The British get ordinary letters for twopence-halfpenny and send air mail letters for sixpence for the first half ounce. The United States servicemen get their mail at the regular civilian rate of 6 cents. The Canadian rates are 5 cents for ordinary letters, which is twice the British rate, and 15 cents for a half ounce air mail. This rate is equivalent to one shilling threepence or three times the British rate. This is not a very important matter, I realize, but it is these little things, I have found in my personal experience, that cause a lot of trouble. These things such as the type of food, the way it is being prepared or served, some of these complaints over mail, are the things that cause a lot of trouble completely out of proportion to their own intrinsic importance. If one looks after a lot of the little things, very frequently you will have a unit in which there is no trouble and where the spirit and morale is very much better than it would be if you let a few of these little things go along with a lot of people labouring under a sense of injustice.
In addition to that, there is another complaint. I am informed that so far as the mail in Canada is concerned people on a station have to get their mail through the station post office. They cannot have a box there or anything along that line. The mail is put in a rack and they have to go and pick it up. They are not allowed to have the mail delivered to the general delivery in the place
[Mr. Harkness.l

where they happen to be or to have a box there. This is another matter that is not very important, but as I say it is the small complaints that cause difficulty. They are matters which I believe the minister should investigate. I have received representations on the actual conditions that exist, and he may perhaps get them corrected.

I agree with the hon. member about the importance of mail. This is something we have been trying to look after very carefully. I must say that I have had very few complaints, generally speaking. The mail seems to have been very well delivered. I have had no complaints at all about delivery to Europe.
I said my reports on the Canadian postal corps were excellent. Everybody agreed they did a good job.

I shall be glad to look into it. If the R.C.A.F. do not carry mail to Europe it may be because their airlift is fully occupied by their own loads. We have hired a good deal of T.C.A. airlift service to Europe to service the R.C.A.F. abroad. There may be something also in connection with licences to carry mail or something of that kind.
Now, with regard to rates, I am very surprised at the complaint. I have never heard the suggestion before that rates were other than reasonable. Ordinary letter rate is 4 cents to the orient.
I was talking about Europe.
The air mail rate to the Orient is 7 cents for the first ounce. The air mail rate to Europe is 15 cents each half ounce.
That is what I said.
The forces letter rate is 5 cents, which would seem to be a very reasonable rate, in view of the distance to Europe.
The point is, as I understand it, that the people in Europe have to pay the regular rate. They do not get a forces letter rate, as the British do.

I was going to speak on the reserve forces.

If we have reached that point I believe I should make a statement. In my opening speech on May 20, and again in reply on May 21, I said that I would make a statement on the reserve forces at this time when

we came to this item. It would seem to be the most appropriate time to do so.
The reserve army, or the non-permanent active militia, as it was called, played the major role in the build-up of the Canadian army during the great war 1914-18 and the second world war, and contributed greatly to the fine record of Canada in both these wars.
Since the end of the second world war, and particularly during the last five years, there have been a number of developments which must be taken into account in considering the organization of the reserve army so as to be best prepared at any given time to meet an emergency if and when it should occur.
These developments include the war in Korea; commitment of an infantry brigade to the NATO forces in western Europe; rotation requirements; increasing emphasis on continental defence; a tenfold increase in the size of the regular army since 1939 and an even more considerable increase in its fighting effectiveness.
It has come to be generally accepted that if there were a third world war it would fall into two or more fairly well-defined stages, and the requirements of the Canadian army in the first stage could only be met by fulltime or regular forces.
The role of the reserve force of the army today is, therefore, to provide a partially trained and equipped force as the nucleus of units to be mobilized and brought up to strength in the case of an emergency. The effectiveness of the reserve force depends upon a strong hard corps of volunteers, and it also depends on the active support of Canadian people throughout the country.
In May of last year the chief of the general staff, on the recommendation of the conference of defence associations and with the concurrence of the Minister of National Defence, established a committee of distinguished soldiers for the purpose of examining, reporting and recommending on the organization, training and administration of the Canadian army reserve force with a view to improving its effectiveness.
This committee was headed by Major General Howard Kennedy, C.B.E., M.C., and had, as additional members, Major General E. J. Renaud, C.B., C.B.E., C.D., and Major General H. F. G. Letson, C.B., C.B.E., M.C., E.D. The wide experience in civil and military affairs of the members of this committee and in particular the close association of Major Generals Kennedy and Letson with the reserve force over a period of many years, made them particularly suited to study and advise on problems of the reserve force.
Supply-National Defence Before beginning their survey, this committee was thoroughly briefed concerning peace and wartime plans for the Canadian forces. In the course of its examination and study the committee visited reserve force units from coast to coast, both at their local headquarters and during annual camp. Discussions were held with senior reserve force officers of all corps. The recommendations of the committee, therefore, were based on long experience and on close and comprehensive study on the ground of conditions and problems.
The report of the committee was submitted to the chief of the general staff in January last. It has been examined by army headquarters and discussed in detail with the conference of defence associations, as well as the general officers commanding the five army commands.
It should be observed that no particular reference is made to the various types of training-at summer or other camps, corps schools, week-end training at areas near unit headquarters, et cetera-because great latitude is already allowed each command, area and unit, so as to enable each unit best to meet local conditions.
As a result of the report and the detailed study and consideration which followed, it has now been decided to take the following steps:
1.	There will be an extensive reorganization of militia units to relate them more closely to possible wartime requirements, effective peacetime training and local support. This reorganization includes:
(a) Present brigade and other formation headquarters will be replaced by a new type to be known as militia group headquarters:
(b)	as the anti-tank defence role has been transferred from the artillery to the armoured corps, a number of artillery units will be converted:
(c)	excess anti-aircraft will be converted to other types of artillery or amalgamated with units of other corps;
(d)	as coast defence has become the primary responsibility of the navy and air force, the coast defence units will become harbour defence batteries:
(e)	as the type of training in field park squadrons is not suited to the reserve force, field park squadrons of the reserve force will be converted to or included in field squadrons:
(f)	two of the signal regiments are to be amalgamated to form one signal regiment;
(g)	the Royal Canadian Army Service Corps, the Royal Canadian Army Medical Corps, and the Royal Canadian Ordnance Corps will be reorganized to reflect as closely as possible the potential support in their localities;
(h)	there will be a number of changes in infantry formations.
2.	The Canadian army (reserve force) is to be renamed the Canadian army (militia).
3.	The Canadian army (active) will be known as the Canadian army (regular).
4.	There will be an adviser to the chief of the general staff in militia matters. The officer to be

Supply-National Defence selected will be a senior officer with extensive service in the reserve. The first officer appointed is Major-General H. F. G. Letson, C.B., C.B.E., M.C.,
E.D.	.	.	.
5.	A new directorate combining militia and cadets will be set up at army headquarters.
6.	Accommodation and training facilities for the militia are being reviewed and new construction and additional facilities will be progressively provided as funds permit.
7.	Steps are being taken to explain, emphasize and enforce the obligations which a man undertakes on joining a unit of the militia.
8.	Minimum attendance, equivalent to 15 days' training, will be necessary before a member of the militia is entitled to receive pay.
9.	The foregoing provision must be taken with a new bonus to be paid to each individual attending annual camp, provided he has attended not less than 75 per cent of local unit training in the six months preceding summer camp.
10.	Training standards will be amended to enable a militia soldier to obtain his qualification in stages and to receive credit for any stage reached.
11.	Field summer uniforms are to be issued for wear at camp and local headquarters training in warm weather.
12.	Qualification badges in various military trades and specialties will be worn on uniforms as well as chevrons to denote length of service in the militia.
13.	Full-time assistance is to be provided on an increased scale to aid militia units in their administration.
14.	Unit allowances are to be simplified and consolidated to reduce the work involved in bookkeeping.
15.	Grants for bands will be increased and provision of suitable instruments will be accelerated under a replacement program.
16. An allowance will be made for a dress uniform for bands.
17.	In order to provide assistance in arranging local publicity for militia units, each HQ and major unit will be able to have an additional militia officer specifically for public relations duties.
18.	There will be a substantial increase in grants to army cadet units and additional clothing will be provided for them.
19.	Officers, serving in various honorary appointments, many of whom have done much to promote interest in the service, will be eligible for 'he Canadian forces decoration.
20.	Income tax will now be deducted at source for all members of the militia unless a member claims that his total net taxable income is below the minimum taxable and requests that no deductions be made.
The action outlined here has been considered with the committee and is in accordance with its views.
In dealing with this matter, I should like to emphasize that the steps being taken with respect to the army reserve force are in effect the views of the reserve force itself, as ascertained and weighed by the committee under Major General Kennedy.
I should add that while the committee under Major General Kennedy made recommendations with regard to specific units, of necessity the list of specific units that were to be affected was not put before the conference and therefore was not specifically

approved by it, though the conference did approve, in principle, the general steps I have outlined.
Not only is this the case but the changes recommended have all been discussed with the conference of defence associations, representing the twelve different corps associations. This body, which represents every single unit in the reserve forces, has unanimously approved the committee's recommendat.'ins to which I have referred, thus indicating that these recommendations have the active support of all its member corps.
The changes proposed are planned to tap the resources of interested and available personnel so as to provide the best basis for the build-up of forces that may be required in the second or later stages of another world war. The over-all number of units will be substantially reduced. It is expected that at the outset these changes may result in some reductions in the total number of officers and men on strength. But it is expected that they will result in more effective use of personnel.
It is hoped to work all these changes out so that there will be as few as possible actual disbandments and no loss of existing support or local interest. Further consideration is being expedited in the hope that all necessary changes will be satisfactorily completed at an early date. The reserve force associations have promised their strong support in carrying all this into effect.
In conclusion, I should like to appeal to the House of Commons sitting in committee and to the public generally to support the steps to which I have referred. The3r are designed to meet anticipated changes in the needs and requirements of the service and to produce increased efficiency and effectiveness of the reserve force of the army, henceforth to be known as the Canadian Army (militia). The support of the reserve force associations will, I am sure, ensure success in carrying out the new policies and changes which I have announced but the degree of that success will rest primarily on the popular support accorded it throughout the country. If this support is not continuously given many of these improvements and changes will be largely vitiated. The role, importance, and potentialities of the reserve force must be understood and acted upon.
The militia units will in no small degree be community units. Community organizations can do much toward educating our youth in the value of our free institutions. They can point out that it is the duty of each individual Canadian to do what he can

to safeguard these institutions by service in the regular or reserve forces. Employers and trade unions can assist by encouraging young men and women to join the militia and by making it possible for them to acquire the necessary training and particularly practical training at summer camps.
The citizen who plays his part in Canada's militia is serving the interests of his country at the expense of his own free time. He must be made to feel that the public appreciates the effort he is making in peacetime just as much as the appreciation shown to those who participate in active service. All our citizens can thus contribute to creating the realization in our youth that service in the militia is an honourable duty which all should discharge in order that as many Canadians as possible may be made ready to defend their country.

Mr. Chairman, of course you will realize it would be extremely difficult to comment adequately upon this important document which we have received only just this minute. In fact very few hon. members have even received a copy, and have to depend upon what they heard the minister say. I cannot help expressing regret that earlier publicity has not been given to the findings of this committee. As long ago as January of this year I asked the minister whether he intended to table the Kennedy report. He said he was not prepared to do that as it was a report prepared at the request of the chief on the general staff but that he would-and these were his words-report to the house very shortly. Well, a good many months have gone by since then, and there has been much uncertainty amongst the units of the Canadian Army (militia), as it is now to be called, because of this long delay.
We are told that the recommendations of the report, which the minister is prepared to accept, have been concurred in by the various defence associations. Of course no reference was made to the recommendations of the report which the minister is not prepared to accept, and that must unfortunately remain a closed book because we are not privileged to see the report. I hope they are not extensive because, as the minister has said, the success of the reserve army, of the militia unit, depends entirely upon the public support that they receive. We all believe that a reserve force is necessary.
General Gruenther has emphasized the importance of the reserves. Well, we cannot have an adequate and an efficient reserve force unless not only members of parliament but the whole public get behind those units.

If there is any comment at the present moment as to the recommendations of this report, I think it is likely to be upon the fact that we really do not know what the Kennedy report says and what their main recommendations or what the other recommendations are that the minister is not prepared to accept.
In those items which were mentioned I note with particular satisfaction that there is to be an adviser to the chief of the general staff on militia matters. The emphasis on our forces has veered in recent years from the reserve forces to the active forces. Remember that in the days before world war II there was a very small active force and the energies of the Department of National Defence and the staffs across the country were mainly directed to increasing the efficiency of the reserve units. After the second world war that emphasis was changed., and there has to a certain extent been a neglect of the reserve units. By appointing a particular adviser to the chief of the general staff and a man of the experience, both with the reserve and in special duties, of Major General Letson, we may rest assured that the requirements of the reserve forces in the future will be vigorously presented to the chief of the general staff.
As lar as I can gather from recommendation No. 9, it would seem that there will be a bonus paid now to men who have completed a certain percentage of their training in camp. That is dependent upon their having carried out a certain number of days' training prior to moving into camp. I think that the change of name and change of status of the brigade commands is a step in the right direction, because quite obviously those brigade commands could not assume the ordinary duties of a brigade headquarters on, mobilization. I do not intend to comment further on this report at the present time. I am pleased that it has been referred to the defence associations. There is merely the announcement that there are going to be many changes and that will continue the uncertainty. Until the changes are published it will be very hard for the commanding officers of the various units to proceed with the training programs.
The one point which strikes me as perhaps not being as sound as I would like to have seen it is the fact that a reduction is being made in the number of anti-aircraft artillery. I should have thought that the reserve army would have been called upon to play a major role in the defence of this country and provide anti-aircraft defence for the localities in which they are stationed. We have heard a good deal about the need for increased emphasis being placed upon civil defence, and the dangers to which this country might be subjected in the event of a third world war. It would seem to me that anti-aircraft artillery units should work in close co-operation with the civil defence organizations of the land, and therefore I am surprised to hear the minister state-and I think I heard correctly-that there was to be a considerable reduction in the number of anti-aircraft units in the reserve army.

Mr. Chairman, since the minister has just made this statement tonight I have had no opportunity of studying it and I propose to make only one or two brief comments on it, particularly in view of the fact that the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, despite the extremely short notice, has covered the report very well. Following the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition
IMr. Pearkes.l

this morning, however, the minister stated in connection with the Kennedy report that there was no reason why the officials of the government should disclose the reasons for any action the government might take. I presume he had in mind the fact that he was going to give us this report tonight and his remarks struck me as rather peculiar because I have always understood that one of the duties of the opposition was to ask questions in regard to the reasons why the government took any particular action, and that one of their functions was to secure and probe into these reasons. I think the statement the minister made to the effect that there was no reason why the government should disclose reasons for any action they may take is directly contrary to our ordinary democratic procedures and the way in which we carry on government in this country.
I am extremely glad we have had this report. From what I could gather as the minister read his statement there are going to be quite a lot of changes which will help improve the reserve forces, which is an aim for which I think we are all striving. However, I am sorry we have not got the Kennedy report itself so that as a result we could form our own conclusions on the evidence presented by units all across Canada and gathered by the three generals who conducted the investigation. In other words, I think we in this house are entitled to have the reasons why the decision which has just been announced was arrived at and to know the basis on which it was arrived at. However, I am glad we at least have the statement made by the minister. One thing I noted in particular was that a definite decision has been taken to transfer the antitank corps at divisional level to the armoured corps, and that a number of anti-tank units will be transferred from artillery to the armoured corps. I am sure the artillery will very much regret losing those units but it will be to gain the advantage of armour and certainly I think it is a proper move to make. I think the self-propelled anti-tank guns in use today can be of better use in the armoured corps than in the artillery, and I think a move in this direction should have been made long before this. As I pointed out earlier, for the past two or three years we have not had any anti-tank units or components in our army at all, and I am extremely glad that we are now going to have these units as part of the armoured corps.

Mr. Chairman, I wanted to say a few words on the reserve army. I refrained this morning from saying anything about the reserve army although I am interested in it. We have a battalion in my area which gained fame during the last war and during the previous one, and I might say to the minister that there has been a great deal of dissatisfaction during the last few months and a lot of rumours due no doubt to the fact that this Kennedy committee has been going around and the officers and men do not know what is going to happen to them. As my colleague said a few minutes ago, I think it is important that the list of these battalions or regiments that are going to be maintained be posted soon. A great many of these units right now do not know what is going to happen. The officers are having a difficult time to get men out. The men are wondering whether the unit is going to be disbanded.
You would be surprised to know, Mr. Chairman, how much information about this report is around the country. How much of it is authentic is what we do not know. I think it is most unfortunate that the government do not see fit to inform members of parliament of the true facts about a report like this. We are the people who are approached when we go back to our constituencies. When we go to our homes these people want to know what is going on in Ottawa. They almost think we are not around in the house and that we do not even ask the department what is going on. When we tell them that the department will not disclose these facts, they are amazed. I want to bring out that point.
I think we are entitled to this information and that we should receive it at an early date. If you expect us and the public to give you the support which you need to have a successful reserve military force, you must pass out the information. That is the first lesson that we all learned in the army. You cannot carry out any successful exercise unless everybody is in the picture. You just cannot take out a few staff officers and a lot of brass and carry out a successful exercise. Anybody who is in the army will agree with me on that point. Everybody must be in the picture.
I believe we should have good reserve forces. I believe that they really will be the first line of defence in case of trouble. The active forces you have are all tied up and they will continue to be tied up, and they will be the last troops to get to the vital places where defence is necessary. Defence is therefore going to fall back on what you are now going to call the reserve or the
Supply-National Defence militia group. You therefore need the support of the public, and you will not get that support unless you put the public in the picture. If you do not put the members of parliament in the picture, you will not get the public in the picture. I therefore think it is important that we be told all the facts and that we be told them at an early date so that we can talk intelligently, so that we can help you, so that you can help the public, and so that we can get together and in cooperation have a good reserve unit.
I know that for a number of years before the last war it was not easy to get a reserve unit up to strength or up to standard. I was one of those who had the experience of spending not only a little bit of money and time but quite a bit of it. I may say that I never regretted it because we had a battalion which, when the war broke out, was one of the best in our brigade. It was selected, thank goodness, because of the fact that it had won the brigade prize for a number of years. That was not done by sitting back and not putting the public in the picture. You cannot expect to have a good reserve unit unless you have the businessmen, the ordinary farmers in the community and all the people behind that unit. In order to do that, you must give some support to the officers and to the members of parliament, the members of the legislature and the businessmen in that community.
I may sound a little bit drastic in this matter but really and truly I have sat back since the war and noticed the reserve unit going down and down. It has been going down because it has not been getting the support of the public; and it has not been getting the support of the public because nobody has ever come down to our area and invited to a meeting the ordinary citizens and the ordinary farmers from which we have to draw our recruits, the people in that community. Nobody has ever asked them to a meeting to explain what the reserve army is for or what role the reserve army is expected to carry out in case of an emergency. Unless you are prepared to do that, you will not get a good reserve unit. I plead with the minister.
Under this reorganization I hope that unit in my area will be one of the units that will be retained. I do not know whether it will be retained or not. It could be possible that it will not be retained. I suppose that better units will be selected. Maybe that matter has all been decided. But if it is retained you could have a good unit, if you give us some support. If you put us into the picture you will get my support and you will get the support of many other reserve officers

Supply-*National Defence who are there. At the moment they will not do one thing because they do not know -and this is a fact-what role the reserve army should be playing. I claim that is the fault of the army. It is not the civilians' fault. I can be backed up in that statement by many other officers with good service in the last war and in the first war and who did good service in the reserve units between the wars.
I impress this point upon the minister. You have got to pass on all the information that you possibly can. If you do that you will get the support of the people who will make a good service unit. Pay is not going to bring them in. Pleasure is not going to bring them in. Security is not going to bring them in, except the type of security that you have got to impress upon those young men. You must impress upon them that they need this training to protect their wives and families in case of emergency. That is the type of training that will bring them in. You have got to give them enthusiasm, not for the few dollars they will earn but because they really believe in a cause, because they believe there may be another war, and that if there were another war their service would be needed. I believe it is needed. I believe that is the type of training these young men need.

Unfortunately I did not make myself too clear at the time. Perhaps I can have this evening an enlargement upon that reply.
I asked the minister this question: In the case of veterans of world war II re-enlisting in the Canadian armed forces is any reference made to world war II records for screening purposes? In reply to that question I received the answer "Yes". I should like to go a little bit further and to ask the minister whether, in the case of these veterans of world war II re-enlisting- whether it be in the air force or in the army -any reference is made to the records of the Department of Veterans Affairs. If that is so it would avoid a situation that crops up periodically in our defence forces where an undesirable recruit seems to slip through the screening net, with considerable embarrassment to the department as well as to himself. I would appreciate it if the minister could reply to the extended question I have presented to him this evening.
I have also been interested in the washout rate among aircrew in particular. It has been suggested from time to time that because of the difficulty of obtaining a desirable type of recruit for aircrew training the wash-out rate is unnecessarily high among our R.C.A.F. recruits. Is it possible to give any information on this score and any statistics which will present a comparison of our wash-out rate with that of trainees from the other NATO countries participating in our air training scheme?
Recently the Department of National Defence has extended its excellent program for training university students in the various branches of the services. I note that on page 27 of the white paper, I believe it is, the total figure is given of the number of students taking part under the R.O.T.P. scheme. The figure for the R.C.A.F. is 1,984. I believe this scheme was further extended recently making it possible for university students to have a short experience in the armed forces during the summer recess with the hope of encouraging such students to participate in the more extensive R.O.T.P. scheme. Does the figure of 1,984 for the air force include this special group or does the total figure of officer cadets for all the armed forces that is given in the white paper, 6,955, include this particular group?
I also note that the expenditure for film displays and other material of that kind is up from $935,000 to $1,509,000 for the current year. This would suggest that the Department of National Defence is contemplating a more vigorous recruiting program than hitherto. It also suggests that perhaps the recruiting program has not been going

as well as anticipated with the result that the department considers there is a necessity of giving further publicity to this important aspect of our whole defence program.

In answer to the hon. member's interesting questions, he asked first whether, in the case of veterans of world war II desiring to enlist, any reference is made to their records in world war II. I am informed that when they apply to join one of the forms they sign is a form dealing with their previous war experience. That form is referred for further inquiry to the Department of Veterans Affairs which keeps the records of veterans of the first and second world wars. My understanding is that the answer is yes, but I do not want to suggest for a moment that this is done sufficiently rapidly to screen out people who may have had bad records. An effort is made, but this is a very large-scale operation. We are dealing with another government department, and I am not sure whether or not that is done in time to turn down a man on the score that he has had a bad record if he does not disclose it himself. However, a check is made.
The hon. member also asked about the wash-out rate for aircrew. This rate is not given in any country. We have checked this, and I think hon. members will appreciate the reasons for not doing so. I am not in a position to give any comparison between the wash-out rate for R.C.A.F. and other trainees. This is a matter which is receiving continuous consideration by everyone concerned in our air force and the other air forces, and we are working together very closely on it. I must say personally that I am reaching the point where, having had some experience and having discussed the matter extensively with experts in this field in other countries, I am beginning to doubt whether increasing the level of selection produces a corresponding decrease in the rate of losses in training. You get to a point where, whatever the rate of refusal on selection is, statistically the rate of losses in training appears to be just about the same, so that you could select out too high a proportion without getting corresponding returns. However, that is an idea of mine. Other people are testing the matter scientifically.
The hon. member also asked whether in the figures given in the white paper for R.O.T.P. personnel we include any of this new group he mentioned. I was not able to hear precisely what he said. If they are officer candidates from the universities or the service colleges then they are included. If, however, they were previously officers and are taking
Supply-National Defence refresher courses they are not included in that figure. The figure in the white paper is for officer candidates only.
The hon. member inquired about the expenditure in an item on page 317, I believe. I understand he was referring to the item for films, displays, broadcasting, advertising and other informational materials, $936,000 for this year and $936,700 for last year. It is very much the same figure. We feel it is desirable to maintain advertising at about the same level, but I can assure the hon. member and the house that this matter is being reviewed within the next two or three weeks to see if we cannot effect some further reduction in recruiting expenses. We have some experience in this regard. We did make a substantial reduction in March, April, May and June of 1950 and the rate of recruiting slipped very materially. We were about reaching our then targets or coming within sight of them. Then we had the Korean affair and it was necessary to build up the program again. Personally I am rather opposed to making too sharp a drop until we see whether or not we are maintaining our present levels in the services and increasing them slightly towards the targets.
Of course, hon. members should appreciate that as we attain our target, not that we will ever have any fixed target because we will be changing from year to year, but as we reach about the targets we will see that wasting will exactly equal intake and intake will equal wastage. We shall have an exact equilibrium. People will talk then about our high rates of wastage. Our aim will be to maintain our intake at precisely the level necessary to meet wastage. As long as we do that, we will be meeting the target.
Naturally, we will always be striving to keep down wastage in order to keep the men of experience. Actually our wastage rates for the three services are I believe very favourable. Let me put it this way, our rates of re-engagement for the three services are very favourable. I have got the rates for other countries and for ours, and they are improving in our country or holding their own, while relative to the others with which we are familiar, they are very much better. This is a good position, but I should like to see it still better.

I should like to ask one further question concerning the use of D.V.A. files. Can the minister indicate whether it has been the practice to refer to D.V.A. files since the beginning of recruiting in connection with the Korean campaign or recruiting since Korea or is it a new practice that has been added in recent times?
