This is relatively recent.

I have just one short question. I am not going to raise the matter which I understand is being discussed between the Department of Transport and the minister of defence, the matter of the skyways for the various planes, but I should like to draw the attention of the minister to the hundreds of millions of dollars Canada has invested in aeroplanes. Surely we do not want to see them damaged if it is at all possible to escape damage. We all know that accidents will happen, but why invite accidents?
The question I should like to ask the minister is: Is it not possible to issue and enforce orders that R.C.A.F. planes shall not deliberately buzz the major cities of the Dominion of Canada? I was home over the Easter week end for a few days, and not one but a number of aeroplanes zoomed and buzzed the major city of Vancouver. It was really frightening. The roar of the planes was such that you would have thought a plane was in trouble and coming down. All the windows rattled. People by the thousands dashed out of their homes to see what was happening. 1 did myself. Here were a number of planes, five or seven, zooming back and forth over the city of Vancouver. If there had been a slight defect in the plane, the pilot and crew were absolutely doomed, as was the property and lives of the people of Vancouver. Why is it allowed to continue? Can it not be stopped?

Both the Royal Canadian
naval air arm and the Royal Canadian Air Force have to fly by the rules regarding civil aviation. They are just as much subject to those rules as commercial aircraft, and that applies to low flying or flying on certain levels, flying by instruments and everything else. They are completely subject to the same rules. I can assure you that in the case of the two service air forces, these rules are strictly enforced. Whenever any infraction is found, severe disciplinary action is taken. When this happens a man may be dismissed from the service, and then very frequently I have representations made that he should be restored.
I know of the incident in Vancouver to which the hon. member referred. It was drawn to my attention before. This was an occasion when the naval air arm had been out doing some exercises at Patricia bay. On the way back from Patricia bay to the east they, as a way of celebrating the Queen's birthday, did a flypast over Vancouver. They understood that this had been advertised and cleared with the local people, the newspapers and so on. Apparently it was not, and it was a surprise. This was planned and organized
[Mr. Dinsdale.l

as a patriotic demonstration, as is done on numerous occasions. We had a magnificent flypast over Ottawa on the occasion of the coronation when 140 aircraft went by. Some of them were below ordinary flying height, but very little danger is involved in that. However, it is disturbing and I am assured there was a misunderstanding about it, otherwise it would not have occurred.
With regard to other matters, we simply are not in a position to say to the R.C.A.F. that they must not fly in or out of the airfields that have been built for the R.C.A.F. at vast expense to the Canadian people, whether they be at Moose Jaw, Saskatoon or any of the other places. Each of these airfields probably represents an investment of $30 million. They have to be located near a city and they are operated as safely as possible. At some of these airfields the trainees rise and descend at the rate of more than one a minute, so that the air may at times be infested with Harvards. If the weather is clear, there is no reason why that should represent a hazard.
In the case of the Moose Jaw business I have nothing to add to the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce who made the statement for the government in that connection. We are looking into it and we are hoping to arrive at some very sensible and reasonable provision which will make it less likely than the almost mathematical impossibility that a collision should occur. It is almost impossible to conceive that a collision should have occurred between those two aircraft in broad daylight; yet it did; that is being investigated.
Earlier in the day the minister indicated his intention of placing on the record a statement regarding fire-fighting equipment and facilities.

Yes, I did. The hon. member asked me about fire in R.C.A.F. hangars, and I promised to give him and other hon. members at various times, information about it. I thought it would be best if I dealt with all the questions at once. At the present time we have 137 hangars for storage or maintenance work. Of this total only 26 were constructed after the second world war. The new hangars are all of fire-resistant construction. The 161 older hangars cost a total of approximately $14 million when they were constructed. They were, of course, rushed up and were of temporary wooden construction. They have lasted much longer than planned, and many of them are still capable of being used, particularly in view of the fact to replace them all with modern fire-resistant types would cost approximately $177 million today. You get into a position

where the interest on the cost of replacement would be far bigger than the average amount of fire loss on this account, which has been about $700,000 a year.
Consequently, we have a replacement program with which we are proceeding, but on the basis of economy we would not be justified in tearing down these old hangars and replacing them even if we had the productive machinery and resources to do it at once.

I should like to stress, of course, that I did not at any time suggest they should tear down the old hangars and replace them. Would the minister indicate the system of fire watching that is maintained? If he recalls, when I was speaking previously, I quoted an editorial from one of the Calgary daily papers in which it was indicated that to the best of their knowledge an adequate system of fire watching was not maintained. I believe they pointed out that with the amount of investment in government hangars they would be warranted in having one person on duty at all times. We realize fully that when a fire starts in a hangar, at least if it makes any headway at all, it is just about impossible to stop it. But it does seem to me that if someone is on the spot at all times that a fire might very easily be detected in its very early stages, and there would probably be some opportunity of stopping it. Just what is the policy with respect to that?

At each air station they have a service fire-fighter squad which is highly trained and fully equipped. In this case it was on the scene of the fire within a minute of discovery. In addition, there are fire prevention services and patrols. They are arranged in accordance with the regulations laid down by headquarters of the three services and with the work of the fire marshals. If we had men constantly on duty at each of say six hangars it would mean 24 men a day, and would amount to a good deal of money.

Mr. Chairman, I have had some complaints from officers who served in the air force during the second world war and then went into civilian life, some of them working for various government departments. They were then called back into the service at the time of the Korean crisis. They were given leave of absence by the departments for only four years. Now they are in the position of either leaving the air force and forfeiting their gratuities-that is, if the air force would let them go; and the air force is under no obligation to do so-or, having overstayed their four years' leave of absence from the department of government, they have lost their jobs in civil employment.
Supply-National Defence What liaison is there between the Department of National Defence and other departments of government?
This is the first time the question has been brought to my attention. I will look into it.

Thank you very much. As a matter of fact I have taken it up with the department concerned. Now, I have a question regarding civil employees. I notice there is a very large increase in some classifications of employees. For example typists, cleaners and helpers. I suppose these are civilians who are employed to replace service personnel?
Yes.

In the case of cleaners and helpers, for instance, the number has increased from 39 to 482, as set out at page 315. Then, there are other large increases in some other trades, although those increases are not as great as the one I have indicated.
This is largely a reclassification by the civil service commission of a number of messmen positions to those of cleaners and helpers.
And I notice the same thing in connection with the corps of commissionaires. Is this just a reclassification?
We are trying so far as possible to replace service personnel by members of the corps of commissionaires.

I believe it is the intention of the air force to move the wing in North Luffenham to the continent, if that has not already been done. Is it the intention to retain North Luffenham as a Canadian air force station, or will that be returned to the R.A.F.?

It will be returned. We do not propose to make the move until the station at Marville in France is built and ready for habitation. Then the move will be made. It was first planned that this move would have taken place in December, but that would not have been a very good time to make a move. As it happens the station is not likely to be ready. Married quarters will not be quite ready and the move will not be made until March or April.

Then a further question. I notice that in the reserve air force there are a group of civilian employees for whom there was no item last year. What is the explanation of that? Is it considered now that it is beneficial to employ civilians in reserve squadrons? I am referring to what appears at page 318.

Supply-National Defence
These have been carried here as part of the active force increment with the reserve squadron.

Would the minister be kind enough to make a very brief statement as to what progress is being made in two regards, first as to the equipping of squadrons stationed in Canada with CF-lOO's and the other as to the equipping of squadrons overseas with Orenda-powered Sabres.

With regard first to the equipping of squadrons with CF-lOO's, I may say that is continuing. As I said before, I expect all the regular squadrons to be equipped with CF-lOO's will be organized and in existence, and at least partly equipped with CF-lOO's, by the end of this year.
The delivery of Orendas for the F-86 is going on apace. Aircraft are being flown across. They are being put on stations. We will be making aircraft available with the J-47 engine when they are released and available for mutual aid.
I think hon. members would be interested in a fact that I believe I can give safely now. I refer to the figures of aircraft we have disposed of to other countries. We transferred to Great Britain 370 Sabres with, of course, American engines and other government-found property representing about 30 per cent of the cost. We sold to the United States 60 Sabres for use in Korea, and 60 for transfer by them to Great Britain. We have now allocated to Greece and Turkey 82 each. If my mental arithmetic is right that represents a total of 594 Sabres that we have made available to other countries, in addition to those necessary to equip ourselves.
We have already produced, of this leading aircraft of this type, over 1,100. And when you speak about the Russians having 20,000 front-line aircraft, of which 50 per cent are jets, it must be kept in mind that we have produced 1,100 of this type alone.

There is one matter, Mr. Chairman, I wish to mention. It has been the subject of correspondence between the two ministers and myself and relates to the construction by the Department of National Defence at the R.C.A.F. station on Avenue road in Toronto of a large three-storey building, which looks like a factory.
This property was sold by the city of Toronto to the crown in 1940 at the urgent request of the government. It is the old Eglinton Hunt Club property. The city conveyed the property at the request of the Department of National Defence to the crown in 1940, in view of a very urgent plea from the department to make the property available for use in connection with the activities of the Department of National Defence. It


has been developed as an R.C.A.F. station; not, of course, an operational station, but known as No. 1 A.T.S.
Last year, without any intimation to the property owners in the neighbourhood, the Department of National Defence erected on what had been the parade ground on Avenue road this building to which I have referred. It is not yet completed. It is a high, three-storey, red brick building, which has all the appearance of a factory. This building is erected in a residential area. All the property in the area is zoned, and the zoning restrictions are quite severe, in the general interest.
But when the Department of National Defence apparently decided that it needed more accommodation it gave no thought whatever to the effect the erection of this ungainly building was going to have upon property in the neighbourhood.
I may say to the committee, Mr. Chairman, that the effect of the erection of that building on that site in a residential area has been to depreciate the value of other residential property in the immediate neighbourhood quite substantially. You can just picture, Mr. Chairman, how you would feel if, living in a residential area, there was built right across from you a tall three-storey building, that has the appearance of a factory. That is how these people whose property has been damaged by the erection of that building feel over what has been done there.
The department can quibble and say: we are not bound by residential restrictions. They can go further and say that when they obtained the property at a very low price, indeed much below the actual value of the property in 1940, from the city of Toronto, it was made possible for them just to go ahead and use the existing buildings for the purpose of an R.C.A.F. station. That is a very different matter, Mr. Chairman, from coming along now and erecting an entirely new building on these premises, one, as I have indicated, which has lowered the value of properties in the neighbourhood very severely.
I brought this matter to the attention of the Minister of National Defence last year when the construction was commenced, and the minister's letter indicated that he would look into it. Then some time later I received a letter from the Associate Minister of National Defence saying in effect that these restrictions did not apply to this property. That is not the spirit of the agreement by which the property was conveyed to the crown in 1940. It happened that at that time I was chairman of the property committee of the city when the crown's representatives came before that committee and asked the city to convey that property. There was

no suggestion then about erecting new buildings on the property. There was a temporary building put up there tor the accommodation of personnel during the war. People did not object to that because it was a temporary building. There is nothing temporary about the building that has been erected now. It is a permanent three-storey brick dwelling, higher than any building in the neighbourhood and damaging all those affected.
Then the associate minister wound up his letter of December 17, 1953, by saying:
While the Royal Canadian Air Force does not wish to interfere with the activities of the community which it serves, it is felt that as reasonable people the citizens of Toronto should be prepared to accept any disadvantages there might be to having this situation in operation as such disadvantages are more than offset by the advantages accruing to the municipality through R.C.A.F. activities.
Mr. Chairman, that is no answer to the complaint of persons whose properties are damaged. The city of Toronto will be second to no municipality or community in this country in the support and loyal assistance that it gives to any activities of the armed forces in this country. It will be second to none in doing its part but, Mr. Chairman, it is a very different matter that citizens of a whole municipality, in this case a million people or more, are prepared to do their part from saying that people in the neighbourhood must submit above all others in the city to the damaging of their properties, and the subtraction of substantial amounts of money from their investments. Some of those people in the neighbourhood affected have invested their life savings in their homes.
I wish to raise again the complaint that I made last year which produced no effect as far as the department is concerned, and to say that I think the department has been very thoughtless, very unfair, in the way it has gone ahead with a project which has brought this damage upon the value of homes in the neighbourhood.

I appreciate the point made by the hon. member. We have been criticized for having too good a building in Washington and not a good enough one in Toronto. I venture to say that if you look at the unit cost of the two buildings, you will find that they are within five cents or ten cents a cubic foot of each other. However, the one in Toronto is unquestionably on too small a lot. I think that really is the point about the building. That is all the area that there was to put it on, so it was put rather flush with the street and interferes with the street line. I certainly would like to have seen it put on a larger lot.

That is not part of the point at all. The point is that this building was erected in a residential area. You do not take three-storey buildings with a factory appearance and erect them in a residential area. I have made a complaint, and I could put it very strongly. I think the department has been very thoughtless and very unfair to these people concerned in going ahead and putting up a building of that kind in the heart of a residential area of the city and in that way inevitably causing damage to the value of their properties. There is no member in this house who would feel otherwise than these people do if the Department of National Defence just went ahead in a residential area right across the road from them and put up a big three-storey brick building that just looks like a factory or warehouse.
It is an office building.

From its appearance it might be a warehouse or a factory. I may tell the minister that this thoughtless action has damaged the value of homes and has subtracted a good many thousands of dollars from the investment that these people in that neighbourhood have in their homes. I raised the objection at the time when I thought it might still have been considered before the building was fully erected. Nothing was done. The plans were carried through and the building is now virtually completed. I think it is most unfair that the crown in a situation of this kind should take advantage of its own immunity from the effect of municipal bylaws in the case of property that it owns in a residential area. This property should never have been developed in this way, and the crown should never have erected this building on the property.

There is one matter I should like to ask the minister a question about. It concerns the notification of next-of-kin when there has been an air crash, and then the subsequent putting out of the information generally. I realize the fact that the next-of-kin must be notified before the information as to who has been killed in an air crash is released, but there is quite a bit of delay before the name is released generally or the names of people who have been killed in one of those crashes. During that intervening time a great deal of mental anguish is caused to parents, wives and so forth, of men who are serving in the same area. For example, a flash comes over the radio that there has been an aeroplane crash in New Brunswick at a certain station, and everybody who has a son or a husband serving there immediately wonders whether it

Supply-National Defence is his son, her husband and so forth. Until the general news is put out as to the name of that person these people of course go through great agonies of mind. As I say,
I appreciate the next-of-kin must be notified first, but I wonder whether it would not be possible to expedite this matter and get the genera] information out so that everybody knows it, and all the relatives know what their situation is more rapidly than has been the case heretofore. It would be a great help to morale and so forth if that could be done.

That is appreciated, Mr. Chairman. As soon as an accident does occur every effort is made through every suitable means to notify the next-of-kin. The best possible means are chosen. If there is an air force padre in the neighbourhood he is at once put on the job by long distance telephone and signal. If not, some other minister, clergyman or priest who has had service connections or an officer commanding, or other suitable person, but we do try to give the first communication to the next-of-kin by word of mouth in person. I find, through a great deal of experience in this, that it is very desirable. Only last week we had a case where it was not possible to do that, where the next-of-kin learned through other sources in advance, and it created very unfortunate and unnecessary shock. As the hon. member said, the next-of-kin must be notified first. We try to do that with the utmost speed, but we have in mind the considerations the hon. member has brought to our attention.
Perhaps the minister did not get my point. I was concerned with the relatives of the people who have not been killed.
Yes, who might have been flying.
Who are extremely worried that it is their relative who is concerned in this crash. My whole point was to try to get out the general information more rapidly than is being done.
I appreciate that.

speechtext:
We shall now turn to Royal Canadian Air Force (reserve).
Royal Canadian Air Force (reserve).

Mr. Chairman, the problem of the reserve in relation to the army has been mentioned earlier this evening and many of these factors relate themselves to the air force because, as has been pointed out, the reserve is the backbone of our defence
fMr. Harkness.]
program. One of the encouraging developments in our air force defence has been the establishment of at least an operational wing of CF-100 fighters. When I say an operational wing that is merely a guess because there is no specific information in the white paper as to the exact number of squadrons which are available for operational work today. But on page 7 of the white paper in the last sentence of paragraph 14 we have reference to the fact that auxiliary squadrons will in due course be converted to CF-100 fighters. I am wondering just what time element is involved in the phrase "in due course".
There have been one or two incidents in Canada during the past two years which have suggested there is a great deal of dissatisfaction among the members of the reserve serving in auxiliary squadrons concerning the type of operational equipment available to them. Their complement consists of Mustangs and Vampires both of which are obsolete and were obsolescent during world war II. It is therefore imperative, if the reserve squadrons are the backbone of our Canadian air defence, that this re-equipping process be brought forward as quickly as possibly. I trust it will be possible for the Minister of National Defence to give us some further details in this regard. I am sure it would mean much to the morale of those who are trying to do a job with equipment that is obviously far from being adequate.
On page 318 of the estimates relative to expenses for the reserve forces I note, and I believe I am right in these figures, that the expenditure last year was $5,750,400, and this year the estimated expenditure is $3,537,000, a decrease of some $2 million covering the activities of the reserve squadrons. I am wondering what this decrease represents. Does it mean that the reserve squadrons are not operating at full strength? I note also that pay and allowances are down and I would like to know how that saving indicated in the blue book is made up by the department.
I notice also that the item for expenditure on the air cadet corps is down slightly from $447,200 to $412,000. The air cadet movement is one of the best sources for potential recruits to the regular Canadian air force. Finally, on this matter of the reserve forces, there is a reference made under this section to a certain contribution made to various military groups and I wonder if the air force association is included in these grants. I have scanned the estimates and I have not been able to locate any reference to grants in aid of activities of this kind. I trust they are being given some support because the air force association, which is made up of

thousands of R.C.A.F. veterans of world war II, is a reservoir for auxiliary service personnel. It is out of the air force association that the participants in the mobilization assignment training program are largely recruited, and these air force associations right across the country are taking advantage of every available opportunity to promote the welfare of members of the R.C.A.F.
In my final word on reserve matters I would like to refer to a communication I received from the minister after our discussion on last year's estimates. Because we adjourned earlier last year than this year it was not possible for the minister to reply verbally to a question I had asked concerning the disposition of reserve units across the country. The minister in his reply dated May 15, 1953 indicated that it is contemplated that several reserve radar units would be established. During the past two years I have urged that an opportunity be given to our air force association wing in the city of Brandon to make a more positive contribution to the defence of Canada. We have one of the best wings in the country but up to the present time its contribution has been restricted largely to maintaining interest locally in air force matters because there has been no possibility of establishing a more or less active reserve unit in the city of Brandon. It occurs to me that one of these radar units, particularly a light warning set, would perhaps meet the need of an air force association such as we have in the city of Brandon. It would not involve too many personnel and would also provide basic training in a most important aspect of air force defence, that is in connection with our radar units. In his general statement the minister made reference to the fact that in the next decade we will be approaching the push button stage of aerial warfare and that, of course, means that radar will be the chief means whereby this will be accomplished. I would appreciate the minister making some comment on the questions I have raised. I would appreciate it if the minister would make some comment on those questions I have asked.

Mr. Chairman, I will answer the hon. member very rapidly. With regard to R.C.A.F. associations grant, if he will look at page 322 of the estimates, he will see provision for grants of $15,000. The reason for the reduction that there is in the air cadet appropriation is that this is more realistically related to what is intended for this year.
With regard to auxiliary squadrons, we expect to begin the equipment of existing
Supply-National Defence squadrons with CF-lOO's in 1955. But preliminary to that we plan this summer to start trying this out with a single squadron on an experimental basis. The problems involved in this operation are extremely complicated. In order to have the squadrons work with CF-lOO's, it will probably be necessary to have about half the strength regular force.
With regard to Mustangs, Mitchells and Vampires, may I say that Mustangs are very good aircraft for catching the kind of bombers that might come over at this particular period. Mitchells are going to continue to be used for the operation of cleaning up any landings that might take place. They are very good aircraft for the purpose. With regard to Brandon having an air station or reserve flight or something of the kind, I think the air force's answer to that would be that it has been found generally desirable to locate these air control and warning units, large or small, at places where active flying is carried on so that they can train on active flying by the R.C.A.F. and where there is not too far away a radar station which they would be mobilized to assist. Those two conditions do not exist at Brandon yet. However, we have to take it into consideration.
Contributions towards the military costs of NATO.

Mr. Chairman, I do not rise to speak on this item of NATO but to say that I think we have had a fairly full day. Here is NATO with an appropriation of $12 million. I think it is about time we called it a day and called it ten o'clock.

Mutual aid.

Before this item is concluded I should like to ask about a project

Supply-National Defence which the department seemed to have under way a short time ago, that of making the Long Branch rifle ranges available, by finding other property, so that they might be used for a housing project or other uses of that kind. Can the minister say how that matter stands?

Yes. About five years ago I was brought into the picture with regard to Long Branch. We decided then, as a matter of policy, to co-operate with the provincial government, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the local community in working out a complete plan under which we would give up Long Branch in exchange for an equally good and convenient bit of land on which to have a range. Owing to one reason or another that kind of arrangement was not carried out. I have since announced repeatedly that we are willing to go through with it so that the department of defence would have equivalent ground for the job somewhere else. We even went so far at one stage as to take expropriation proceedings to secure ground north of Toronto. I thought this was being done without objection from the local community. There were very few farmers concerned. However, in the end they objected strenuously and we dropped the matter. Now we are exploring the possibility of seeing whether, with the improved transportation facilities in Toronto and area, it may not be possible to use Borden. That suggestion is being explored.
Items agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall I rise, report progress and request leave to sit again?
Agreed.

If you have not left the chair, Mr. Chairman, may I express to hon. members appreciation for their co-operation.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On Saturday evening I set out the agenda for this week. Subject to any unexpected changes we shall follow the order of departments as I set them out. That would mean that tomorrow we would begin with defence production, then take national health and welfare and follow with those that were indicated for tomorrow in the statement I made on Saturday evening.

Might I ask the house leader this question? Since we were co-operative in allowing this big item with regard to NATO to pass and in view of the fact that there are many items here that could conceivably come
under defence production, I am just wondering if he would like to co-operate with us a little bit and might suggest that we might be able to discuss this item on defence production.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not sure that I understand what my hon. friend is referring to. But certainly, at any rate, he has banked a little bit of good will on my part tonight.
